articles.title: The Marker Drift Problem: Measuring LLM-Assisted Writing with Unstable Lexical Indicators
articles.authors: Serhii Nazarovets
articles.abstract: Lexical markers are increasingly used to estimate the prevalence of large language model (LLM)-assisted writing across large publication corpora. However, longitudinal applications of this approach rely on an important assumption: that the relationship between these markers and LLM use remains sufficiently stable over time. Recent research suggests that once publicly identified, individual markers may lose their diagnostic value due to adaptation by users and the evolution of language models. Furthermore, lexical markers may reflect not only LLM use, but also linguistic competence, AI-assisted editing, and broader forms of stylistic convergence. This paper introduces the Marker Drift Problem to describe a methodological challenge in which indicators change alongside the phenomenon they are intended to measure. Marker drift raises questions about temporal comparability, as observed changes in marker prevalence may reflect changes in LLM use, changes in the indicators themselves, or both. Without attention to the temporal stability and construct validity of lexical indicators, increasingly precise estimates of LLM-assisted writing may be based on unstable measurement instruments.

articles.title: Open Here, There and Everywhere? A Comparative Review of Open Access Definitions and Typologies in Monitoring Instruments
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Didier Torny
articles.abstract: Open Access (OA) monitoring has become a policy instrument for governments, institutions, and research funders globally, yet the typologies and definitions underlying OA monitors have never been systematically compared. Drawing on a global dataset of 30 OA monitors, we conduct the first systematic comparative review of their operational OA definitions and typologies. Our findings reveal dynamics of standardization, as well as enduring differences. Unpaywall/OpenAlex occupies a near-hegemonic position as metadata provider (77% of monitors), shaping classification choices across the landscape. Nevertheless, significant heterogeneity persists: monitors diverge on whether Bronze publications constitute true OA, on how to count Green OA publications, on the relevance of open licenses, and on whether economic dimensions (APCs, Diamond OA) belong in typologies at all. Only two monitors share both a common typology and identical operational criteria. These divergences pose challenges for cross-national comparability and call for greater methodological transparency in open science monitoring infrastructures.

articles.title: Crossref as a source of open bibliographic metadata
articles.authors: Nees Jan van Eck; Ludo Waltman
articles.abstract: There is a growing recognition of the importance of open availability of bibliographic metadata of scholarly publications. We present an up-to-date overview of the open availability of bibliographic metadata through the infrastructure of Crossref, focusing on six metadata elements: reference lists, abstracts, ORCIDs, author affiliations, funding information, and license information. Our analysis shows that the availability of these metadata elements has improved over time, at least for journal articles. However, the analysis also shows that many publishers need to make additional efforts to realize full openness of bibliographic metadata.

articles.title: Credit, recognition, and reward for non-traditional research artefacts in the Life Sciences
articles.authors: Gavin Farrell; Eva Alloza; Adel Bouhraoua; Salvador Capella-Gutierrez; Carole Goble; Henning Hermjakob; Maria Makaronidou; Andrew Smith; Shoaib Sufi; Thanasis Vergoulis
articles.abstract: Publication metrics remain the primary academic performance assessment in modern academia. This focus has fostered the publish or perish culture, negatively impacting research output quantity and quality. Consequently, a gap exists in the recognition and reward of impactful non-traditional research artefacts, such as curated datasets, research software, and training materials. To address this, we share perspectives to expand the assessment consideration for researchers producing these outputs. We also highlight the dedicated roles and need for wider consideration of career paths of digital research technical professionals, including academic data curators, research software engineers and domain expert trainers. Through a mapping of valuable non-traditional artefacts illustrated by Life Science examples of ELIXIR Europe, we aim to foster a productive and sustainable Open Science ecosystem where these outputs are made visible and considered. We examine the technical solutions for credit and sociological barriers to recognition and reward, while also considering the impacts of generative AI. Furthermore, we discuss policy and funder mandate reforms to ensure those responsible for non-traditional research artefacts are properly recognised and rewarded, to accelerate global scientific discovery.

articles_hidden.title: Automatic Prompt Optimization for Policy Documents Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Hanif Sajid
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, I leverage three automatic prompt optimization (APO) algorithms to search for optimal prompts that enable large language models to classify policy documents accurately, without requiring task-specific training data. I evaluate the performance of these optimized prompts using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini model, comparing them against prompts created by domain experts as a baseline. Experimental results show that all three algorithms significantly outperform the baseline. Among the algorithms, APE, which induces simple prompts from input-output example pairs, significantly outperforms GRIPS and performs comparably to ProTeGi. Additionally, ProTeGi demonstrates similar performance to GRIPS. However, neither the optimized prompts nor the human-designed ones achieve a research-grade performance (defined as an F1-score of 70%) with the GPT-4o-mini model. To reach research-grade performance in policy document classification using APO methods, future work could explore the use of more powerful models, hybrid APO systems, cross-model evaluations, and inference-time enhancements.

articles_hidden.title: Guidance for defining outcomes in clinical trials
articles_hidden.authors: Xiangji Ying; Tianjing Li; Joanne McKenzie; Matthew James Page; Kiran Ninan; Jean-Pierre Oberste; Colby J. Vorland; Andrew William Brown; Riaz Qureshi; Nicholas J DeVito
articles_hidden.abstract:
Defining outcomes completely before conducting clinical trials helps to mitigate reporting biases; however, there is limited guidance to help investigators define outcomes completely. We aimed to develop a structured approach for defining trial outcomes completely and consistently.
We reviewed literature, developed preliminary rules for defining outcomes, and refined them iteratively. We randomly selected randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on ClinicalTrials.gov that registered before their start dates and posted results by January 4, 2024. The 225 included RCTs evaluated 3,424 outcomes. Two raters independently applied preliminary rules to define each outcome. When raters encountered outcomes they could not define, we refined the rules. We continued this process until no further changes were needed. We discussed and finalized our approach in a consensus meeting.
We define an “outcome” as a value for each participant that will be used in analysis to generate study results. A complete outcome definition includes six elements: outcome domain, specific measurement, specific metric, cutoff, variable type, and timepoint. We developed rules for naming specific measurements for both subjective and objective outcomes. We expanded on prior work by developing more comprehensive categories for specific metrics. We introduced "cutoff" as a distinct element with three subelements. To clarify the boundary between outcome definitions and statistical methods, we replaced a previously described element, "method of aggregation," with "variable type," which refers to whether the value for each individual is continuous or categorical.
Trialists and sponsors could use this approach alongside other guidelines to define outcomes in trial registrations, protocols, and result reports.

articles.title: Online Discourse is Falsely Polarized by Self-Selection
articles.authors: Will Schulz; Claire Elizabeth Robertson; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ashwini Ashokkumar; Lisa Oswald; JungHwan Yang; Simon Munzert; Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Andrew Markus Guess
articles.abstract: We present comprehensive evidence quantifying the magnitude and scope of false polarization (i.e. the impression that opinions on political issues are more polarized than they actually are) on social media, driven by users' selective posting behavior. Using more than a decade of social media behavior connected to individual ideological attitudes in 1.7 million posts, a series of controlled experiments, and a large global survey covering 40 countries (total N = 49,222), we find that (1) strong ideologues post their opinions significantly more often than moderate individuals, and (2) extreme attitudes are posted more often than moderate attitudes. This general pattern replicates robustly across 40 countries, spanning diverse political cultures. Indeed, across studies we find extreme opinions are overrepresented on social media by at least 6% and up to 22% compared to their true prevalence in our samples. Furthermore, the opinions that users post are more hostile and toxic than the beliefs they keep to themselves.  These results were not explained by political interest or consistent left-right differences, suggesting that political extremity has an independent effect on social media behavior. Thus, most of the observed polarization of online discourse in recent years may be attributable to the systematic over-representation of pre-existing extreme political views, rather than the causal effects of platforms.

articles.title: Social Isolation and Ambition: A Two-Wave Correlational Study of School Ostracism and Goal Abandonment in High-Achieving Adolescents
articles.authors: Aleksandr Anikeev
articles.abstract: Independent student research project examining the relationship between chronic school peer ostracism and thoughts of abandoning ambitious personal goals in high-achieving adolescents. Across two independent samples (Wave 1, N = 82, CIS-based Co-founder ecosystem; Wave 2, N = 35, international communities), we find a robust positive correlation between school ostracism and goal-abandonment ideation (pooled N = 117; r ≈ 0.61). A formal Baron-Kenny mediation analysis supports full mediation through school burnout. This OSF project contains the manuscript, anonymized Wave 2 data, and a reproducibility analysis script.

articles.title: Perceptions and Outcomes of Artificial Intelligence Among Back-office Employees: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.authors: Maria Igorevna Efremova; Oliver Runswick; Myanna Duncan
articles.abstract:
Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace is rapidly evolving. Employees’ perceptions of AI are of increasing interest, particularly in relation to their psychological wellbeing and performance outcomes. This systematic review extends existing research by synthesising recent empirical evidence on the impact of AI among back-office employees across a range of industries and functions, an occupational group that is particularly exposed to AI-driven technologies. Following PRISMA guidelines, eight databases were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published in English between January 2022 and January 2026. A total of 40 eligible studies were included in the review. Findings indicated that employee perceptions of AI were largely positive, although experiences across industries and occupations varied. AI adoption and performance outcomes were commonly related to perceived usefulness, ease of use, and the extent to which the organisation was ready to adopt AI. These outcomes were also associated with fears of job displacement and de-skilling, but these relationships were unexamined quantitatively. AI’s workplace value appears contingent on employee perceptions and organisational context, rather than just on the technology. 

Key words: AI at work, AI adoption, back-office employees, technology acceptance

articles.title: Reframing Acculturation:  When (and Why) Acculturation Science Warrants a Systems Explanation
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Karen Phalet
articles.abstract: Acculturation has always been understood as a process of change, and contemporary research examines that change from several complementary perspectives, including developmental trajectories, reciprocal intergroup relations, ecological contexts, situated cultural processes, and multilevel social change. The field therefore contains many elements of a systems account without a shared architecture for relating them. This article offers a selective integrative review and metatheoretical synthesis using complex dynamic systems theory (CDST). CDST provides a coordinating framework that complements existing acculturation theories and encounter-level models of adaptation. It distinguishes five explanatory questions distributed across different traditions: what form change takes, who or what influences whom, how change moves across levels of organisation, where broader conditions become relevant, and how processes unfolding at different rates become linked. We organise these questions through five dimensions: nonlinear dynamism, relational reciprocity, multilevel emergence, situated adaptation, and multiscale temporality. Together, they provide a way to examine how patterns of acculturative change depend on prior experience, relationships, local conditions, levels of organisation, and processes unfolding at different rates. For each type of systems claim, we specify a linear-additive alternative and the evidence needed to distinguish between them. Power differences and prior history are treated as conditions that can shape how the system operates and changes. The framework therefore shifts attention from average associations between acculturation variables and outcomes toward explaining how acculturative change is organised, when different processes become connected, and when a systems explanation adds value beyond conventional models.

articles.title: Acculturation as a Situated Transactional Process
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract: Acculturation research commonly links broad preferences for heritage-culture maintenance and participation in the receiving society to psychological and sociocultural adjustment. Yet meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence shows that these associations are often weak, heterogeneous, and limited over time, suggesting that broad preferences alone cannot explain why cultural engagement leads to different outcomes across situations. This conceptual article develops a situated transactional framework within a broader complex dynamic systems account. Building on established work showing that acculturation is contextual, domain-specific, and interactional, the framework specifies how these influences come together within concrete encounters. It proposes a process in which locally relevant conditions shape appraisal, the mobilization of culturally patterned resources, response, relational and institutional reception, multidimensional outcomes, and feedback into later encounters. The article also distinguishes the adaptation process, understood as the continuing person-environment transaction, from adaptation outcomes, including psychological, sociocultural, relational, and externally observed consequences. By organizing these elements into an explicit recursive architecture, the framework generates testable predictions about context-specific responses, reception, multidimensional outcomes, learned response patterns, and structural change. It thereby provides a concrete empirical agenda for testing whether these mechanisms improve explanation and prediction beyond broad-orientation and contextual-moderation accounts.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Gaze on IPCC climate maps carries behaviour-specific signals for intended low-carbon action
articles.authors: Étienne Serbe-Kamp; Ayshan Aliyeva; Candelaria Belen Krick; Candela I. Jantus; Yaning Han; Joaquin Navajas; Bahador Bahrami; Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Climate maps are among the most widely shared products of climate science, yet their effect on the people who look at them is measured almost entirely with questionnaires. We recorded gaze with mobile eye-trackers while people freely viewed climate-projection maps from the IPCC Interactive Atlas, and asked whether how someone looks carries information questionnaires miss. It does, for only one of the three outcomes we tested. Gaze improved prediction of intended low-carbon behaviour in viewers the models had never seen, beyond a broad battery of climate measures and in every model tried. The same features said nothing about how anxious those viewers were, or which audience segment they placed themselves in. Attention to climate information is therefore not a general marker of engagement. It tracks readiness to act. Because a visualisation can be designed around where people look, this opens a route to evaluating climate communication while people are looking.

articles.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic lives. This raises the question of which individuals are more likely to rely on GenAI in their schoolwork, with reliance defined as a dispositional tendency to turn to GenAI in preference to one’s own effort or teacher support, as well as difficulty initiating schoolwork without it. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model of the associations between executive functioning (EF) difficulties and reliance on GenAI through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage= 17.4 years, 55.2% girls), with analytic samples of 735 and 839 GenAI users, respectively. Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.33, ps < .001). Consistent with the hypothesized model, a sequential indirect association through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Specific indirect associations through perceived usefulness were consistently observed in both groups, whereas those through habitual use alone received more limited support despite the strong association between habitual use and reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF difficulties as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be particularly relevant to understanding the indirect association between EF difficulties and reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the relevance of self-regulatory capacities for understanding individual differences in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: ‘Why me?’ - The influence of perceived fairness of climate policies on adoption intentions of high impact climate actions across cultural contexts
articles.authors: Mario Herberz; Tobias Brosch; Claudia R. Schneider
articles.abstract: The unresolved question of how efforts to reduce carbon emissions should be fairly distributed across society constitutes a major hurdle to widespread cooperation on climate change mitigation. While perceived fairness has been established as a key characteristic of broadly supported climate policies, its affective underpinnings and its relevance for individual-level adoption of climate actions, as well as the added value of addressing fairness concerns in climate policies remain understudied. Here, we investigate the association between the perceived fairness of governments promoting the adoption of high impact climate actions and adoption intentions, the affective processes involved in fairness judgments, and the extent to which two climate policies addressing perceptions of unfairness succeed in increasing intentions to adopt climate actions. Across three pre-registered studies conducted in Switzerland, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom (Ntotal = 1063) we demonstrate that perceived fairness positively predicts adoption intentions, and this more strongly so than the perceived impact of climate actions. We found anger, psychological reactance, and lack of enthusiasm to be affective correlates of lower perceived fairness. Reducing the cost of adopting high impact climate actions and mandating societies’ highest emitters to reduce their carbon emissions to increase self-interested and distributional fairness, respectively, successfully increased adoption intentions. Evidence on potential moderators of these effects remained largely inconclusive. While practical challenges in the study of the behavioural effects of climate policy design remain, systematically accounting for inequalities and perceived unfairness seems to be key to the widespread adoption of high impact climate actions.

articles.title: Assessing complex belief structures with the triads task: Reliability and validity
articles.authors: René Dutschke; Gundula Thiele; Martin Schoemann; Caroline Surrey; Stefan Scherbaum
articles.abstract:
Research on attitudes and beliefs often relies on assessing people’s agreement with several explicit
statements. We promote a different approach, focusing on the interconnectedness of beliefs and
their cognitive and affective components. Here, we present the triads task as a procedure to
measure complex belief networks. Leaning on similarity and difference judgments for three
concepts at a time, the triads task allows us to derive similarity scores for each pair of concepts in
a topic domain, which provide insights into belief networks of individuals and groups.
Furthermore, we propose a procedure to translate similarity scores into belief network
visualizations, inspired by cognitive-affective maps (CAMs). For a sample of 56 participants, we
show that similarity scores are retest reliable in a two week interval (averaged individual retest
correlation: r = .78) and that participants communicatively validate our visualization procedure.
We highlight the benefits of the triads task in measuring belief networks and further discuss this
procedure with regards to its potential as a research and intervention tool.

articles.title: Emotional Crying as a Dynamic Multilevel Regulatory Process: A Scoping Review and Integrative Framework
articles.authors: Francesco Giaquinto
articles.abstract: Despite decades of research, emotional crying remains an insufficiently integrated phenomenon, with its biological, cognitive, and interpersonal functions often investigated independently. This scoping review maps the existing literature on emotional crying and proposes a multilevel conceptual model of crying as a context-dependent regulatory process. Fifty-seven studies were included (44 primary studies and 13 theoretical or review papers). Evidence was organized according to both crier and observer perspectives, revealing a multilevel architecture linking antecedent appraisals, physiological regulation, neural mechanisms, cognitive representations, and interpersonal communication. Across studies, crying was associated with experiences of helplessness, emotional overload, and meaning-making, while also functioning as a social signal capable of influencing support-related responses and interpersonal dynamics. Observer-focused research further indicated that the effects of visible tears depend strongly on contextual, relational, and interpretative factors. Overall, these findings suggest that crying is better understood as an emergent multilevel regulatory process rather than as a simple emotional discharge. The proposed framework highlights dynamic interactions among biological, cognitive, and social systems that shape internal regulation and organism–environment exchanges. Within this perspective, emotional crying can be interpreted through the Thermodynamics of Mind framework as a process involving hierarchical transitions between mental states. Ultimately, this model integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal accounts of crying while providing a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical investigation.

articles.title: How Many Factors Underlie the WAIS-5? Evidence From the Australian and New Zealand Standardization Sample.
articles.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles.abstract:
The latent structure of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fifth Edition (WAIS-5) is the subject of recent psychometric debate. Although the publisher's initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a theoretically derived five-factor model, a recent independent evaluation of the US standardisation sample found that complementary exploratory and confirmatory analyses favoured a hierarchical four-factor representation. The present study examined whether these findings could be independently replicated using the published WAIS-5 Australasian standardisation sample (N = 677).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation, followed by Schmid-Leiman transformation and model-based reliability and dimensionality analyses. Confirmatory analyses compared competing oblique, higher-order, and bifactor models evaluated in the US sample.
Factor-retention procedures did not support the proposed five-factor structure. Exploratory analyses consistently recovered four interpretable factors corresponding to Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, with Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning failing to emerge as distinct latent constructs. Confirmatory analyses identified the same higher-order (4h3) and bifactor (4b3) models as the preferred representations of the data. Model-based reliability analyses indicated a dominant general factor with smaller contributions from the broad cognitive abilities. Despite modest differences in model parameters, the central conclusions closely replicated those of the US sample.

articles.title: AI’s Frontline
articles.authors: Alex Taylor; Jina Suh; Marlyn Thomas Savio; Sinead O'Dwyer; John Caesar De Villa
articles.abstract:
1.	AI’s safety and reliability depend on a globally distributed workforce
2.	Data workers feel an ambivalence towards their work: operating in a space of tension between monotonous and potentially emotionally taxing work, and feelings of individual and collective agency in contributing to new tech. 
3.	The space of tension opens up a space for thinking productively about the importance of data work and the active role data workers can play in shaping AI development.

articles.title: The cascade from basic visual processing to social dysfunction: An extended path model in a transdiagnostic sample of youth.
articles.authors: Kelly Mathis; Scott D. Blain; Laura Rose Locarno; Carly A Lasagna; Colombi Costanza; Katharine N. Thakkar; Cynthia Z. Burton; Ivy Fei Tso
articles.abstract:
Background
Social dysfunction is widespread across psychiatric disorders, but treatments remain limited. Identifying underlying mechanisms could inform novel treatment approaches that meaningfully improve clinical outcomes. We previously showed that basic visual processing deficits cascade through gaze perception and emotion recognition to impair theory of mind. Here, we test an extended model assessing whether this cascade ultimately predicts real-world social dysfunction via theory of mind in an expanded sample.

Methods
A combined sample of 202 psychiatric patients with varying levels of social dysfunction and healthy individuals completed basic visual processing tasks, a multi-level social cognition battery that included measures of gaze perception, emotion recognition, and theory of mind, and clinical assessments of social functioning. A five-level path model evaluated the sequential cascade from visual processing to gaze perception, emotion recognition, theory of mind, and social functioning.

Results
The extended five-level path model demonstrated good fit to the data. Poorer basic visual processing sequentially predicted deficits across intermediate social cognitive domains, culminating in theory of mind, which directly predicted worse social functioning.

Conclusion
These findings indicate that basic visual deficits cascade through social cognitive steps to impair everyday social functioning. As a candidate shared mechanism contributing to social dysfunction, basic visual processing represents a promising target for psychiatric interventions.

articles.title: Collaboration, Creation, & Imagination: Exploring the Effects of Co-Imagination on Divergent Thinking
articles.authors: Zoe Fowler; Clin KY Lai; Roger Beaty; Brendan Bo O'Connor
articles.abstract: Creativity is essential in adaptively navigating the challenges of the future. While creativity research reveals the complex ways social context can influence creative outcomes, research on how we imagine the future has only just begun to explore imagination as a collaborative process (i.e., collaborative imagination, or co-imagination). How does collaborative imagination influence creative cognition? Across two studies (N = 162), we assess how imagining the future collaboratively rather than individually influences engagement in divergent thinking during imagination. This work quantified divergent thinking by measuring the semantic distance between all words spoken by a given participant in the narrative (i.e., Divergent Semantic Integration, or DSI). Study 1, run with university students in-lab, found no significant effects of collaborative imagine vs. individual imagine tasks on DSI scores. Exploratory analyses including social connection found that participants in the co-imagine condition had significantly higher DSI scores, though this model also revealed social connection related negatively to DSI scores. Study 2, run over video call with Prolific participants, did not replicate these findings. Together, these studies consider underexplored questions at the intersection of collaboration, imagination, and creativity, and provide tools for future research to investigate creative cognition in co-imagination.

articles.title: Chatbot and Problematic Integration: Two Tests among U.S. Users
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are token-based, probabilistic engines that produce most likely answers based on trained models and user input. In this work, I draw upon the problematic integration (PI) theory to conceptualize human-AI interaction (HAII) as communication processes that are aimed to address users’ problematic probabilistic orientations (PP). I propose that (1) PP prompt people to seek answers from AI chatbots and (2) that the extent to which chatbot responses address PP shapes interaction outcomes. Two studies tested these propositions using national age-matching samples of AI chatbot users in the United States (age range=18-85 years; mean age=41 years). Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey and Study 2 was an interactive experiment where participants talked to chatbots about one of twenty validated and pretested life concerns and rated chatbot-generated responses addressing their concern. Findings lend partial support to my propositions and offer insights into how AI chatbots may shape communication and human cognition.

articles.title: Now You See Me: Associations between Student Outcomes and Instructor Visibility in Online Learning Contexts
articles.authors: Lindsay Ackerman; William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Online classroom environments may be associated with compromised student engagement and learning outcomes and behaviors, partially arising from a lack of instructor visibility. We tested the effect of watching instructor-led videos on learning outcomes in online environments. Study 1 (N = 600) was a randomized experiment testing whether participants who watched videos of an instructor delivering information reported higher engagement and understanding compared to participants who read equivalent text. In a small, applied Study 2 (N = 30, in an online course), we investigated classroom associations between watching instructor-led videos and subjective (e.g., self-reported engagement) and objective (e.g., time spent on course page) student learning outcomes and behaviors. In the classroom study, watching the instructor-led videos was associated with course engagement, connection to the instructor, and objective learning behaviors. However, in the experimental study, those who read the text performed better than those who watched the videos, though applications to classroom contexts may be limited. This work provides insight into the utility of visual and audio instructor representation in facilitating positive learning outcomes for students in online classrooms and invites educators to consider how best to engage students in online courses.

articles.title: From Friend to Foe: Stereotypes of Dogs are Ambivalent
articles.authors: Lindsay Palmer; Remy Frost; Sophia Ruppel; Anamarie C Johnson; Andrew Johnson; Clive DL Wynne
articles.abstract: Research on animal stereotypes often lacks nuance, focusing on animals broadly rather than specific subgroups or contexts. In Study 1, 172 participants listed stereotypes about Dogs, Aggressive Dogs, and Friendly Dogs in open-ended responses. We identified 17 themes for Dogs (e.g., “good companions”), 15 for Aggressive Dogs (e.g., “dangerous to children”), and 20 for Friendly Dogs (e.g., “affiliative”). In Study 2, we examined stereotype endorsement, policy support, and how related belief systems influenced endorsement. Using items created from Study 1 responses, 305 participants rated their personal endorsement of stereotypes (Dogs, Friendly Dogs, or Aggressive Dogs). We found that greater belief in stereotypes about Dogs and Aggressive Dogs decreased support for policies to improve welfare, and only stereotypes about Aggressive Dogs predicted increased support for restrictive policies. We found that beliefs in essentialism and dominance theory consistently predicted greater stereotype endorsement.

articles.title: An Open-Source Standardized Pipeline for Equitable Observations of Interactive Behavioral Dynamics: Theory-driven Measurement, Analysis, and Masking
articles.authors: Arkadiusz Białek; Wim Pouw; James Trujillo; Fred Hasselman; Babajide Owoyele; Natalia Siekiera; Joanna Raczaszek-Leonardi; Travis J. Witshire
articles.abstract: Behavioral observation has a longstanding tradition in psychology. However, its reliance on manual coding makes observational methods costly and prone to biases that arise from the inherent limits of coding schemes and from the subjectivity of human raters. Behavioral observation research therefore has drawbacks in terms of applicability, accessibility, reproducibility, and equitability. Computer vision (CV) methods have promise in this regard. In the context of quantifying human movement, CV approaches to pose estimation are becoming increasingly precise and have the benefit of being non-intrusive, reproducible, and low-cost. With such methods, human movement in videos can be processed as multivariate time-series data, offering a basis for a more comprehensive analysis of individual, interpersonal, and social dynamics, opening up the possibility for the widespread study of diverse populations in out-of-lab real-world contexts. Fulfilling such a promise goes beyond technical progress, it requires a theory-driven implementation of new accessible observational methods made equitable to learn. To showcase this promise, we present a CV pipeline with analyses of the temporal dynamics of dyadic interactions, including a cross-cultural investigation of movement fluidity in sibling cooperation during task-focused interactions and longitudinal assessments of infant-caregiver coordination during free-play sessions. The pipeline incorporates a pedagogical computational notebook, pose estimation (YOLOv8), theory-driven linear and non-linear time series analysis, and a CV method for more privacy-aware video data archiving. Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it.

articles.title: Beyond Pre-Post Comparisons: A Comprehensive Effect Size Framework for Intensive Longitudinal Interventions via Time-Varying Modeling
articles.authors: Xiaohui Luo; Yue Liu; Hongyun Liu; Laura Francina Bringmann
articles.abstract: Intensive longitudinal interventions (ILIs), which deliver repeated interventions in people’s daily lives while intensively tracking their psychological states, offer unique opportunities for ecologically valid, real-time, and personalized support. However, there is a striking mismatch between the richness of the data these studies generate and the simplicity of the methods used to evaluate them: evaluations still rely largely on pre-post mean comparisons that collapse dozens or even hundreds of observations per person into a few summary statistics. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a comprehensive effect size framework based on Bayesian multilevel time-varying autoregressive (TV-AR) models within the generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) approach. The framework organizes effect sizes along four dimensions: subject level (population-average, individual-specific, and between-group), parameter type (mean level, autoregressive effect, and variance), temporal scale (integrated and time-specific), and study phase (active intervention and post-intervention decay). These metrics move researchers beyond whether an intervention works to when effects emerge, plateau, or fade, how the intervention reshapes the dynamics and stability of a process, and for whom it is effective. We demonstrate the framework with data from a mindfulness-based ILI targeting negative affect, in which an intervention and a control group were assessed before and during the intervention, and provide openly available annotated R code and a tutorial. Overall, the framework provides a practical and flexible toolkit for evaluating ILIs, supporting the broader shift toward a more dynamic, process-oriented, and personalized intervention science.

articles.title: Steering Generative AI Toward Developmentally Supportive Learning: The SCAFFOLD Framework and a Pilot in a School Setting
articles.authors: Olga Muss
articles.abstract: Adolescents are the fastest-growing users of Large Language Models (LLMs) and many LLM-powered toys are entering homes, transforming their environment. Yet these tools were not designed for their educational, emotional, and developmental needs. Children are particularly vulnerable because their skills are immature, knowledge limited and they are undergoing sensitive periods of development, when the foundations are being laid. Safe, developmentally and pedagogically grounded design for interactions with LLMs are therefore essential for limiting risks and harvesting benefits of this technology. This thesis presents the Steered Contextual AI Framework for Orchestrating Learning Dialogue (SCAFFOLD), which builds upon its technical framework, a layered reliability framework that surrounds LLM-generated text and speech with external verification, targeted repair, and safe fallback, to enable to steer LLM’s behavior towards its conceptual framework that operationalizes the knowledge from developmental psychology and neuroscience, science of learning, science of education and pedagogy and the science of human-computer interactions. Model-agnostic and privacy-preserving, SCAFFOLD helps educators to configure interactions with AI that support safety, learning and development, with transparency and modularity. The thesis includes a piloted minimal SCAFFOLD prototype tested in a classroom with 12–16-year-olds using an LLM-powered social robot in a multi-user co-creation task, where students collaboratively designed a mnemonic on a previously covered topic. Preliminary findings showed that, compared to a prompt-only LLM, the SCAFFOLD prototype elicited more student activity, engagement, and on-topic participation. Co-creation level was associated with post-test knowledge scores after controlling for prior knowledge. These findings provide initial evidence for SCAFFOLD's feasibility and potential to support engagement and learning in educational settings.

articles.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles.title: Attention Bias in Perfectionism:  Prolonged Dwell Time on Critical Faces Partially Mediates a Link Between Perfectionistic Concerns and Psychological Distress
articles.authors: Elisabeth Prestele; Christine Altstötter-Gleich; Stephan Koenig; Ulrike Basten
articles.abstract: Perfectionism is a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor implicated in emotional disorders, including depression and anxiety. Yet, the mechanisms through which perfectionism contributes to psychological distress are only partly understood. A candidate mechanism is attention allocation during social interactions, as attention to evaluative cues may influence subsequent perceptions and affective responses. The present study used eye tracking to examine whether perfectionistic concerns (PC) and perfectionistic strivings (PS) are associated with attention biases toward socially evaluative cues, as indicated by prolonged dwell time on facial expressions of criticism as opposed to appreciation in a free viewing task. For 148 participants (82% female, 1% diverse; age: 18 – 57 years, M = 24 years, SD = 6.4), the proportional dwell-time on critical faces was related to self-reported PC as well as state and trait measures of psychological distress (unpleasant mood and depressiveness). In latent-variable analyses, PC showed small to moderate positive unique associations with the proportional dwell time on critical faces. Path analyses further indicated that this dwell time partially mediated the associations of PC with unpleasant mood and depressiveness. These findings provide novel evidence that PC are linked to biases in attention toward social cues of criticism, suggesting a pathway through which PC may contribute to psychological distress. More broadly, the results underscore the importance of considering attentional mechanisms in models of perfectionism and emotional disorders.

articles.title: Why the body comes first: Effects of experimenter touch on infants’ word finding
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; Ruth Tincoff; Christopher Baker; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
The lexicon of 6-month-olds is comprised of names and body part words. Unlike names, body part words do not often occur in isolation in the input. This presents a puzzle: How have infants been able to pull out these words from the continuous stream of speech at such a young age? We hypothesize that caregivers’ interactions directed at and on the infant’s body may be at the root of their early acquisition of body part words. An
artificial language segmentation study shows that experimenter-provided synchronous tactile cues help 4-month-olds to find words in continuous speech. A follow-up study suggests that this facilitation cannot be reduced to the highly social situation in which the directed interaction occurs. Taken together, these studies suggests that direct caregiver-infant interaction, exemplified in this study by touch cues, may play a key role
in infants’ ability to find word boundaries and suggests that words linked with caregiver touches may comprise early vocabulary items.

articles.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Realistic, misleading AI-generated audio content is a new threat to digital-media consumers. This study examined the effects of misleading AI-generated podcasts that presented false claims about nanoparticles in sunscreen (Experiment 1; N = 463), or microwaves damaging foods (Experiment 2; N = 500). U.S. participants either received a misleading podcast, misleading article, or a neutral podcast (control). To test interventions, misleading podcasts were preceded by either a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can deceive, an active inoculation that added an educational activity, or no intervention. The podcast and article produced comparable increases in misinformed beliefs. Both inoculations significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information and attenuated the podcast’s impact on beliefs. Results demonstrate that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as text-based misinformation, and that brief AI-source-focused inoculations can mitigate, but not eliminate, its persuasive impact. Findings inform interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.

articles.title: Gambling disorder symptoms as an indirect marker of microtransaction spending in video games
articles.authors: Charles-Etienne Benoit; Szymon Pałubinski; Akito Miura; Takahide Etani; Floris Tijmen van Vugt; Piotr Kałowski; Andrzej Cudo
articles.abstract: Video games have gained a lot of popularity over the past decades, generating large global revenue, mostly through in-game monetization referred to as microtransactions. Game developers have studied the psychological mechanisms in video game monetization presumably to increase potential revenues, which could for some gamers exacerbate negative personality traits. This is particularly true for microtransactions which may associate with gaming disorder symptoms and gambling disorder symptoms. There is currently insufficient research as to how the various forms of microtransactions relate to symptoms of gaming disorder and gambling disorder. We collected questionnaire data from 461 gamer participants. In order to explore the structure and interrelations between the variables, network analysis was applied. Our results align with previous findings that showed that the amount of money individuals spend on microtransactions increases with the risk of gaming disorder symptoms. However, we demonstrate that gambling disorder symptoms relate only indirectly to online spending through a direct link to physical game purchases. This finding is interesting considering the immaterial nature of microtransactions. Altogether, our findings highlight the need to disentangle gaming and gambling disorder symptoms and microtransactions, isolate psychological markers of problematic behavior, and aim to develop support or preventive technologies to come to the help of vulnerable gamers.

articles.title: Designing for Realistic Self-Assessment: Reducing Illusions of Competence in Human–Technology Interaction
articles.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Humans frequently overestimate their unaided problem-solving abilities after receiving cognitive support—a bias known as illusion of competence. Such miscalibration harms the ability to seek and sustain support and thus undermines adaptive reliance on technology. In four experiments, we examined how subtle interventions can reduce this bias during technology-assisted problem solving. In Experiment 1, short metacognitive prompts inviting reflection on the contribution of cognitive support abolished the bias. In Experiment 2, the intervention of emphasizing the external origin of the support was tested. The emphasis was implemented by framing the support as coming from a humanlike (a robot face) or a nonhumanlike (a soft-ware window) entity. Both emphases of external origin reduced the bias to a similar extent. Moreover, engaging in unaided problem solving also abolished and even reversed the bias, leading to an illusion of incompetence. We failed to replicate these findings after methodolog-ical refinement in Experiment 3 that included more pronounced external support. When keep-ing refinements but again using less pronounced support, replications succeeded in Experiment 4. Our findings demonstrate that minimal interventions can enhance a problem solver’s meta-cognitive accuracy when receiving cognitive support. We discuss implications for the design of cognitive human-computer interactions that promote realistic self-assessment and thus sus-tainable collaborations.

articles.title: Material Life Satisfaction Increases Willingness to Engage in Costly Climate Action
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change requires sustained public support for policies and willingness to engage in actions that may incur personal costs. Understanding the social conditions under which citizens are willing to support such measures is important for assessing the feasibility of ambitious climate action. Using data from a large, population-weighted survey of Dutch citizens (N = 22,749) and covariate adjustments informed by directed acyclic graphs, we estimate the effect of different facets of life satisfaction on willingness to contribute 1% of monthly household income to address climate change. We find a strong effect of material life satisfaction: individuals who are very satisfied with their material conditions are more than three times more likely to be willing to contribute than those who are not satisfied at all. In contrast, satisfaction with social life, physical health, and mental health show weak or negligible independent effects on willingness once material life satisfaction and relevant background variables are taken into account. We discuss the implications of our results for the design and acceptability of climate policies that are perceived as placing burdens on households.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: Trust and Intellectual Humility as Necessary Conditions for AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Recently, AI models demonstrated a remarkable ability to facilitate opinion change, a notoriously difficult task between human communicators. Here, we focus on the dispositions that characterize message recipients, specifically identifying trust in AI, intellectual humility (IH), and their interplay as key factors in acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Across two studies with an online British sample (N=294), we replicated findings showing significant attitude change regarding legal immigrants following brief interactions with GPT. Crucially, our findings reveal that opinion change is contingent on higher IH and greater trust in AI, independently and jointly, predicting greater acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Experimentally capturing the centrality of open-mindedness (IH) and source sensitivity (Trust) highlights how epistemic vigilance constrains AI’s persuasive impact and sheds new light on the persuasion literature by revisiting the role of source credibility. Future research should examine whether these dispositional effects extend to long-term behavioral patterns across broader real-world contexts.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles.title: How Employees Experience (Im)balance with W-ICTs: an Ideal Type Analysis of Digital Well-being
articles.authors: Lore Geldof; Ann DeSmet; Alice Verlinden; Elfi Baillien
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The rapid digitalization of work has intensified employees' connectivity to work-related information and communication technologies (W-ICTs), creating both opportunities and risks for digital well-being. While prior research highlights these ambivalent effects, little is known about how employees emotionally experience digital (im)balance with W-ICTs. Hence, we aim to develop a typology detailing such emotional experiences.
Design/Methodology/Approach: Drawing on 40 qualitative interviews (60% female; Mage = 40.25; SD = 9.16), this study abductively develops an experiential typology of digital (im)balance with W-ICT using Ideal Type Analysis. The identified types capture variations in emotional experiences (i.e., affective and cognitive) and digital connectivity processes (DCPs; i.e., interference, boundary blurring, exposure, and time displacement).
Findings: Eight Ideal Types are identified, comprising four experiences of digital imbalance and four experiences of digital balance. The types differ in emotional valence with configurations of DCPs. A comparison of the types show distinct emotional experiences while similar DCPs may occur. This is contextualized in the organisational setting.
Originality: By integrating emotional experiences and DCPs, the typology advances a configurational understanding of employee digital well-being. By contextualizing the types in organizational conditions, the findings suggest that highly connected work environments are not inherently tied to experiences of imbalance.

articles.title: Social readiness and public legitimacy of vaccine mandates: comparative evidence from three countries
articles.authors: Uwana Evers; Joshua Lake; Katie Attwell
articles.abstract: Vaccine mandates are used to increase vaccine uptake during infectious disease emergencies; however, they expose enduring tensions between collective protection and individual autonomy. Existing research treats public opinion toward mandates as a binary – recording only whether people support or oppose them. This study conceptualizes mandate attitudes as comprising two distinct dimensions – perceived public-health protection and concern for rights/autonomy – and examines these in survey data from Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973). In this framework, mandate legitimacy encompasses both perceived collective benefits and perceived infringements on individual autonomy. Analysis revealed divergent patterns: the protection dimension was more strongly associated with institutional trust and vaccination behavior across all three countries, while rights-based attitudes were more variable. Moreover, trust in health-relevant institutions was more robustly associated with the protection dimension than trust in political institutions or media, but this did not extend uniformly to rights-based attitudes. In France, rights-based attitudes were independent of health system trust; in Italy, rights attitudes were unrelated to national government trust, suggesting rights-based objections operate partly independently of institutional confidence. Feeling compelled to vaccinate against COVID-19 was negatively associated with both dimensions across all countries, indicating coercive vaccination experiences may deplete legitimacy capital available for future mandate deployment. Findings suggest that general mandate approval can conceal substantial rights-based resistance, and that institutional trust is insufficient to reduce rights-based mandate resistance Communication strategies that build health institution trust, minimize coercive framing, and are sensitive to political contexts might sustain the public legitimacy required for effective pandemic preparedness.

articles.title: Narrative Entropy
articles.authors: Devin R Wright; Fritz Breithaupt; Anthony F. Beavers; Jacob G. Foster; Jisun An
articles.abstract: Narrative Entropy Theory (NET) proposes that we inhabit narrative environments: ecosystems of cultures, communities, and personal histories constructed from overlapping stories. Narrative entropy is a dynamic, relational property of these ecosystems: the degree of constraint and uncertainty over the interpretive possibility space available within them. At relatively lower entropy, interpretive activity concentrates around recurrent structures, makes narrative and shared worlds easier to navigate and facilitates shared meaning and experience. At relatively higher entropy, more possibilities remain available, which makes interpretation less anticipable and preserves opportunities for interpretive plurality, perspective-taking, and the generation of new meaning. In this way, narrative environments shape how meaning is interpreted and shared and which experiences and perspectives become available for recognition. NET connects the structure of these environments to cognition, communication, and social coordination while treating narrative as both organized structure and embodied activity. We provide an initial empirical demonstration using 475,716 English-language news articles from sources in 65 countries. We operationalize narrative entropy through topic attention, microframe complexity, and narrative fluency (the compressibility of traversal through narrative networks) and compare these measures with national indices of expressive freedom. All measures covary with these indices in the predicted directions and together account for more than one-third of the cross-national variance in the World Press Freedom Index. Together, these results show that narrative environments leave measurable traces in the artifacts they produce, making their structure empirically tractable for scientific inquiry.

articles.title: Educator Preparedness in Navigating Inclusive Education and Sensory Differences in Autism: Qualitative Exploration in Ontario, Canada
articles.authors: Stephanie Larmer; Gabrielle Czichrak; Ryan A Stevenson
articles.abstract: Although Ontario, Canada follows an inclusive education model, little is known about the current status regarding the education of autistic students. Specifically, limited research has explored relevant facets of educator experiences and needs, a crucial component of successful inclusive education in autism. We aimed to explore existing gaps through open-ended questions in a questionnaire and follow-up interviews. First, educators and pre-service educators completed the open-ended questions as part of a larger questionnaire. Then, those who opted to participate completed follow-up interviews on their responses to the open-ended questions. The results revealed a pervasive lack of support for educators and pre-service educators and the consequences it can have for both them and autistic students. Specifically, participants detailed a wide range of desired professional development in autism and outlined a high prevalence of sensory experiences with autistic students, desiring guidance. Ultimately, participants emphasized the existing barriers to successful inclusive education in autism and explained the changes that would help in overcoming them. It was evident participants care for autistic students and desire change that leads to greater inclusion and success. This research demonstrates the value in listening to those responsible for implementing inclusive education in autism, providing decision makers with updated evidence based on direct experience that can guide professional development design and policies and may serve as an example for inclusive education more broadly.

articles.title: Recent Clinical Encounters for Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviours: Disclosure, Assessment, Missed Opportunities, and Implications for Practice
articles.authors: Jennifer Q. P. Nguyen; Glenn A Melvin; David John Hallford
articles.abstract:
Objective: Many individuals who die by suicide have contact with healthcare services in the months preceding their death, making these interactions critical opportunities for identification, intervention, and support. However, little is known about how individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STBs) perceive recent clinical encounters, including how these experiences are discussed and managed.
Method: Australian adults (N = 266; Mage = 32.9; range = 18-71 years) who had experienced STBs and consulted with a mental health professional within the past two weeks completed an online survey examining suicide-related enquiry, disclosure experiences, clinician responses, and satisfaction.
Results: Psychologists were the most commonly consulted clinicians (49.2%), and 90.8% reported having seen the same clinician previously. Although 95.7% of participants considered discussing their STBs at least somewhat important, only 67.9% reported discussing these experiences with clinicians. Among those who did not discuss STBs, 50.0% reported that they had not been asked. Participants also reported that clinicians more frequently enquired about general emotional wellbeing (80.6%) than directly about STBs (55.3%). Among participants who did discuss STBs, 52.1% reported withholding information, while 46.2% reported feeling hesitant to disclose. Safety planning (36.9%) and follow-up (37.4%) were reported infrequently despite being viewed as important and helpful. Nevertheless, 75.4% reported being satisfied with their recent interactions.
Conclusions: Despite generally positive experiences with these interactions, the findings highlight opportunities to strengthen suicide prevention by creating opportunities to discuss STBs beyond initial clinical encounters, supporting disclosure through compassionate care, and ensuring that suicide-specific care is provided where appropriate following identification.
Key words: suicide; suicidal ideation; suicidal behaviour; disclosure; non-disclosure; clinician-patient communication

articles.title: BoundBase-EN (BBEN): A database of English bound bases in texts for children and young people
articles.authors: Maria Korochkina; Nicola Dawson; Danielle Colenbrander
articles.abstract: Sensitivity to morphological structure is considered a hallmark of skilled reading; however, much of the extant literature has focused on affixation (e.g., -er in teacher) and complex words with free bases (e.g., teach in teacher). This focus has left bound bases (e.g., ceiv(e) in receive) relatively unexplored, despite their prevalence in English and potential importance as a source of morphological regularity in print experience. Using a combination of automated and manual procedures, we developed BoundBase-EN (BBEN), a publicly available database providing lexical statistics and etymological information for 328 English bound bases occurring in texts for readers from age 5 to young adulthood. The BBEN data provide key insights into the distributional properties of these units. First, most bound bases occur infrequently and in a limited number of distinct words, with only a small set accounting for the majority of readers’ exposure. Second, children encounter bound-base words from the earliest years of independent reading, with developmental increases in exposure reflecting greater token frequency (i.e., more encounters with the same words) rather than type frequency (i.e., greater diversity in words containing bound bases). Third, although relatively infrequent overall, many bound-base words occur more frequently than complex words containing free bases, suggesting that they occupy a middle ground in children’s experience of morphological regularities. These findings highlight the importance of investigating bound bases for understanding how morphological knowledge is acquired and processed, and for informing approaches to morphology instruction. The BBEN database provides a foundation for such research.

articles.title: Preschoolers can coordinate with each other to communicate about novel referents
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Robert Zane Sparks; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring sustained interactive communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4-5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children's referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 4 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N=158), we found that 4-5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner's. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

articles.title: Dynamic attribute activation explains gaze biases in choice.
articles.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Sudeep Bhatia
articles.abstract:
People tend to choose the options they look at more. Prior work explains this effect by assuming that visual attention increases preference for the attended option. However, it remains unclear why looking at an option increases its preference and when this relationship is
weakened. Using an experimental paradigm that combines eye-tracking and a think-aloud protocol, we provide evidence that visual attention shapes preference by activating attributes associated with the attended option. Critically, the content of these activated attributes
depends on contextual factors such as stimulus desirability and behavioral goals. In standard choice settings, where the goal is to choose the preferred option, visual attention primarily activates positive attributes. In contrast, when these contextual factors are incongruent, activated attributes become less positive, reducing the influence of visual attention on choice. To account for these patterns, we propose a new computational model of gaze-driven attribute activation. Our model subsumes existing theories as special cases, and uniquely predicts which attributes are brought to mind by gaze and how they shape downstream decisions. Together, our work offers a mechanistic explanation of a fundamental driver of choice as well as its boundary conditions.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Social Sharing of Emotion: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sarah Taylor O'Brien; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Sooyeon Kim; Peter Koval; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: After experiencing an emotional event, people almost always talk to other people about their experience. People generally believe this process—labelled social sharing of emotion—is beneficial, but empirical findings on the outcomes are mixed. We argue that underlying these mixed findings is an issue with the conceptual clarity of social sharing. In pursuit of conceptual clarity and in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we conducted a scoping review to map how social sharing has been defined and operationalized in the literature. Our review included 99 articles, including 128 studies, empirically investigating social sharing of emotion (sourced from PsychInfo (Ovid), ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, PsyArXiv, and PubMed). From these articles, we identified common features of researchers’ definitions and operationalizations of social sharing, highlighting what researchers deem central to the process. We found large heterogeneity in how social sharing has been conceptualized, which may contribute to the mixed findings on sharing thus far. For instance, we identified 16 unique features of social sharing in researchers’ definitions, 11 unique features in self-report study operationalizations, and 10 unique features in manipulation study operationalizations. Based on our findings, we propose a new consensus definition of social sharing, outlining necessary and sufficient features of the process. In all, this review elucidates a common behavior that is gaining relevance in a world with more ways to connect with each other than ever before.

articles.title: Theoretical Considerations of the Common Factor Model and its Alternatives
articles.authors: Danielle Siegel; Mijke Rhemtulla
articles.abstract: Accurate psychological measurement typically relies on the common factor model, which assumes observed items reflect an underlying latent construct plus measurement error. However, growing evidence suggests that the factor model is not appropriate for all psychological constructs, and applying it when its assumptions are violated can bias both the measurement and structural parameters in structural equation models (SEMs). The paper reviews the common factor model along with a range of alternative measurement approaches, including composite models with prespecified and estimated weights, psychometric network models, and models that treat individual scale items as unique predictors. We describe the theoretical assumptions, strengths, and limitations of each approach, with particular attention to recent methodological developments that all factor-based and composite-based models to be statistically compared within the SEM framework. Using a running empirical example from Milas et al., (2021), we illustrate how the choice of measurement model changes parameter estimates, model fit, and the substantive interpretation of results. We conclude that researchers should select a measurement approach based on the theoretical relations they hypothesize among their scale items rather than defaulting to the common factor model. We offer recommendations for evaluating and comparing candidate measurement models.

articles.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles.title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Research in Aphasia: An AI-Assisted Scoping Review and Semantic Network Analysis
articles.authors: Mengyang Qiu; Siena Sun; Sara NassrElgrgawi; Zirui Feng
articles.abstract:
Purpose: A shared view of artificial intelligence (AI) research in aphasia is needed to locate related work across clinical and computing publications. This scoping review mapped research topics and connections, AI method families over time, and reported evaluation and participant characteristics relevant to clinical applicability.
Method: Seven sources were searched for publications from January 2010 through June 2026. Two large language models (LLMs) independently screened records and extracted information from publication abstracts. Disagreements within and across LLMs were manually reviewed and resolved. To check screening accuracy, three human reviewers independently screened a sample without seeing model responses. Semantic network analysis of the abstracts identified research communities and connecting studies.
Results: LLM-assisted screening identified 412 primary studies. Its decisions agreed with the human majority on 91% of 145 sampled records. Network analysis identified 12 communities, with partial separation between clinical and computing publications and general separation between post-stroke aphasia and primary progressive aphasia studies. Deep learning and generative AI first appeared in clinical and computing publications in the same respective years and represented larger proportions of computing publications. Abstracts often lacked key evaluation and participant information: only 28 abstracts (7%) reported independent model testing, 21 (5%) clinical evaluation, and 34 (8%) aphasia severity.
Conclusions: The map provides entry points for exploring related research, and the workflow offers a foundation for future evidence syntheses in communication disorders. Clearer reporting of evaluation and participant characteristics could improve communication across disciplines and help readers identify relevant publications.

articles.title: Popular nonfiction can durably shift politically relevant attitudes—and so can a much shorter AI summary
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Adam J. Berinsky; James Patoriza; David Gertler Rand
