articles.abstract: Can reading a chapter of popular nonfiction shift politically relevant attitudes among resistant partisans, and, if so, can an AI-generated summary do so just as effectively? In a preregistered experiment, N = 555 Republicans were randomized to read “The Cyber Sleuth” by Geraldine Brooks—a profile of IRS cybercrime investigators from Michael Lewis’s Who Is Government?—or a control text, and further randomized to either the full text (∼5300 words) or a much shorter AI-generated summary (∼1400 words). Reading “The Cyber Sleuth” produced wide-ranging attitude change relative to control: IRS favorability increased substantially (d = 0.62), with spillover to civil-service favorability (d = 0.37) and opposition to DOGE-led workforce reductions (d = 0.40). These effects remained significant two months later (ds 0.14–0.19). Strikingly, the AI-generated summary produced effects statistically indistinguishable from the full text. Popular nonfiction, and an AI summary thereof, can be an effective tool for politically relevant attitude change, even on a polarized, partisan issue.

articles.title: What Race Means for Health among Black Americans: How Microaggressions Shape Self-Efficacy and Readiness for Behavior Change
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives: Persistent racial disparities in cardiovascular health among Black Americans reflect not only structural inequities in the United States, but also the racialized meanings of cardiovascular disease reproduced through public and private health communication. Drawing on ecological systems theory, this research examines how beliefs linking race and cardiovascular disease are reinforced through routine clinical interactions and how these meanings shape health behavior change. Method: Across two experimental mixed-methods studies, a model integrating ecological, social–cognitive, and behavior-change frameworks was tested. In Study 1 (N = 374), health-message framing was experimentally manipulated to examine effects on self-efficacy and decisional balance while controlling for prior experiences of racial microaggression in medical contexts. Study 2 (N = 589) extended this work by testing whether conceptualizations of race as biological/genetic and social/political moderated these effects. A subset of participants (n = 57) voluntarily provided narratives of racially charged healthcare experiences, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Results: Racial microaggressions from health professionals disrupted self-efficacy and decisional balance for cardiovascular health behaviors. Endorsement of biological versus social race beliefs moderated these effects, shaping both their magnitude and direction. Qualitative findings revealed how everyday clinical interactions reproduce racialized meanings of disease risk and personal control. Conclusions: These findings identify clinical communication as a consequential site where racial meanings of disease are constructed and psychologically internalized, influencing motivation for health behavior change. Addressing biologically essentialist framing in healthcare may therefore be critical for strengthening self-regulation and reducing cardiovascular disparities among Black Americans.

Keywords: racial microaggressions; health communication; self-efficacy; decisional balance; Transtheoretical Model; ecological systems theory; racial essentialism; cardiovascular health disparities

Public significance statement: How health professionals and public campaigns talk about race matters for behavior change. This research shows that subtle racialized cues in medicine can weaken Black patients’ sense of control and readiness to take preventive action. Training clinicians to avoid biological essentialist framing may improve patient engagement and help reduce cardiovascular health disparities.

articles.title: Taking the speaker’s perspective? Investigating quantifier and implicature processing in an AI-language training paradigm using EEG-VR
articles.authors: Maria Spychalska; Ludmila Reimer; Marjolijn Dijkhuis; Peter Hagoort
articles.abstract:
Interpreting speaker meaning requires taking into account the speaker’s epistemic perspective, i.e., their access to relevant information. The extent to which listeners integrate this perspective during comprehension is known as the perspective-taking problem. We present the first EEG study to investigate the role of perspective-taking in the processing of quantifiers and scalar implicatures. Using immersive virtual reality, we asked participants to assist an AI, represented by a virtual agent, in learning to use quantifiers appropriately. Critically, the agent had limited access to the reference domain compared to the participant.

Our results show that when the speaker’s information access is restricted, listeners initially process the semantic content of quantified statements from an egocentric perspective. Effects of the speaker’s perspective emerge only later, reflected in a sustained anterior negativity. For pragmatically ambiguous sentences containing ``some", we observe neither an effect of speaker perspective nor evidence for scalar implicature processing. We argue that contexts requiring consideration of the speaker’s knowledge primarily support Gricean, weak implicatures, which are computed relatively late as post-propositional inferences.

articles.title: All BANG, little buck: Basic psychological needs are weakly linked with video gaming behavior
articles.authors: Nick Ballou; Tamás Andrei Földes; Matti Vuorre; Thomas Hakman; Kristoffer Magnusson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: Psychological theories of media use often assume that subjective motivation affects observable behavior. Using video games as a test case, we examine this assumption by pairing repeated self-reports of motivation with objective digital trace data at scale. Across two datasets comprising tens of thousands of hours of gaming behavior, we test predictions derived from self-determination theory and the Basic Needs in Games (BANG) model, which posit that autonomy, competence, and relatedness experiences drive engagement. Study 1 (preregistered) analyzes 11k daily observations from 555 U.S. players with 30 days of multi-platform digital trace data. Study 2 (exploratory) examines 102k sessions from 9k PowerWash Simulator players, linking in-game experience prompts to behavioral logs. In both studies, need satisfaction was robustly associated with subjective states but showed weak or null associations with short-term gaming behavior, including subsequent play, session length, and return latency, across extensive preregistered and robustness analyses. These findings reveal a substantial motivation–behavior gap and suggest that SDT-based accounts may overestimate the role of need satisfaction in explaining when or how much people play. Data and code are available under a CC0 license at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18352505.

articles.title: Schizotypy and Autistic Traits in Bilinguals: Associations with Language Deficits Across Native and Non-Native Languages
articles.authors: Arthur Hamilton; Synthia Guimond; Olessia Jouravlev
articles.abstract:
Background: Schizotypal and autistic traits are increasingly understood as existing on continuous dimensions extending from subclinical variation to clinical schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), respectively. Language deficits are well documented in SZ and ASD but research on their relationship to subclinical schizotypal and autistic traits remains limited. Moreover, while evidence suggests SZ symptoms manifest more strongly in bilinguals’ native (L1) than non-native (L2) language, little is known about whether associated language deficits similarly differ between L1 and L2.
Methods: The present study examined associations between schizotypy, autistic traits, and language performance in 503 bilinguals (436 English–French and 67 French–English) from the general population. Participants completed lexical, semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic language tasks in both L1 and L2, together with questionnaires on schizotypy and autistic traits.
Results: Higher schizotypy was associated with poorer syntactic and pragmatic performance in both languages and lexical performance in L1 only, while no association was found with semantic performance. Higher schizotypy was also associated with a reduced L1 advantage in lexical performance, but not in other linguistic domains. Autistic traits showed no independent association with linguistic performance or L1-vs-L2 differences. However, autistic traits moderated the relationship between schizotypy and language performance: higher autistic traits attenuated the negative association between schizotypy and performance in L1 while strengthening it in L2.
Conclusion: Overall, the findings partially support dimensional understandings of SZ by showing that some language deficits associated with clinical SZ extend to subclinical schizotypy, without providing clear evidence that ASD-associated language deficits extend to subclinical autistic traits.

articles.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a higher distribution of web surveys was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles.title: Humanlike AI May Strengthen Women’s Agreement With Sexist Stereotypes
articles.authors: Sterling Williams-Ceci; Rachel Minkowitz; Lior Zalmanson; Michael MACY; Mor Naaman
articles.abstract: AI can influence societally-consequential attitudes by generating biased arguments – but can it influence our attitudes without changing its arguments at all? In four experiments (N = 2,762), we show that the mere presence of humanlike features in an AI chatbot influences women to more strongly accept ideologically-compatible sexist stereotypes, biases that often resist influence and have societal harm. This influence operates indirectly by increasing “mind perception” – the belief that AI is conscious and thinking – which increases perceptions of its trustworthiness. Our contribution is that anthropomorphism’s influence extends beyond increased trust toward AI itself, impacting women’s broader attitudes about their competence and status. This influence happens when women are attentive during conversations with AI. As developers add more anthropomorphic features to AI, the harms of stereotypes it repeats will increase for vulnerable groups – but making AI appear less humanlike can mitigate this risk.

articles.title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
articles.authors: Paul McKee; Gregory Russell Samanez-Larkin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles.abstract: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

articles.title: Context Sensitivity Underlies Emotional Intelligence and Flexible Emotion Regulation in Daily Life
articles.authors: Riley Leckie; Carolyn MacCann
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies depends on situation factors, such that effective emotion regulation involves regulatory flexibility (flexibly matching the regulation strategies you use to the context you are in). Recent research shows that two emotional intelligence abilities (emotion understanding and management) predict regulatory flexibility. This connection is assumed to be based on individual differences in context sensitivity (which underpin both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility). The current pre-registered study tests this assumption, aiming to replicate the emotional intelligence/regulatory flexibility link while adding a novel measure of context sensitivity in daily life. Participants (N = 131) completed baseline assessments of emotional intelligence and up to 30 experience sampling surveys (n = 2,901) across five days. Surveys measured four emotion regulation strategies and five appraisals of emotionally relevant situational features. Variability in strategies and appraisals was used to derive regulatory flexibility and context sensitivity metrics both in each situation (between-strategy and between-appraisal variability) and across situations (within-strategy and within-appraisal variability). All prior effects linking emotional intelligence to regulatory flexibility were replicated and there were two new findings. First, both emotional intelligence abilities predicted higher context sensitivity in each situation (between-appraisal variability), but not across situations (within-appraisal variability). Second, higher context sensitivity predicted higher regulatory flexibility at both the within-person and between-person level. These findings support the assumption that context sensitivity underlies both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility. To refine proposed measures of context sensitivity in daily life, future research should look to disentangle general appraisals of pronounced changes in the objective characteristics of the world from sensitivity to more nuanced changes.

articles.title: Predictive coding unifies neural and behavioral signatures of contextual facilitation
articles.authors: Samer Nour Eddine; Anthony Yacovone; Gina R. Kuperberg
articles.abstract: During comprehension, words that are primed or predictable are processed more quickly and elicit smaller N400 responses than words that are less consistent with their preceding context. Although these behavioral and neural effects are both commonly interpreted as evidence of facilitated processing, they have typically been explained within different computational frameworks that impose seemingly conflicting constraints: behavioral facilitation requires more activity to accumulate over expected representations, allowing a decision threshold to be reached earlier, whereas N400 facilitation requires less neural activity to be generated overall. Here, we show that an implemented model of predictive coding provides a unified mechanistic account of both phenomena and, in doing so, resolves three longstanding puzzles. First, it explains how facilitated processing can simultaneously produce faster behavioral responses and reduced neural activity: expected representations accumulate activity more rapidly in state units while generating less activity in error units. Second, an asymmetry between top-down priors and bottom-up evidence allows context to pre-activate multiple lexical candidates without inducing premature competition or misprediction costs. Third, it reconciles apparently conflicting claims about the timing of contextual facilitation by showing that behavioral and neural measures can reflect different phases along a single continuous trajectory of lexico-semantic processing, rather than distinct processing stages.

articles.title: Self-reported emotional change in conversations with an emotional support assistant: an observational analysis in TerapIA
articles.authors: Alejandro Vaca Serrano; Alberto Vaca Escribano; José María González de Echevarri
articles.abstract: People who talk to an emotional support assistant usually want to feel a bit better by the time they stop talking. Measuring whether that happens, and under what conditions, is a different thing from proving clinical efficacy. We analyze the change in a continuous emotional score in [0, 1] that users record at the beginning and at the end of their conversation with Pía, the assistant of the TerapIA app. The analysis is restricted to conversations where both ratings are present, where the slider was moved away from the interface default at both ends, and where the dialogue reached at least ten user messages. Once we discount the automatic greeting that opens the chat, that threshold amounts in practice to a conversation with actual content. Over n = 1935 conversations from 909 people, the mean score went from 0.42 at the beginning to 0.56 at the end (Δ = +0.138; 95% CI by user-clustered bootstrap [+0.121, +0.155]; dz = 0.54; Wilcoxon p < 0.001), and 63.4% of conversations improved. The mean change is zero in very short dialogues and consistently positive from ten user messages onwards, with an association between length and improvement that is statistically significant and robust to clustering by person. The result holds, and is in fact slightly larger, if only the first eligible conversation of each person is used (Δ = +0.147; dz = 0.57). Among the people who contributed at least three such conversations, the end score of the last one minus the start score of the first was +0.195, and 70% of them went up; the emotional starting point also rises with the number of accumulated conversations within each person. The design is observational: there is no control group, filling in the rating is optional, the score is a self-report, and regression to the mean is present. We do not infer causality, and we do not claim equivalence with a clinical outcome. What we do document is a robust association between talking with Pía for enough turns and a better self-reported emotional state at the end, of a magnitude close to the one observed in other deployed conversational agents with a pre/post within-session measure.

articles.title: Educational Neuroscience Outreach Programs for School-Aged Students: From Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation to Career Development
articles.authors: Arash Khojasteh Zonoozi; Benjamin Ostow; Sepehr Mortaheb; Steven Jillings; Shiva Sharifi; Hamed Ekhtiari; Ghazaleh Soleimani
articles.abstract: Educational neuroscience outreach programs promote neuroscience literacy, science interest, and brain health among school-aged students, ranging from neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to engagement for neuroscience careers. However, their implementation, delivery, and evaluation remain poorly understood. This chapter examined programs through three questions: (1) Where and in what institutional contexts were students targeted? (2) How were programs delivered? and (3) What neuroscience content was taught and what outcomes were reported. A PRISMA-guided review searched PubMed from inception to 2025 for empirical studies of neuroscience-based educational/outreach programs targeting students aged ~5–18 years. Eligible studies reported outcomes of structured neuroscience education in school/community settings. Data included characteristics, design, content, delivery, implementation, and outcomes, and findings informed a translational roadmap. Forty-three studies met the inclusion criteria. Publications increased substantially after 2019, with approximately 65% of studies published during this period. Most programs were conducted in the United States (67.4%), implemented in schools (76.7%), and targeted high school students (58.1%). Activity-based programs were most common (41.9%), often single-day interventions (44.2%), with teachers’ moderators (44.2%) rather than trained implementers (23.3%). Content most commonly addressed addiction (25.6%), cellular/molecular (23.3%), and cognitive neuroscience (20.9%). Knowledge gain (27.9%) and attitudes/interest toward neuroscience (25.6%) were frequently evaluated. The findings provide a foundation for applying neuroscience education to NIPE-oriented goals, including brain and mental health literacy, skills and competencies, and health-related decision-making, while also supporting STEM and neuroscience career engagement. The proposed translational roadmap emphasizes global access, developmental tailoring, stronger school–academic partnerships, sustainable implementation, and rigorous, standardized evaluation to guide future educational neuroscience outreach and NIPE-informed education.

articles.title: Negative Word Production in Bilinguals Triggers Inhibitory Mechanisms: Evidence from Mass Univariate Time-Frequency Analysis
articles.authors: Rafał Jończyk; Marcin Naranowicz; Guillaume Thierry
articles.abstract: Semantic processing of negative content is attenuated when bilinguals read for comprehension in their second language (L2). This phenomenon, well studied in comprehension, has seldom been studied in production or the auditory modality. Here, we show that the dampening of negative emotional content also applies in a production context, albeit to a different extent in the visual and the auditory modalities, and likely entails inhibitory control when bilinguals translate negative words from L2 to L1. Polish–English bilinguals orally translated written (Experiment 1) or spoken (Experiment 2) negative and neutral words either from L2–to–L1 or L1–to–L2. Event-Related Potential results suggested differential processing of negative and neutral words only in the L2–to–L1 translation direction and only in Experiment 1, between 300–750 ms after stimulus onset. Hierarchical linear modeling of neural oscillation power over time revealed a two-step modulation of alpha power in the case of negative L2 words suggesting reduced sensitivity at the stage of stimulus integration (240–365 ms) and enhanced inhibitory control during the preparation of L1 production (620–800 ms). In Experiment 2, we found modulations of theta and alpha power by valence regardless of language of operation, which may be explained by evolutionary precedence of auditory over visual language processing and may be specific to the current production context. We thus show that data-driven time-frequency analysis reveals language-emotion interactions in the course of speech preparation and offers more sensitivity than traditional mean voltage amplitude approaches.

articles.title: Electrophysiological Correlates of Maladaptive Daydreaming: An Exploratory Resting-State EEG Study
articles.authors: Mohammad Atashrooz; Amir Sam Kianimoghadam; Reza Khosrowabadi; Hoda Doosalivand
articles.abstract:
Objective: Maladaptive daydreaming (MD) is characterized by extensive and immersive fantasy activity associated with distress or functional impairment, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly understood. This study examined resting-state electrophysiological differences associated with probable MD.
Methods: Resting-state EEG was recorded from 42 participants (20 probable MDer, 22 screen-negative) during eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Absolute and relative spectral power and sensor-level functional connectivity were examined using linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to demographic, imagery-related, and affective covariates.
Results: Participants meeting the MDS-16 cutoff for probable MD (≥50) showed greater posterior alpha power than screen-negative participants (pFDR = .015), with estimated between-group differences of 0.83 dB during eyes-open (95% CI [0.06, 1.60]) and 1.38 dB during eyes-closed rest (95% CI [0.60, 2.15]). Significant group × condition interactions emerged for frontal theta and theta/beta activity (both pFDR = .007), reflecting stronger eyes-closed-related modulation in probable MD. Relative-power analyses similarly showed greater proportional alpha activity (both posterior and frontal pFDR = .005), with corresponding reductions in several non-alpha bands. These spectral findings remained robust to demographic, imagery-related, and affective covariates. Exploratory analyses also suggested greater sensor-level wPLI connectivity in probable MD.
Conclusion: Probable MD was associated with greater posterior alpha power, condition-dependent frontal theta modulation, and preliminarily elevated functional connectivity. This pattern is consistent with a bias toward internally directed attention rather than heightened imagery vividness, but because ongoing thought content was not sampled during recording, and group classification relied on self-report rather than clinical diagnosis, these findings should be treated as an initial electrophysiological characterization rather than an MD-specific signature.
Keywords: maladaptive daydreaming; resting-state EEG; quantitative EEG; posterior alpha; frontal theta; internally generated cognition; functional connectivity

articles.title: The Adaptation Dilemma: Cultural Fit Does Not Guarantee Safety in Mental-Health LLMs
articles.authors: Maya Low; Ian Gold; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: People increasingly take mental-health concerns to general-purpose AI chatbots. A first wave of safety research has begun to map LLM failure points in this context. When that work considers culture, it usually reads the problem as a lack of fit: if the model does not match the user, the fix is to make it match more closely. We argue that this perspective is incomplete, because cultural fit and safety are not the same thing. By safety we mean the absence of harm caused by the interaction itself. We sort these harms into two classes: imposition, where the model forces its default on a user it does not fit, and collusion, where it adapts to a framing that keeps the user unwell. Because a response that fits a user’s own framing is more credible to them, moving a model toward that framing lowers the risk of imposition while raising both the likelihood of collusion and the damage collusion does when it occurs, so improved cultural sensitivity trades one exposure for another rather than reducing exposure overall. We argue that the reinforcement learning layer increasingly pushes these models toward collusion, while the safeguards in current use are poorly suited to detecting that failure or to limiting the harm it does. We propose a taxonomy of six culture-related failure modes, three of imposition and three of collusion. We argue that evaluating safety requires an anchor outside the user’s in-the-moment approval: responses must be assessed against the harms and benefits the interaction produces for the user, judged both by an external standard and against the goals the user has stated for their care.

articles.title: Recovery from Work via Physical Activity: A Longitudinal Study Among Workers with Intellectual Disabilities
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract: Beyond the established physical and mental health benefits for people with intellectual disabilities (PwID), physical activity may also enhance workplace well-being, as demonstrated in the general population. Given that PwID are susceptible to work-related exhaustion, the restorative role of physical activity could be particularly relevant. This study aimed to investigate recovery processes engaged through off-job physical activity and their contribution to the workplace well-being of PwID. To address this objective, forty-two workers were followed over a six-week cycle of physical activities. Participants reported recovery experiences (i.e., psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery, control, affiliation, and affect) after each session, while trainers recorded session characteristics (i.e., duration and intensity). Workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, need for recovery, and vigor) was assessed at the beginning and end of the cycle. Multilevel analyses revealed only one significant relationship: a positive association between session duration (between-person level) and mastery experience. Regression analyses indicated that relaxation positively predicted exhaustion, while detachment positively predicted cognitive impairment and need for recovery. Conversely, mastery and affiliation were positively associated with physical vigor. These exploratory findings provide initial empirical evidence regarding the recovery role of physical activity for PwID. Further research is needed to validate and expand upon these results.

articles.title: Parent-reported strengths in children with ADHD, autism, and AuDHD
articles.authors: Lessa Madelief Schippers; Amy De Roubaix; Sander Begeer; Corina Greven; Martine Hoogman
articles.abstract:
Background
Traditionally, research on neurodevelopmental conditions has focused on challenges, while strengths received less attention, despite relevance to clinical practice and well-being. To date, few studies have investigated strengths in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Moreover, no studies directly compared strengths of children with ADHD, autistic children, and children with co-occurring ADHD and autism (AuDHD), leaving open questions about specificity of strengths for these groups.
Method
For the current study, we used data from a large Dutch National registry study, In Kaart. We qualitatively investigated parent-reported data from Dutch children (n = 143) aged 5-16 years with (suspected) ADHD, autism or AuDHD. Parents reported on strengths related to the diagnoses of their child. We used content analysis to identify strengths in children with ADHD, in autistic children and in children with AuDHD.
Results
Across all diagnostic groups, parents reported a wide range of strengths. Children with ADHD and autistic children showed both overlapping and unique strengths, whereas the strengths reported for AuDHD children reflected a combination of both groups. Strengths fell within the categories of ‘Courage’, ‘Higher order cognitive skills’, ‘Humanity’, ‘Justice’, ‘Motor skills’, ‘Temperance’, ‘Transcendence’, ‘Wisdom’ and ‘Other skill’. For children with ADHD, creativity and zest were most prominent, whereas attention to detail and honesty were most prominent in autistic children. 
Conclusion
The variety and frequency of reported strengths suggest that positive aspects are not uncommon for children with ADHD and/or autism and may offer opportunities for a more balanced perspective on these conditions. Our results can feed strength-based approaches for use in clinical practice, assessment, and support, helping children with ADHD and/or autism flourish.

articles.title: Synchronised group singing enhances social bonding more than group conversation or recitation does: A Registered Report across 30 languages
articles.authors: Zixuan Jia; Yuto Ozaki; Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; jiawen huang; Emmanouil Benetos; Uswatun Khasanah; Sasha Calhoun; Gakuto Chiba; Yoichi Kitayama; Shinya Fujii
articles.abstract: The evolution of music, language, and prosociality has been debated since before Darwin. The social bonding hypothesis proposes that these phenomena may be interlinked: musicality may have facilitated the evolution of social bonding beyond the possibilities of spoken language. Although dozens of experimental studies have argued that synchronised rhythms can promote bonding, methodological issues including publication bias, sample bias, experimenter effects, and appropriateness of experimental controls make it unclear whether synchronous singing reliably and generally enhances bonding relative to speaking. Following a peer-reviewed Stage 1 Registered Report protocol, we collected data from randomized controlled in-person experiments with 1,017 participants singing and speaking in groups of 5-10 in 30 diverse languages (N = 901 participants after planned quality control exclusions). Our results strongly supported all three of our pre-registered confirmatory hypotheses (all Bayes Factors > 30): (i) synchronised group singing enhances self-reported social bonding (20.9% mean increase), a significantly greater increase than (ii) group conversation (12.9% increase) or (iii) synchronous recitation (15.2% increase). Unregistered exploratory analyses suggested that perceived synchronisation and enjoyment are key predictors of social bonding, results are not artefacts of expectancy or group size, and singing’s bonding effects may be stronger in non-Western than Western contexts. Group singing may serve as a better bonding activity than speaking activities in settings such as school or workplace orientation events. Our study provides strong cross-cultural empirical evidence that music is not merely “auditory cheesecake” that is “useless” compared with language (Pinker, 1997). All forms of vocal communication increase social bonding, but group singing bonds us together over 1.5 times more on average than spoken conversation does.

articles.title: Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO): First- and Second Language Book Reading in Adults with Dyslexia
articles.authors: Sam Boeve; Lore FranÃ§ois; Ella Salgado Salgado Figueroa; Esperanza Badaya; Louisa Bogaerts; Nicolas Dirix
articles.abstract: Openly available eye-tracking corpora have been indispensable for the progress of psycholinguistic theories of reading. Past corpus work extensively covered typical reading in a range of languages, but left reading difficulties relatively under documented. In this article, we present a novel corpus, the Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO). It includes eye-tracking data collected from 20 Dutch - English bilingual adults with a diagnosis of developmental dyslexia. They read an entire novel (almost 60.000 words), with one half presented in their first language (Dutch) and the other half in their second language (English). After each chapter the participants answered multiple reading comprehension questions. Additionally, all participants completed several measures of linguistic abilities, including vocabulary, spelling, a one-minute reading test and a language questionnaire. This corpus is the largest of its kind and is a direct extension of the existing GECO corpus of typical reading (Cop, Dirix, Drieghe & Duyck, 2017). In combination with GECO, it provides researchers with a unique resource to study naturalistic reading in dyslexia and its intersection with bilingualism. All data and materials will be made available upon publication.

articles.title: Evaluating Open-Weight Large Language Models for Structured Depression Assessment from Clinical Interviews
articles.authors: Jeffrey M. Girard; Gaossou Youssouf Kebe; Louis-Philippe Morency; Fernando De la Torre; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles.abstract: The administration of semi-structured clinical interviews for depression assessment is resource-intensive and susceptible to rater drift. While large language models (LLMs) offer potential for automated quality assurance, reliance on proprietary models creates data privacy barriers incompatible with secure clinical workflows. This study evaluates a privacy-preserving pipeline using open-weight LLMs to perform item-level scoring of the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) directly from interview transcripts. The sample included 541 video-recorded English-language interviews with 277 psychiatric inpatients diagnosed with diverse affective and psychotic disorders. Benchmarking 25 architectures, we found that an indirect scoring strategy, where models predict individual item scores that are subsequently summed, significantly outperformed direct total score prediction. This suggests that decomposing the assessment into intermediate reasoning steps improves performance. The best-performing models achieved “good” error rates and “excellent” correlations with trusted human labels, approaching established benchmarks for human inter-rater reliability. To determine the active ingredients of effective prompting, we conducted an ablation study. Results revealed that descriptive cues (scoring criteria) were the primary driver of performance, whereas few-shot examples provided negligible additional benefit, suggesting that zero-shot prompting is a viable, efficient strategy. However, error analysis identified a multimodal gap, where text-only models struggled more with items dependent on nonverbal behavior. We conclude that open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong potential to serve as secure “digital second opinions,” representing a promising step toward augmenting clinical decision-making without compromising patient privacy.

articles.title: A Computational Account of Approach-Avoidance Conflict in a Foraging-Inspired Search Paradigm
articles.authors: Franziska Usée; Christiane A. Melzig; Dirk Ostwald; Anne Collins
articles.abstract:
An approach-avoidance conflict (AAC) arises when the same action promises reward but also carries potential harm. Here, we examined how humans
initiate and sustain engagement under such conflict using an online foraging-inspired AAC task. Eighty-seven participants repeatedly encountered
visual search fields associated with four instructed reward-punishment states and decided whether to enter each field and how extensively to search it,
allowing us to distinguish passive avoidance as withheld entry from active within-field avoidance as early search termination. Participants committed to
search more often and explored more extensively when expected rewards were high and punishments were low. Agent-based behavioral modeling indicated that initial
and sustained engagement could be characterized at different levels of behavioral granularity: commitment to search was best explained by additive
reward-punishment evaluation with state-independent trial drift, whereas search extent was best captured by a click-wise stopping process inspired by the
marginal value theorem, a foraging account of when to leave a current patch for alternatives. These findings suggest that avoidance under conflict is
not a single decision, but unfolds across separable decisions about whether to engage, how long to persist, and when to leave.

articles.title: Barriers and enablers to implementing and using surveillance technology for suicide prevention in public places
articles.authors: Bethany Cliffe; Alex Dark; Ian Marsh; Penny Phillips; Andy Willis; Laura Joyner; Lisa Marzano; Peter Craig; Keith Hawton; Jay-Marie Mackenzie
articles.abstract: This research sought to understand the barriers and enablers of implementing surveillance technologies for suicide prevention in public spaces. To explore a range of professional stakeholders’ experiences of and attitudes towards surveillance technologies, we drew on ethnography of three public sites that have high suicide rates, and seven focus groups with 56 stakeholders working there. Framework analysis was used, and ethnography notes were triangulated with this. We learnt that there were four stages at which barriers and enablers exist: 1) decision making, 2) procurement, 3) implementation and 4) perceived effectiveness. During decision making, barriers included lacking specialist expertise to know what technology to implement and how to implement it, and the organisational and personal risks around assuming responsibility for suicide prevention. During procurement, the costs were a notable challenge, with stakeholders having limited budgets to purchase the technology and ensure its sustainability. Factors which enabled implementation of the technology were having a suitable response mechanism so that interventions could be delivered, and making sure the technology was appropriate for the location/context. Technology was perceived to be effective when it enabled identification of/ response to incidents, but not when it generated false alerts or carried risks like displacement to other locations.

articles.title: Non-word repetition in bilingual children: the role of language exposure, vocabulary scores and environmental factors
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Gianmatteo Farabolini; pasquale rinaldi; Maria Cristina Caselli; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Assessing language development in bilingual children is challenging in geographical areas where bilinguals have different native languages. Lexical development measures are often used as a starting point to study linguistic abilities in bilingual children. Non-word repetition (NWR) has been found to be very informative in detecting variation. The present study contributes to the broader research aim of documenting bilinguals' language skills. In a sample of 19 Italian-speaking bilingual children with different native languages, correlations among performance on an Italian-like NWR and receptive vocabulary score (Italian PPVT-R), cumulative exposure, age of first exposure to Italian, current Italian exposure, maternal education, parental concerns and vocabulary in toddlerhood (MB-CDI) were calculated. NWR performances correlated with PPVT-R and parental concerns, but not with maternal education and language exposure measures. Neither NWR scores nor PPVT-R scores were related to Italian vocabulary size in toddlerhood (MB-CDI). We integrate our results with those of others and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of administering NWR to bilingual children, and more generally how to perform early bilingual language assessments.

articles.title: Sensitivity to Prosody at 6 Months Predicts Vocabulary at 24 Months
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl
articles.abstract: Children’s language acquisition appears effortless, and advances enormously between the first word period, at about 12 months, to the stage at which complete and often complex sentences are produced, at about 3 years. However, this apparently miraculous process may in fact rely on knowledge that the child has began to accumulate even before birth. Indeed, work on infant speech perception in the last 40 years suggests that infants begin to attune to their native language during the first year of life.

articles.title: Ethical Considerations Around Surveillance Technologies for Suicide Prevention in Public Places: Bringing Together Staff and Lived/Living Experience Perspectives
articles.authors: Bethany Cliffe; Ian Marsh; Alex Dark; Andy Willis; Penny Phillips; Laura Joyner; Lisa Marzano; Keith Hawton; Carlisle George; Peter Craig
articles.abstract: This research brings together lived/living experience and professional stakeholder perspectives to explore ethical considerations around the use of surveillance technologies for suicide prevention in public places. The study employed qualitative interviews with people who have lived/living experience, focus groups with professional stakeholders, online ethnography of suicide discussion forums, and ethnography at public sites which have high rates of suicides. Framework analysis was used to interpret the interview and focus group data, which was then triangulated with ethnography notes to develop three themes: 1) Expectations around surveillance in public; 2) Experiences of surveillance: balancing harms with saving lives, and 3) Human response matters: experiences of intervention. Our findings show that surveillance technologies are typically associated more so with criminality than suicide, which can lead to anxieties around possible consequences of their use for suicide prevention. We also identified tensions between the pressures on staff to prevent suicides, through using surveillance technologies for example, versus the risk of causing harm in the process. Additionally, surveillance may detect someone in distress, but the prevention comes from the human intervention, which needs to prioritise empathy, retaining autonomy and ongoing care to support the individual. A key conclusion from this work is that surveillance technologies do not operate in isolation and so the broader context and systems should be considered to ensure that suicide prevention is done so in ways that are ethical and that aim to reduce harm.

articles.title: The psychological burden of “mild” aphasia: Greater associations with psychosocial well-being than with language severity
articles.authors: Deborah Levy; Kent Meinert; Katelyn Urena; Julianne M Alexander; Davida Fromm; Brian MacWhinney; Brielle C Stark
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Depression is common following stroke and neural injury, and individuals who develop aphasia—a language disorder—face an increased risk. However, people with aphasia are rarely assessed, referred, or treated for post-injury depression, an issue that may be further exacerbated in mild cases that lead to direct discharge home. Here, we examined the prevalence and correlates of depression in a cohort characterized, on average, by very mild or “latent” aphasia.  

Methods: Using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB), we investigated relationships between depression and aphasia in 79 individuals with and 73 individuals without aphasia. Subgroup analyses investigated (a) sentiment in response to the open-ended question “How do you think your speech is these days?” and (b) self-reported psychosocial quality of life (Stroke Aphasia Quality of Life; SAQOL-39). 

Results: Individuals with aphasia showed higher rates of depression than neurologically healthy peers. Depression severity did not relate to aphasia severity. However, depression severity did relate to (a) the emotional valence of participants’ descriptions of their speech, (b) younger age, and (c) poorer psychosocial quality of life.  

Conclusions: These findings indicate that depressive symptoms are elevated even among individuals with very mild aphasia, and are more closely associated with younger age, negative valence about speech, and poorer psychosocial quality of life than with objectively measured aphasia severity. This underscores the importance of assessing the lived impact of communication changes across the full spectrum of post-injury aphasia.

articles.title: Communicating causal effect heterogeneity
articles.authors: Matti Vuorre; Matthew Kay; Niall Bolger
articles.abstract: Advances in experimental, data collection, and analysis methods have brought population variability in psychological phenomena to the fore. Yet, current practices for interpreting such heterogeneity do not appropriately treat the uncertainty inevitable in any statistical summary. Heterogeneity is best thought of as a distribution of features with a mean (average person’s effect) and variance (between-person differences). This expected heterogeneity distribution can be further summarized e.g. as a heterogeneity interval (Bolger et al., 2019). However, because empirical studies estimate the underlying mean and variance parameters with uncertainty, the expected distribution and interval will underestimate the actual range of plausible effects in the population. Using Bayesian hierarchical models, and with the aid of empirical datasets from social and cognitive psychology, we provide a walk-through of effective heterogeneity reporting and display tools that appropriately convey measures of uncertainty. We cover interval, proportion, and ratio measures of heterogeneity and their estimation and interpretation. These tools can be a spur to theory building, allowing researchers to widen their focus from population averages to population heterogeneity in psychological phenomena.

articles.title: Conceptual combination as a window on representational format:  scope relations between “all” and “not” in combination with representations of “same.”
articles.authors: Jean-Rémy Hochmann; Rebecca Zhu; Susan Carey
articles.abstract: In Array Match to Sample (AMTS), participants are trained to sort arrays (e.g., of 16 items) containing  identical icons (16s) with other 16s arrays and arrays containing uniquely different icons (16d) with other 16d arrays.   This training is consistent with several different bases of sorting; 1) low entropy (variability) goes with low entropy, high entropy goes with high entropy, 2) match all same with all same, not all same with not all same; 3) match all same with all same, all not same with all not same, and 4) match all different with all different, not all different with not all different.  Testing with intermediate samples (i.e., 12s-4d, 8s-8d, 4s-12-d), keeping the choice cards the same (16s, 16d) probes the basis of each individual’s sorting behavior.  By age 4, more than ½ of humans sort by categorical rules 2 or 3 above, combining a representation of same with representations of all and not under one of two scope relations between all and not.  Animals and almost all 3-year-olds sort by entropy, an analog magnitude ensemble statistics, and animals cannot be taught to sort according to a criterion that combines all, not, and same as in 2 or 3 above.  No population sorts according to rule 4, combining “all,” “not” and “different.”.  Here we told participants a rule to follow; rule 2 in Experiments 1 and 2 and rule 4 in Experiment 3.  We found that the proportion of child participants sorting categorically matched the proportion of children who know the words “same” and “different”, and that telling children the rule increased sorting categorically at age 3, and increased sorting according to the stated rule in 4-year-olds and adults.  Both 4-year-olds and adults, equally and catastrophically, failed to follow rule 4 when instructed, instead sorting on the basis of the categorical distinction between all same and not all same.  We discuss the implications of these results for characterizing the development of the capacity to combine all and not under consistent scope relations, and for characterizing the formats of prelinguistic and linguistic representations of sameness and difference.

articles.title: Implementing an evidence-based 'identification-to-intervention' approach through school Mental Health Support Teams: A qualitative study of expected implementation determinants
articles.authors: Alice Rose Phillips; Rosie Underhill; Michael Larkin; Cathy Creswell; Rachel McGuire; Hollie Edwards; Catherine Gallop; Ian MacDonald; Falko Sniehotta; Tessa Reardon
articles.abstract:
Background: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent in childhood and are associated with academic and social difficulties. Although effective early interventions exist, many children do not access support due to complex referral routes and limited-service provision. ‘Identification-to-intervention’ (i2i) approaches address these barriers by combining universal screening with a targeted therapist-guided parent-led online intervention. In England, Mental Health Support Teams (MHSTs) deliver evidence-based interventions in schools so may be well-placed to implement i2i approaches. We lack understanding of factors which might influence implementation of i2i for child anxiety problems in a routine practice context. 

Method: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with MHST staff (n=16), primary school staff (n=6), and parents/carers (n=6) across England. Interviews were guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0)’s implementation determinants and analysed using template analysis. 

Findings: i2i was viewed as a simplified and accessible route to early mental health support. Participants identified barriers to parents/carers accessing i2i, including stigma-related concerns, literacy or language challenges, and limited familiarity with MHSTs. MHST staff felt i2i aligned with their remit and current skillset. Although some school and MHST staff viewed i2i as timesaving, others anticipated workload increases. Usual referral and clinical data management systems would need adjustment to allow direct contact from parents and the collection of screening data. 

Conclusions: i2i approaches are considered acceptable and appropriate across parents/carers, school staff and MHSTs, but structural barriers associated with MHSTs would need to be addressed to optimise implementation.

articles.title: They’re All Like That! The Universality Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: This paper investigates how humans store information within the thousands of concepts that structure thought, belief, and action. Building on recent work suggesting that each concept has a central form—a core representational structure that triggers strong beliefs when properties are encoded into it—this paper introduces and tests a new form-triggered belief: a default universality belief. Across two experiments, participants judged central form properties as universally true of all category members. They rejected this belief for properties that were highly prototypical or causally important, if they were not part of the concept's form. This effect held across both familiar and novel categories, and across domains including animals, artifacts, institutions, places, and events. These findings suggest a domain-general mechanism underlying universality judgments, with implications for theories of stereotyping, trauma, and ideology. More broadly, they help to explain how humans construct complex thoughts by reducing complex concepts down to a limited set of core properties, and they resolve a longstanding puzzle about why people assume universality despite its rarity in the natural world.

articles.title: Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0
articles.authors: Daniel Skorich
articles.abstract: Self-Categorization Theory is a theory of the way in which human beings come to represent themselves cognitively as group members. In this paper, I present 5 critiques of Self-Categorization Theory, with the goal of further refining it: (1) categorization into equivalence classes is neither sufficient nor necessary for perceiving groups as entities; (2) the boundary conditions on self-categorization (vs. categorization) are underspecified; (3) the person level is relatively underexamined; (4) meta-contrast is implausible as a basis for entity formation; and (5) comparative and correlational relations are overemphasized. I propose as resolutions to these critiques that: self-categorization is the categorization of intentional agents; groups are holistic entities, perceptually triggered by cues to collective intentionality, and cognitively represented as “conceptual atoms” with an associated object file; group phenomena have person equivalents and vice-versa; and relations between intentional entities and between intentional entities and their properties are represented propositionally in a “language of thought”. Taken together these resolutions result in an updated Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 (SCT2.0). I discuss this expanded theory in general terms, and then further elaborate on the key mechanisms of salience, depersonalization, and prototypicality. I conclude by emphasizing the way in which SCT2.0 builds on the legacy of its predecessor.

articles.title: Experienced vs. actual gaze reciprocity in repeated social interactions: A gateway toward social connectedness
articles.authors: Julian Gutzeit; Luise Hölting; Antonia Sophie van Duijn; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: In many contexts, direct gaze is regarded as a socially rewarding signal that promotes positive interpersonal evaluations, yet most evidence stems from single, in-the-moment judgments of briefly presented faces. Across three eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether repeated gaze-contingent interactions shape more enduring social evaluations. Participants repeatedly exchanged gaze with a few on-screen virtual partners who reciprocated their gaze with systematically different probabilities. Afterwards, participants estimated gaze reciprocity rates for each partner and completed several ratings (e.g., feelings of social connectedness, social agency). Notably, participants reliably distinguished between gaze reciprocity rates of interaction partners even when differences in actual gaze reciprocity were small and close to chance (40% vs. 60%), though estimates were compressed toward the middle of the range. Critically, while objective gaze reciprocity rates showed little consistent relation to social evaluations, subjectively perceived reciprocity rates were robustly associated with social connectedness and social agency across experiments. Additionally, some experiments pointed to associations with likability and trust (entrusted money in an economic Trust Game). However, these associations did not extend to implicit behavioral measures (free-choice gaze selection, gaze cueing). A pooled multilevel mediation analysis confirmed that objective gaze reciprocity rates predicted connectedness indirectly, via subjective perception. Together, these findings suggest that social evaluation is shaped more by the experience of being looked at than by objective gaze reciprocity itself, at least when gaze reciprocity levels are somewhat difficult to differentiate.

articles.title: FEED your mind: The evolutionary roots of human food cognition
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Raffaella I Rumiati; Annie E. Wertz; Carol Coricelli
articles.abstract: Research on food cognition has largely overlooked that our modern food environment strongly differs from the environment in which our ancestors lived. When foraging for food in wild environments, our ancestors had to distinguish edible food resources from myriad inedible and potentially toxic entities. In contrast, in most cultures today, many decisions about food are made during a trip to the grocery store or a meal at a restaurant, where we might ask ourselves: Is this item healthy? but certainly not: Is this item edible or poisonous? Here we argue that the scope of the problem humans faced with respect to food included navigating through wild environments to Find candidate food items, Excluding the costs of making a mistake and consuming a harmful food item, Evaluating the nutritional benefits of the potential foods and Deciding which food items to include in their diet. We call this the FEED problem and argue that it provides an organizing framework for thinking about the wide array of cognitive processes involved in human food psychology. The FEED problem can also be used as a generative theory to produce new testable empirical predictions about what cognitive mechanisms drive our modern food behaviors and provides a roadmap for future research in the field of food cognition.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of peer victimization on prosocial behavior in adolescents: A reanalysis of Guo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Guo et al., we reassessed the evidence supporting their mediation model relating peer victimization to lower levels of prosocial behavior among adolescents. We demonstrate that the empirical associations can be reproduced with high accuracy by an alternative latent-variable model that does not depend on the order of influence proposed in the original article. In this model, self-reported peer victimization, psychological capital, empathy, and prosocial behavior are conceptualized as indicators of a broader latent construct, namely core self-evaluation. The findings illustrate a fundamental issue in observational research: different theoretical models may account equally well for the same covariance structure. Consequently, correlational data alone provide limited grounds for favoring one specific explanatory mechanism over competing alternatives. Consequently, researchers should consider alternative specifications before drawing strong conclusions about underlying processes.

articles.title: The Long Shadow of the Wall: Socialization Signatures in Public-Events Knowledge Across East and West Germany
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract: Germany’s division and subsequent reunification provide a rare historical possibility to examine how regionally segregated information environments are reflected in what people know and how long such differences persist. In a national sample of 1,012 German adults aged 30–80 years, participants completed a 120-item multiple-choice test of public-events knowledge spanning 1960–2019, including items specifically targeting East- and West-German events from the pre-1990 period. While overall knowledge levels were similar among East- and West-socialized respondents, the item-level differences were pronounced, especially for East-specific items in pop culture, arts and literature. Nested cross-validated elastic-net models yielded near-perfect discrimination between East and West socialization in older cohorts (ages 51–80; AUCs > .96), slightly lower discrimination among ages 41–50 (AUC = .93), and a sharp drop in the youngest cohort (ages 30–40; AUC = .67). East-specific items contributed most strongly to classification, which is consistent with the concept of cultural hegemony and an asymmetric information flow. Despite post-1990 convergence, persistent geographic patterns in knowledge profiles remain. Public-events knowledge thus carries a cohort-dependent socialization signature, leaving detectable traces of historical division even after societal convergence.

articles.title: What motivates support for mandatory vaccination? Trust as a moderator of relations between personal values and support for coercive policy measures
articles.authors: Joshua Lake; Uwana Evers; Katie Attwell
articles.abstract: Public debates about vaccination mandates often pit collective welfare against individual autonomy, yet little is known about how personal values relate to mandate support. In late 2025/early 2026 we surveyed adults in Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973); personal values were measured with the Best-Worst Refined Values scale; vaccination trust with the Vaccination Trust Indicator; and attitudes toward mandatory vaccination with the Vaccination Mandate Attitudes Scale. We examined value-attitude relations by country for each of the 10 basic personal values, and the role of trust as a moderator. Vaccination trust moderated associations between values and mandate attitudes for 8/10 values in Australia, and 9/10 values in France and Italy. Across countries, when vaccination trust was high, growth oriented values (benevolence; universalism; self direction) and security values, were associated with increased mandate support, however when trust was low, they were associated with reduced support. Self enhancement values (achievement; power) and tradition values generally showed the opposite pattern of effects, while conformity values displayed a relatively stronger (positive) direct effect. Findings identify vaccination trust as a moderating factor in the attitudinal expression of value priorities, suggesting that future research on policy design and communication should examine how trust and value-congruent framing jointly shape public acceptability.

articles.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. We conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. Fourteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. The recruitment target (N=25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. Acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. Two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. Exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 52% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. Our pilot study indicates that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial.

articles.title: Infant-directed songs as a source of language input: Do infants segment words from playsongs?
articles.authors: Arina Shandala; Eniko Ladanyi; Mridula Sharma; Natalie Boll-Avetisyan
articles.abstract: Singing is an important communicative feature in caregiver-infant interaction that potentially provides infants with linguistic information. Nonetheless, little is known about how infants process words in songs. Therefore, the present study investigated infants’ ability to segment words from playsongs. German-learning 8-9- and 11-12-month-olds (n = 67, 43% female, 57% male) were familiarized with playsongs containing repetitions of a pseudoword. Subsequently, their word recognition was tested by measuring their looking behavior while listening to spoken familiar and novel pseudowords. Results revealed a significant listening preference for novel over familiar pseudowords in 11-12-month-olds, indicating their ability to segment pseudowords encountered in playsongs (β = -0.14, p = .014). In 8-9-month-olds, no group-level evidence for a preference was detected. Exploratory analyses of music-related questionnaires revealed no links with task performance. Our results provide the first findings that by their first birthday, infants are able to segment words from playsongs, a song genre whose value for learning is commonly assumed but has rarely been studied empirically.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Equivalence Testing with the Updated TOSTER R Package
articles_hidden.authors: Aaron R Caldwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of methodological guidance, researchers continue to misinterpret non-significant results as evidence for the absence of an effect. Equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST) provides a principled alternative, but adoption remains limited by software accessibility and lack of training. The TOSTER R package, originally developed by Lakens (2017), made TOST accessible to experimental psychologists. This paper describes a major update to the package that expands its scope with (1) a unified t-test interface supporting both equivalence and minimal effect testing, (2) a simplified hypothesis testing interface returning standard R objects, (3) tools for computing and testing standardized effect sizes and correlations, (4) robust and resampling-based alternatives including bootstrap and permutation tests, (5) equivalence testing for ANOVAs, and (6) power analysis and sample size planning. Each capability is demonstrated with worked examples. TOSTER is also available as a jamovi module for researchers who prefer a graphical interface.

articles_hidden.title: Cox versus Discrete-Time Models in Behavioral Research: A Simulation Study of Predictive Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Hyungjun Park; Mike W.-L. Cheung
articles_hidden.abstract: The Cox proportional-hazards model is the standard for survival prediction, although discrete-time models are often recommended as an alternative in behavioral research. Discrete-time models theoretically handle the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events better, but whether this theoretical advantage translates to better predictions under behavioral-research conditions has not been systematically tested. The present study compared six survival prediction models (Cox, elastic-net Cox, gradient-boosted Cox, random survival forest, logistic hazards, and multi-task logistic regression) via simulation under all combinations of sample size, number of time points, event rate, and hazard distribution. Each model's predictive performance was evaluated by the concordance index, mean absolute error, and integrated Brier score. Results on the concordance index and mean absolute error were broadly comparable across all six models in every condition tested. Results on the integrated Brier score showed that the Cox-family models consistently performed worse than the discrete-time models and random survival forest, although this was attributed to how the Cox-family models estimate baseline hazards, not how they handle the proportional-hazards assumption or tied events. Overall, concerns about the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events overstate the case against the Cox model. The Cox model remains a reasonable default for prediction, with discrete-time alternatives favored when probabilistic calibration matters; whether the calibration advantage is substantial enough to justify the additional implementation effort remains unclear. Possible directions for future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A scoping review of community engagement and implementation outcomes for approaches  to adapt mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Tschida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth are commonly adapted for use in community-based settings and, more increasingly, with community-engaged  research methods (Stahmer et al., 2005). However, it is unknown which adaptation method, including what level of community engagement, may be most effective and feasible for (1) enhancing the fit of mental and behavioral health EBPs with autistic client needs in a community 
service context and, (2) improving implementation and intervention outcomes (Dickson et al., 2021). Using the Model for Adaptation Design and Impact (MADI; Kirk et al., 2020) and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research (Key et al., 2019), this scoping review aimed to fill this research gap by assessing approaches to adapt mental and behavioral health EBPs for autistic youth served in community-based settings from existing literature. Data sources included PsycInfo, PubMed, and Web of Science. Article eligibility criteria included (a) reported in English, (b) describes EBP adaptation, (c) includes children with autism spectrum diagnoses and/or their caregivers, and (d) considers community-based mental and behavioral health settings. Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines, an initial literature search (n = 349) was followed by title and abstract screening (n = 230), full text review (n = 121), and data charting and analysis (n = 37). Frequencies were obtained for MADI and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research domains reported and assessed across studies. Qualitative content analysis also was used to yield more nuanced descriptions of each adaptation approach and related context, feasibility, and empirical support (Graneheim & Lundman, 2004). Context 
surrounding adaptation, common factors for feasible and effective adaptation methods, and two effective and feasible exemplar methods to were identified. Overall, this scoping review contributes to science found at the intersection of autism research, implementation science, and community-engaged research. Further, it has the potential to inform and improve efforts to adapt and implement EBPs in community-based settings and consequently improve wellbeing among 
autistic youth and their families.

articles_hidden.title: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation as a tool to causally modulate the human hippocampus
articles_hidden.authors: Craig McFarland; Miriam Klein-Flugge; Helen Barron; Valentina Mancini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Non-invasive brain stimulation has, until recently, had limited effect on deep brain circuits critical for memory. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising tool to address this limitation. By delivering spatially focused acoustic energy, TUS enables targeted modulation of deep brain structures such as the hippocampus. TUS therefore provides new opportunities to causally modulate activity in neural circuits important for memory.
Objective: This perspective discusses how TUS provides a potential methodological advance for human memory research, examining the mechanistic basis of the technology, emerging empirical evidence, and outstanding interpretative and technical limitations.
Methods: We synthesise human and animal TUS studies targeting hippocampal and other memory-relevant circuits, compare TUS with alternative brain stimulation approaches and discuss potential clinical applications for TUS in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and medial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE).
Results: TUS provides a tool to modulate activity in deep circuits that have been inaccessible to other forms of non-invasive brain stimulation. Human TUS studies to date document changes in neurochemistry, functional connectivity, and memory-relevant behaviour. Moreover, clinical studies in AD and mTLE report memory improvement and seizure reduction, respectively. To guide future work, we outline five critical considerations: uncertain directionality of effects, individual differences in delivered acoustic dose, state-dependence of outcomes, evidence of lasting synaptic modification, and standardisation of protocols.
Conclusions: TUS holds promise for studying and enhancing human memory. Realising this potential will require concurrent neuroimaging or electrophysiology to verify target engagement, and close attention to individual differences in dose and brain state, together with cross-laboratory standardisation.

articles_hidden.title: Shared Dimensions, Divergent Patterns: Multidimensional Well-Being Among Cultural Majority and Minoritized Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Jozefien De Leersnyder
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents adapt constantly to their social environments, which can support certain functions while limiting others. In intercultural contexts, adolescents share institutions but hold different social positions and cultural references. Consequently, similar overall well-being scores can mask entirely different combinations of health, relationships, and material conditions—a limitation of single total scores. Well-being and acculturation research approach this problem differently. Well-being research provides broad theories but typically focuses on global indicators within Western majority samples, while acculturation research studies adaptation in intercultural contexts but primarily examines minorities and separates psychological adjustment from sociocultural competence. Researchers currently lack a common multidimensional framework to capture well-being variations among adolescents sharing an intercultural environment. We addressed this gap in 1,385 Belgian-majority and Turkish–Moroccan minoritized adolescents using exploratory and multigroup factor analyses, which supported a broadly comparable five-domain structure. This demonstrates that a common framework can apply across groups while accommodating meaningful differences in how well-being is experienced and organized. Item-level differences formed a mixed profile rather than a consistent advantage for either group. Cross-sectional Gaussian graphical models revealed differences in overall edge-weight structure and global strength, with greater aggregate connectivity in the Turkish–Moroccan network, though no individual edge difference survived correction. Across both groups, the strongest associations clustered within domains alongside cross-domain links. These findings suggest that adolescent well-being is better understood as a multidimensional system than as a single score: shared dimensions can coexist with different profiles and relational organization. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these patterns reflect contextual conditions, cultural orientations, or their interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Fetching a Problem's Solution from a Computer Does Not Lead to an Impoverished Affective Footprint
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Johannes Bernau; Wilfried Kunde
articles_hidden.abstract: Problem solving relies on purely internal processing (IP) or extended processing (EP) which additionally draws on external resources like computerized equipment. IP can initially cause negative affect due to effort or cognitive conflict, followed by positive affect after success. Such affective dynamics matter as they influence learning, well-being, and cognitive control. Yet, little is known about affect in EP, which this study examined. Participants solved alpha-numeric problems (is “D+4=I” correct?). IP required mentally counting up letters from “D”, while EP involved revealing the correct answer (“H”) by hovering a cursor over a box. Affect was measured using affective priming (Experiment 1), facial muscle activity (Experiment 2), and explicit ratings. We hypothesized that IP produces more negative affect during problem solving but more positive affect afterwards compared to EP. Results provided little support for such a general claim. Affective priming suggests that IP-related operations like matching men-tal representations to sensory input can indeed cause positive affect, which can however also be part of EP. Facial muscle data indicated broadly comparable affective dynamics between IP and EP. These results add an affective spin to the cognitive impartiality hypotheses (Clark 2011), which suggests that neither IP nor EP is privileged by problem solvers.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring cultural and individual differences in the hierarchy of moral concern: Evidence from student samples across 41 cultural groups
articles_hidden.authors: Işıl Ayça Akkuş; Charlie R Crimston; Kelly Kirkland; Brock Bastian; Bastian Jaeger
articles_hidden.abstract: Disagreement about the rights and protections owed to different individuals underpins many important historical and current debates (e.g., on the abolishment of slavery, the feminist movement, abortion, and environmental protection). Recent work on moral concern (i.e., the subjectively felt moral obligation to consider an individual’s welfare and interests) has uncovered a seemingly robust hierarchy.
