Comparing decision sequences in groups with a solo baseline, complemented with agent-based simulations, showed that this strategy gave rise to mild information cascades, with decisions in groups being more similar to each other than in a solo baseline. Our results reveal how social influence shapes search, stopping, and choice, and how these individual-level decision rules scale up to collective dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: The context-dependent evolution of structure learning and metacognition
articles_hidden.authors: Rochelle Kaper; Megan A. K. Peters
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans learn multiple probabilistic regularities at once, and often without feedback, which may be aided by metacognitive evaluations throughout learning. To understand this learning-metacognition relationship, we must first characterize how both capacities co-evolve as environmental structures are internalized, especially when feedback is unavailable. Here, participants learned a two-level probabilistic environment in which stimulus co-occurrences were embedded within a sequence, using unfamiliar fractals and familiar line drawings in a two-session, within-subjects design (N=63; N=50 completed both sessions). For each stimulus set, we measured learning across six repeating exposure-test cycles, using a cover task during exposure phases and forced-choice questions in test phases; test questions also included confidence judgments. Results revealed stimulus- and structure-dependent learning and metacognitive signatures. First, learning dynamics differed across stimuli: fractal sequence test accuracy outpaced co-occurrence accuracy, but vice versa for line drawings. Further, confidence increased across blocks, and was higher for line drawings as well as co-occurrences and first but not second sequence selections. Finally, both metacognitive sensitivity and test accuracy increased in successive exposure-test cycles for fractals, but metacognitive sensitivity remained stagnant for line drawings even as test accuracy improved. These results demonstrate that structure learning and metacognitive processes are highly context- and complexity-dependent rather than being completely generalizable. This study informs future directions for refining theories of learning without feedback, including how people evaluate their own learning and uncertainty and the interaction of both cognitive abilities with task design, stimuli, and environmental structures.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating science and design in the development of Detour: A mobile intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles_hidden.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Maartje Luijten; Ken Koontz; Hanneke Scholten
articles_hidden.abstract: Digital smoking cessation interventions for adolescents and young adults (AYAs) often either lack a strong evidence base or fail to engage their intended users. Integrating psychological science with design-based methods offers a promising route to interventions, yet the processes behind such integration are rarely reported in detail. In this paper, we describe the development of Detour, a mobile smoking cessation intervention for AYAs, redesigned from an earlier app (HitnRun) using the Bloombox Toolkit to integrate science and design throughout. We describe how six psychological mechanisms including smoking cue devaluation and delay discounting were translated into intervention components. We used an iterative, interdisciplinary process involving behavioural scientists, app designers, and an ongoing youth advisory board. Additionally, we included over 380 AYAs across focus groups, play tests, and qualitative questionnaires. We then reflect on our experience integrating design and science for intervention development and share practical challenges encountered, including budgeting for interdisciplinary teams, retaining youth participants, and regulatory delays. By reporting these processes and challenges transparently, we aim to support other researchers in designing digital health interventions that are both scientifically grounded and engaging for their target users.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial biases in Arithmetic: The Effect of Operation Order and Visual Spacing on Calculations
articles_hidden.authors: Martyna Sroka; Michał Obidziński; Krzysztof Cipora; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual layout is known to affect computational performance, yet its relation to response format and numerical proficiency remains unclear. This preregistered study examined whether spatial presentation modulates arithmetic problem-solving. We conceptually replicated Experiment 3 of Landy and Goldstone's (2010) study using the Precedence and Proximity Task in a forced-choice format. Additionally, we assessed arithmetic fluency using a speeded test. A total of 201 adults solved 200 mixed addition–multiplication expressions in which spacing either aligned or conflicted with order-of-operations rules. Operation order was also manipulated. Participants were faster and more accurate in congruent spacing conditions, whereas incongruent spacing increased operation-order errors, especially when problems began with addition. A subgroup of participants showed disproportionately poor performance under incongruent spacing, suggesting a prepotent susceptibility to misleading grouping cues. The spacing effect persisted despite differences in task format and response procedure compared to the original study, supporting its robustness. Higher arithmetic fluency was associated with higher accuracy and shorter reaction times in the Precedence and Proximity Task. These findings corroborate that visuospatial layout biases symbolic computation and that individuals differ in their susceptibility to it.

articles_hidden.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles_hidden.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles_hidden.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Apples to apples: Stability and flexibility trade off only when measured at the same processing level.
articles_hidden.authors: Luca Moretti; Iring Koch; Tobias Egner
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive stability and cognitive flexibility are two crucial abilities supporting goal-directed behaviour. While cognitive stability designates our ability to maintain task-relevant information and shield it against distraction, flexibility allows to choose which information constitutes the task focus. Because of their complementary role, it has long been assumed that cognitive stability and flexibility are inversely related, such that promoting stability should impair flexibility, and vice versa. Recently however, a series of task-switching experiments have failed to observe such a mandatory trade-off, prompting a lively debate on the stability-flexibility relationship. In the present study, we aim to reconcile these findings with the trade-off view, by testing whether the stability and flexibility trade-off depends on the operationalization of these constructs. While previous studies gauged stability via the congruency effect and flexibility via task-switch costs, we here additionally measured cognitive stability via the valency effect. While the congruency effect indexes cross-task interference at the level of response selection, the valency effect is thought to reflect such interference at the level of task selection, which may more closely align with task-switching. Across three experiments and a re-analysis, we provide consistent evidence that manipulations reducing task switch cost increase the valency effect (and vice versa), but do not modulate the congruency effect. These findings suggest that stability and flexibility do trade off, but only when measured at the same level of processing (here, the task-selection level). We discuss the possible reasons why trade-offs may be level-specific, and future approaches to further investigate the stability-flexibility relationship.

articles_hidden.title: Normative and Maladaptive Personality Traits in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative and Hierarchical Analysis of HEXACO and PID-5
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Weiß; Johanna Hepp; Katja Isabell Seitz; Yun-Loe Laura Lai; Nikolaus Kleindienst; Sylvia Steinmann; Katja Bertsch; Inga Niedtfeld
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of personality pathology invite the question of how normative and maladaptive trait systems jointly characterize borderline personality disorder (BPD). This study examined how the HEXACO model of personality and the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders trait system, operationalized with the Personality Inventory for DSM–5, differentiate individuals with BPD from mentally healthy control (HC) individuals, both separately and jointly.
Methods: Data from two assessment waves of a large clinical research program were combined into a final sample of 575 participants (233 with BPD, 342 HC). A joint item-level PCA was conducted to examine seven- and eleven-component solutions, and a Bass-Ackwards principal components analysis was conducted to examine the joint hierarchical structure of HEXACO and PID-5 items. Both instruments were administered as self-reports. 
Results: Compared with HC, individuals with BPD showed lower HEXACO Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness, and higher Emotionality, as well as higher scores on all PID-5 domains, particularly Negative Affectivity and Disinhibition. In the combined domain model, low Extraversion and high  PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism uniquely predicted BPD status. At the facet level, low Social Self-Esteem (HEXACO) and high Emotional Lability (PID-5) were especially discriminative. Joint item analyses yielded a sevencomponent solution in which six components corresponded closely to the six HEXACO factors and a dominant seventh component represented broad maladaptivity, with PID-5 items loading positively and HEXACO items largely loading inversely. Group differences were almost entirely confined to this broad component. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that BPD is characterized by both a broad maladaptivity dimension and a more specific trait profile involving affective instability, interpersonal insecurity, irritability, and reduced behavioral control. The findings support integrating normative and maladaptive trait models in  the dimensional description of BPD, while indicating that the dominant joint dimension cannot be interpreted unambiguously as a substantive general factor of personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: Translation and Validation of the Japanese version of the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (J-APEQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto; Shuhei Iimura
articles_hidden.abstract: Picky eating is a multidimensional eating behavior that has been studied primarily in children, although it is also observed in adults. The Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ) was developed to assess multiple dimensions of picky eating in adults, but a validated Japanese version has not been available. The present study aimed to develop and validate a Japanese version of the APEQ (J-APEQ) (Researcher-led translation) and to compare it with a translation generated using generative artificial intelligence (AI-generated translation). The researcher-led translation was completed by 892 Japanese adults, with 210 participants completing the scale again after three weeks. A separate sample of 939 participants completed an AI-generated translation. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original four-factor structure of the researcher-led J-APEQ, and a second-order factor model also showed acceptable fit. The composite score showed adequate internal consistency, while reliability was lower for some subscales, particularly Meal Disengagement and Taste Aversion. Test–retest reliability was moderate, and correlations with food neophobia, disgust, and eating-attitude measures generally supported convergent validity. The AI-generated translation showed a factor structure and reliability broadly comparable to those of the researcher-led translation. Measurement invariance analyses supported configural, threshold, metric, and partial scalar invariance between the two versions. In the present study, however, the researcher-led translation was the version formally validated and established as the Japanese APEQ (J-APEQ), whereas the AI-generated translation was included for comparison. These findings support the use of the J-APEQ for assessing picky eating in Japanese adults and suggest that generative AI may be useful as a tool for psychological scale translation, although human review and validation remain necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Memory reactivation levels remain unaffected by anticipated interference
articles_hidden.authors: Nursena Ataseven; I. Efsane Algın; Duygu Yucel; Berna Güler; Lara Todorova; Keisuke Fukuda; Eren Gunseli
articles_hidden.abstract: Most daily tasks require frequent information exchange between working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM). However, the factors that modulate the reactivation of LTMs in WM remain to be explored. Here, we tested the effects of anticipated perceptual interference (in Experiment 1) and anticipated dual task interference (in Experiment 2) on reactivation of LTMs in WM using contralateral delay activity (CDA) in the EEG. On each trial, participants saw one or three previously studied or novel objects that were tested after a brief retention interval. In half of the blocks, the retention contained perceptual distractors (Experiment 1) or dual task interference (Experiment 2). In both experiments, the CDA prior to the interference period was similar regardless of the anticipated interference. Additionally, we measured contralateral alpha power suppression as an index of spatial attention. We found that spatial attention allocated to the memorized objects’ locations also was not modulated with anticipated interference. These findings indicate that anticipating interference does not influence the extent to which WM is engaged in representing information stored in LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Healthy attachment for the parents? An investigation on the association between attachment parenting and parental mental health.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Hanna Laura Meder; Mira-Pauline Grapentin; Nora Imlau
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. Attachment parenting (AP) became popular for it promotes responsive caregiving, but has been criticized for over-extensively translating attachment research into challenging parenting standards, mirroring detrimental intensive-parenting beliefs that adversely affect parental health. Meanwhile, evidence on AP remains limited and assessments of AP-beliefs and AP-practice are lacking. This study aims to develop and validate an AP-questionnaire and test the associations between AP and parental mental health and explore the mediating role of intensive-parenting beliefs.
Methods. In a preregistered cross-sectional online-survey, 1664 parents (98.5% mothers) of children aged up to six years answered an extensive item-list assessing AP-beliefs and AP implementation into practice, an intensive parenting questionnaire, and mental health measures. Confirmatory factor analyses were used for AP-questionnaire validation and correlation- and mediation-analyses for exploring the association between AP and mental health.
Results. A 26-item AP-questionnaire was extracted that assesses AP-beliefs and AP- practice, both for the global AP-approach and seven individual core-principles. AP-indicators consistently showed small/minimal correlations with better mental health, whereas mediation analyses revealed parallel, opposing pathways: a positive, direct association from AP to mental health (possibly explained via parental fulfilment) and adverse indirect pathways through intensive-parenting beliefs (challenge-/self-sacrifice and essentialist-beliefs).
Conclusion. AP may be neither uniformly beneficial nor harmful. Rather, it can foster parental fulfilment which increases parental well-being, but also instil dysfunctional beliefs about sacrifice and unavoidable strain that increase parental-stress. To improve evidence-based personalized parenting-recommendations, longitudinal research is needed to disentangle when AP fosters positive parental identity and when it reinforces parental vulnerabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Human outcome-irrelevant value learning is insensitive to its monetary cost
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: When learning from reinforcement, individuals should assign credit selectively to features of their actions that causally determine outcomes. Yet, even when explicit instructions and extensive experience clarify which action features predict reward, humans assign credit to outcome-irrelevant features, leading to suboptimal choices. Here, we use computational modeling to test if this suboptimal credit assignment can be controlled depending on the monetary cost at stake. Specifically, we tested whether higher payoffs can increase control over outcome-irrelevant credit assignment. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task under low and high monetary stakes. Higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but, strikingly, had no influence on outcome-irrelevant values, which influenced choices to a similar degree. These findings demonstrate the automatic nature of credit assignment to outcome-irrelevant features, suggesting that associations between features and reward are formed despite clear instructions and their detrimental consequences for monetary gains.

articles_hidden.title: Selective reproduction of spatial–emotional mappings in large language models
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Fumiya Yonemitsu; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: The vertical-valence metaphor refers to the association between emotional valence and vertical space, whereby positive and negative emotions are linked to upward and downward directions, respectively. While this mapping has been robustly observed in human cognition, it remains unclear whether such associations are also reproduced in artificial intelligence systems. The present study investigated the vertical-valence metaphor in ChatGPT. In Experiments 1–3, ChatGPT-4 showed a consistent pattern in which “up” was evaluated more positively than “down,” and emotional words were spatially organized such that “joy” was placed above “sadness,” with “surprise” positioned in between. This pattern persisted even when the coordinate system was reversed. In Experiments 4–6, we compared silicon and human samples and observed a more nuanced pattern. While the vertical-valence mapping was largely preserved across both groups, the intermediate positioning of “surprise” was not consistently reproduced in ChatGPT-5.2. An additional pilot experiment indicates that this reduction in differentiation may be influenced by prompt language, although the relative contributions of model characteristics and language could not be determined. Exploratory analyses revealed that the horizontal-valence metaphor showed less consistent patterns across all the experiments, indicating lower robustness. Taken together, these findings suggest that large language models do not uniformly reproduce human cognitive mappings but instead exhibit a graded pattern of representation. Robust mappings are preserved, whereas intermediate or weaker mappings may be compressed or destabilized.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles_hidden.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles_hidden.title: Physical endpoint contact enhances visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback in virtual reality
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan George King; Guy Wallis
articles_hidden.abstract: When reaching for a visually defined target, sensory information not only guides the preparation and execution of the reaching response but also serves as a crucial source of error feedback. Research on visually guided reaching has typically emphasised the contribution of visual feedback to movement preparation and execution.  However, visually guided reaching also depends on non-visual sensory information. Here, we focus on the role of haptic endpoint feedback and visual hand feedback and how they interact to regulate behaviour. Thirty-six participants completed a rapid reaching task using a virtual reality head-mounted display, allowing us to manipulate endpoint haptic feedback and visual feedback of the moving hand. Participants completed a vibrotactile feedback condition, providing vibration feedback to the fingertip upon target touch, and a vibrotactile and physical contact feedback condition, providing additional physical surface contact. On 25% of trials, the virtual hand disappeared after movement initiation. The addition of physical contact led participants to initiate movement earlier, increase movement times, and spend proportionally more time decelerating, resulting in improved endpoint accuracy. Across kinematic measures, the effects of physical contact did not interact with visual hand feedback. Additionally, of six presence and embodiment items, only the item asking whether touch felt like one's own differed between conditions. Overall, these findings suggest physical contact improves visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback alone. However, this advantage appears to be selective, increasing the realism of touch rather than overall presence or embodiment and not compensating for a loss of visual feedback of the hand.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles_hidden.title: The Unified Model Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Hsiu Ting Ting Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists describe their statistical models with diagrams. The conventions in use, path diagrams, multilevel panels, plate notation, and causal graphs, each grew inside one modeling tradition, and they disagree on basic symbols. As a result, one figure can stand for two different models. An ellipse with three arrows can show a factor model or a latent profile model. A labeled arrow can show a fixed slope or a person-varying slope. A mediation triangle can show a regression decomposition or a causal claim. This article introduces the Unified Model Graph (UMG), a notation built so that the figure identifies the model that was fitted. Three visual cues type every quantity: fill for observed versus latent, shape for continuous versus categorical, and outline for inferential role. Four edge types separate regression, covariance, deterministic, and mixture relations. Plates mark replication, and a badge states whether the figure makes a causal claim. Every well-formed UMG corresponds to exactly one family of distributions, and path diagrams, plate notation, and causal graphs are special cases; the formal results and proofs are in the supplemental material. The accompanying R package \pkg{} builds diagrams from code or from fitted lavaan, lme4, mirt, and brms objects, validates them, translates them to and from lavaan syntax, checks necessary identification conditions, derives testable implications, and generates model-implied data displays. A benchmark of eight R diagramming packages on ten representational features and ten operations locates what the notation adds. All materials, scripts, and outputs are openly archived.

articles_hidden.title: The Liege Mind-Blanking Scale: a comprehensive scale to assess the heterogeneity of mind-blanking cognitive and experiential aspects
articles_hidden.authors: Paradeisios Alexandros Boulakis; Marion Balla; Agustina Aragón-Daud; David Stawarczyk; Giovanni Briganti; Athena Demertzi; Steve Majerus
articles_hidden.abstract: Our minds are not always full of thoughts. Occasionally, people will report absence of any mental content, an experience termed mind-blanking (MB). So far, MB has been primarily quantified through experience-sampling paradigms. While experience-sampling has allowed researchers to study the behavioural and neurophysiological profile of MB, the practice of asking participants for thought categories, such as “an empty mind”, might undermine the richness and diversity of MB instances. In the present study, we adopted a self-reported, trait approach to MB. We developed a novel MB scale, the Liege Mind-Blanking Scale (L-MBS), with the aim to probe distinct types of MB experiences and relate them to different cognitive functions. A sample of 644 participants completed the L-MBS alongside a cohort of self-report questionnaires measuring trait mind-wandering, attention, memory, metacognition and arousal. The L-MBS showed adequate psychometric properties. Factor analysis validated the presence of 3 discrete factors: one related to the perceived experience of MB, one related to memory failures, and one related to blanking under pressure. Network analysis linked these factors to discrete cognitive domains. The experience of blanking correlated with metacognitive monitoring, while memory failures were associated with autobiographical memory difficulties. Overall, the L-MBS provides a quick, accessible and psychometrically validated measure of an individual’s beliefs about their blank experiences. At the same time, the presence of multiple MB factors suggests that MB is not necessarily a unitary phenomenon and most likely represents a clustering of different moments of no content.

articles_hidden.title: Learning from others’ mistakes: differential effects of observing target errors versus adaptation errors
articles_hidden.authors: Beverley Larssen; Anthony Sze; Ryan Jin; Sarah N Kraeutner; Nicola Jane Hodges
articles_hidden.abstract: How we learn from observing others perform reaching tasks is debated in the adaptation literature. When observers see a hand intentionally miss a target to correctly counteract rotated visual feedback (adaptation error), after-effects are typically absent. In contrast, observing consistent target errors, has resulted in unintended compensatory after-effects. The type of observed “error” (adaptation versus target error) may therefore have different effects on observation-induced behaviour, although this has not been tested within the same experiment. We compared participants in a four-group orthogonal design, who saw a model hit or miss a target, with or without rotated cursor feedback. Small compensatory after-effects (pre- to post-test) were seen when reaching to perceived midline in groups that observed target errors (misses). However, there were also small imitative after-effects after observing adaptation errors without target errors, but only when reaching to visual targets. Observing adaptation errors with or without target misses aided later performance in the same rotated environment and was accompanied by explicit knowledge of the rotation. Knowing the task goal is relevant information for eliciting small compensatory aiming biases in observers, perhaps because target errors matter more than adaptation errors when observing, leading to an unintended resolution not needed for “correct” actions.

articles_hidden.title: Time pressure modulates resource-rational planning in online chess
articles_hidden.authors: Ionatan Kuperwajs; Evan Russek; Lisa Schut; Yotam Sagiv; Wei Ji Ma; Tom Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Human planning is incredibly efficient. Even in complex situations with many possible courses of action, people are able to make good decisions. Recent proposals suggest that a primary contributor to this efficiency is the intelligent use of cognitive resources, but how people allocate these resources under time constraints is not fully understood. In this work, we conduct a resource-rational analysis of planning in a large data set of online chess games. We first demonstrate that players spent more time thinking when they had more time to do so, and that this effect was especially prevalent when computation was more valuable. Then, we show that additional time spent planning resulted in better selected moves when one existed, and highlight the role of expertise in this setting. Finally, we scale our analysis by showing that changes in move time, move quality, and move entropy as a function of time control setting correlate across board positions. Our results provide evidence that people make resource-rational choices when planning under time pressure.

articles_hidden.title: Hypothesis Spaces: How Structural Beliefs Shape Uncertainty in the Anxious Mind
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Benita Senfft; Ondrej Zika
articles_hidden.abstract: While uncertainty is ubiquitous, not all uncertainty is the same. In this review, we dissociate between uncertainty in aspects of known problem spaces (e.g. how long are hospital waiting times; “parameter uncertainty”) and uncertainty arising from unknown structure or even the nature of a problem (e.g. how do I get medical help in a new country; “structural uncertainty”). We suggest that much everyday uncertainty is structural: uncertainty about which model of the world applies in the first place. We bring research on uncertainty and structure learning together through the concept of hypothesis spaces - sets of candidate generative structures that an individual considers plausible, together with distribution of beliefs over their likelihood. We propose that properties of these spaces, including their size, complexity and entropy, provide a systematic framework for understanding structural uncertainty and may help explain characteristic features of anxious thought such as worry, overthinking, catastrophizing and overgeneralization. This perspective also offers a way to refine broad constructs such as intolerance of uncertainty by linking them to specific representational and inferential processes and their properties. We suggest that revisiting the role of uncertainty in anxiety from the viewpoint of structural inference holds the key for mechanistic understanding of clinical observations and closer alignment with fundamental research in cognitive neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Educator Preparedness in Navigating Inclusive Education and Sensory Differences in Autism: Quantitative Exploration in Ontario, Canada
articles_hidden.authors: Stephanie Larmer; Gabrielle Czichrak; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Ontario, Canada follows an inclusive education model, however, little is known about the current status of the education of autistic students in this model. Specifically, educators are a crucial component of successful inclusive education in autism, yet there is a dearth of research exploring which educator characteristics and experiences are relevant to successful inclusive education in autism, and whether educator needs are being met. We aimed to explore existing gaps through an online questionnaire evaluating educators’ and pre-service educators’ experience, self-efficacy, and knowledge of autism, both in general and sensory processing, which is particularly relevant in educational settings. Additionally, we explored educators’ needs related to autism and educating autistic students. The results revealed experience, specifically number of autistic students, contributed to greater self-efficacy in educating autistic students. Furthermore, there was a significant impact of professional development in autism on self-efficacy in educating autistic students and a near-unanimous desire for more professional development in autism, underlining the need for more professional development in autism to build valuable qualities in educators and pre-service educators. Also, there was a significant difference and relationship between general and sensory processing knowledge of autism, where general knowledge was greater and predictive of sensory processing knowledge, suggesting professional development should explore more specific components of autism, especially one so relevant at school, and be scaffolding. This research provides decision makers with updated evidence that can guide professional development design and policies related to inclusive education in autism to make improvements that benefit both educators and autistic students.

articles_hidden.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles_hidden.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles_hidden.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles_hidden.title: Blending Sources of Evidence: Meta-Analysis Combining Aggregated Data and Individual Participant Data from Multilab Replications
articles_hidden.authors: Jingru Zhang; James E Pustejovsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional meta-analyses synthesize average treatment effects from sample-level aggregated data (AD) and are limited to addressing questions of moderation only at the sample level. Although associations between study-mean covariates and effect sizes need not reflect individual-level relations, individual-level moderating effects can be investigated using individual participant data (IPD). Multilab replication projects have recently made large, preregistered IPD collections publicly available for effects also synthesized in conventional meta-analyses, so the two data sources could, in principle, be combined. Determining whether they should be combined, however, requires judgment about their compatibility. We propose four guiding questions for the preliminary evaluation of such syntheses, concerning outcome measurement, primary study sample sizes, the distribution of study features, and publication bias, and show how graphical and tabular summaries can inform each consideration. We then describe meta-analytic models for combining AD and IPD from studies with continuous outcomes. We review two-stage and one-stage approaches for estimating the overall effect distribution and study-level moderation, as well as for separating within-study from between-study moderation of individual characteristics, including a novel bivariate two-stage formulation that jointly synthesizes treatment and moderation effects. We illustrate the framework with two examples, each pairing an AD meta-analysis with a multilab replication of the same effect. In an example of moral licensing effects, the preliminary evaluation indicates that combining the sources is not warranted; in an example of social heuristics effects, synthesizing across data sources is warranted. Together, the examples show that whether two sources can be combined is an empirical question best settled before modeling begins, and that the specification that follows should be tailored to the features of the data that the preliminary evaluation brings to light.

articles_hidden.title: Student Attention During Learning Activities: Variability across Instructional Contexts and Student Characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Zoe Mao; Fang Yu Chang; Maya Khalil; Andrea Dillon; Mark Rapport; Sandra Loo; Agatha Lenartowicz; Jennie K Grammer
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s ability to pay attention during instruction is foundational for learning. The growing use of online learning has introduced important questions about how attentional engagement varies across instructional contexts, particularly of those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Measuring children’s attention in real-world contexts, however, remains challenging. In this semi-naturalistic experiment, we examined attentional behaviors of children with and without an ADHD diagnosis (N = 80; ages 6-10; 37.5% female; 32.5% ADHD) as they participated in four one-on-one science learning activities with an instructor. Activities varied along two instructional dimensions: modality (in-person vs. synchronous online vs. asynchronous video-based) and management of learning (teacher-led vs. student-led). Continuous behavioral coding using the newly developed Student Attention Tracking (SAT) protocol revealed variability in children’s attention both between individuals and across instructional contexts. Linear mixed-effects models, controlling for age, sex at birth, and family socioeconomic status indicated that children’s attentional patterns during synchronous online instruction were comparable to in-person learning, when the amount of teacher-student interaction was comparable. Children also demonstrated lower fidgeting and off-task behaviors during asynchronous video-based learning. Compared to teacher-led in-person instruction, student-led individual learning was associated with higher engagement and lower fidgeting. A significant interaction with ADHD diagnosis indicated that the increases in engagement and decreases in fidgeting were greater for children with ADHD. Furthermore, instructional context accounted for substantially more variance in attentional behaviors than diagnostic status. Together, findings suggest that features of instructional design may play a larger role in shaping children’s attentional engagement during learning than diagnostic differences alone.

articles_hidden.title: Cue–Appraisal Learning in Organizations: A Theory of Conditioned Appraisal Meaning
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Umbra
articles_hidden.abstract: Employees often respond to recurring workplace cues as if those cues carry the meaning of prior experience. A performance review, complaint channel, supervisor phrase, meeting routine, or organizational space may be appraised differently across employees even when the formal cue is the same. This article develops a theory of cue–appraisal learning in organizations. The theory proposes that recurring organizational cues become psychologically consequential when employees repeatedly encounter them in episodes appraised in similar, concern-relevant ways. Over time, employees may develop conditioned appraisal meanings: learned relations between recurring organizational cues and specific appraisal meanings that become more likely to be activated when those cues are encountered again. This cue-level perspective explains how prior organizational experience can shape appraisal activation before a current event has fully unfolded. It also clarifies how learned cue meanings may influence workplace emotion and action tendencies through appraisal processes that remain sensitive to situational, regulatory, and behavioral constraints. The article defines conditioned appraisal meaning, distinguishes it from adjacent constructs, develops propositions concerning acquisition, appraisal specificity, generalization, discrimination, revision, and downstream response, and outlines implications for research and practice.

articles_hidden.title: A Spanish-Language Version of the Emotion Reactivity Scale: Psychometric Properties, Measurement Invariance, and Criterion Validity in a Large Adolescent Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua B Gilbert; Zachary Himmelsbach; Matthew Nock; Nicole R. DeTore; Randi M. Schuster
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) is a widely used self-report measure of the sensitivity, intensity, and persistence of emotional responses. It has been translated and evaluated in Dutch, French, German, Portuguese, and Farsi samples, and has been separately adapted into a brief six-item short form in English. However, no validated Spanish-language version currently exists despite Spanish being the most common non-English language spoken in U.S. schools.

Methods: We provide a Spanish translation of the ERS and evaluate its psychometric properties using data from 522 Spanish-language adolescent respondents and a demographically matched sample of 522 English-language adolescent respondents drawn from a school-based survey. We use multigroup item response theory to test measurement invariance across survey language and regularized differential item functioning (DIF) analysis to identify specific noninvariant items. We evaluate criterion validity through association with the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4).

Results: Multigroup item response theory analyses support metric but not scalar invariance across survey languages, with intercept differences identified for four items, none of which appear on the short form. Despite this evidence of differential item functioning, its practical impact is negligible, as adjusted and unadjusted scores are nearly perfectly correlated ($r > .99$). ERS scores show strong and statistically equivalent criterion validity across language groups in predicting concurrent psychological distress on the PHQ-4.

Conclusions: Both the long and short forms of the Spanish ERS are reliable and criterion-valid measures of emotion reactivity for use with Spanish-speaking adolescents.

articles_hidden.title: Intuitions about trait responsibilities
articles_hidden.authors: Yang Xiang; Stephanie Hsu; Samuel J. Gershman
articles_hidden.abstract: Popular depictions of mental life often feature a bustling society of personality traits—distinctive characters whose actions collectively determine behavior, much like how the actions of individual people collectively determine the behavior of a group. Do these depictions capture something important about folk psychology? One implication is that people should reason about trait responsibility similarly to how they reason about personal responsibility in groups. To test this implication quantitatively, we first collected data on judgments about the predictive relationship between traits and actions (Experiment 1), and then elicited trait responsibility judgments for the same actions (Experiment 2). The data from Experiment 1 were used to construct models of responsibility attribution (adapted from prior work on personal responsibility in groups), which we then compared to data from Experiment 2. We found that participants treated personality traits as entities that can bear responsibility for behavior, and their responsibility judgments were best explained by an actual contribution model that assigns responsibility based on a trait’s predictive contribution to behavior. In contrast to findings from studies of personal responsibility, counterfactual-style models did not fare as well. These findings reveal both similarities and differences between responsibility attribution to traits within a person vs. people within a group.

articles_hidden.title: Group One Session Treatment: A Feasibility Study in Highly Spider Fearful Youth
articles_hidden.authors: Raphael Gutzweiler; Lou Aberfeld; Léonie Rodon; Boris Tolstich
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: One Session Treatments (OST) represent an intensive and efficacious therapeutic modality for the treatment of anxiety disorders. To date, research has been predominantly focused on individual OST in adults. Research on group OST with children and adolescents is scarce. The objective of the present study is to examine the feasibility of a group OST for highly spider fearful children and adolescents, and to conduct an initial evaluation of this treatment.
Methods: A total of 19 children and adolescents (M = 11.95 years, SD = 2.66) participated in the group OST. We assessed fear of spiders using questionnaires, a clinical interview, and a behavioural approach task. Furthermore, an assessment of disgust sensitivity was conducted. Assessments were administered prior to, at the end of (post), and three months following (FU) the group OST.
Results: Participants reported a high reduction in levels of spider fear (Hedges' g = 2.00 (post), g = 1.7 (FU)), increase in behavioural approach, and full remission (in 84% of cases). Participants, their caregivers, and therapists rated overall moderate to high improvements. No effects were found regarding disgust sensitivity. Group OST effects remained stable during the 3-month FU-interval.
Implications: Group OST in spider fearful children and adolescents provided evidence for feasibility and efficiency.

articles_hidden.title: People make inferences from policy decisions regarding default options:  Replication and extension of McKenzie et al. (2006)
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoru Teng; Ka Wai LAU; Tsz King Ng; Chan Ka Po; Yeung Wing; Siu Kit Yeung; Gilad Feldman
articles_hidden.abstract: Default effect refers to the phenomenon that people tend to choose the default option in a choice-set. McKenzie et al. (2006) showed that one mechanism for the effect is that defaults are perceived as an implicit endorsement and a recommended option by the policy makers that set the defaults. In a pre-registered experiment with a Prolific online sample from the United States (N = 602), we conducted replications and extensions of Studies 1, 2, and 3 from McKenzie et al. (2006). Across the nine target-article tests, the adjusted Cramer's V effects ranged from .24 to .86 with corresponding replication estimates ranging from .41 to .80. We concluded a successful replication of all three studies, with support for their findings showing that: 1) people who report willingness to be organ donors, and people who think others ought to be donors, are more likely to select organ donation as the policy default, and that in turn: 2) people make inferences from policymaker’s set defaults (Study 2: organ donations; Study 3: retirement plans) regarding the policymakers’ own preferences regarding enrollment, and their views regarding whether others should enroll. In our extension we added a control condition with no defaults, finding that 1) people still make inferences about choice architects’ attitudes, even when defaults were not set, and 2) that setting defaults to not act (not enroll) is perceived as closer to no defaults than setting defaults to act (to enroll). Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E5K4J.

articles_hidden.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles_hidden.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles_hidden.title: Covariate Selection for Doubly Robust Double/debiased Machine Learning Estimators for Causal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: High-dimensional data create challenges for causal effect estimation because identifying the covariates needed for correct model specification becomes increasingly difficult. Double/debiased machine learning (DML) facilitates the use of machine learning (ML) for causal inference by mitigating regularization and overfitting bias, but comparatively less attention has been given to covariate selection in relation to the double robustness (DR) property possessed by some DML estimators. In particular, ML-based covariate selection may result in differential covariate selection or in misspecification of both models, thereby limiting the practical utility of the DR property. To address these issues, we propose using the union of the covariates selected by the propensity score (PS) and outcome ML models to re-estimate both models. Simulation results show that using the union consistently reduces more confounding bias than using separate selected covariate sets. The results also show that ML-based estimation does not uniformly outperform conventional DR estimation, even under conditions favorable to the Lasso, and that post-Lasso reduces more confounding bias than standard Lasso. These findings demonstrate that successful use of ML for causal inference depends not only on the ML algorithm but also on how the information obtained through covariate selection is incorporated into causal effect estimation.

articles_hidden.title: Within-Person Symptom Dynamics in Serious Mental Illness: Insights from Daily Self-reports and Audio Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Daiil Jun; Jeffrey M. Girard; Yoonho Chung; Scott L. Rauch; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how clinical symptoms fluctuate within individuals is crucial for developing personalized treatment, yet these dynamics remain understudied. We examined whether daily self-reports and speech features from audio journals predicted monthly fluctuations in clinician-rated symptoms among 54 outpatients with affective and psychotic disorders. We identified seven within-person symptom dimensions: disorganized thinking, mania, social withdrawal, inexpressivity, affective depression, cognitive depression, and anxiety. Daily self-reports and speech features were summarized on a monthly level across different temporal windows highlighting 3, 7, 14, and 28 days of daily data prior to the clinical interview to assess the predictive value of emphasizing more or less recent daily histories. Bayesian multilevel models indicated that both the intensity and day-to-day variability of daily experiences and speech features tracked month-to-month symptom fluctuations. Daily Positive Affect and speech sentiment were the most broadly informative indicators of fluctuations across symptom domains. Greater Daily Positive Affect or more positive sentiment predicted increased mania, whereas lower levels tracked increased other symptoms except for disorganized thinking. Model comparisons across temporal windows showed that models using daily self-reports were generally robust to different windows, although social withdrawal showed improved performance highlighting longer daily histories. Models using speech features generally performed better with longer temporal windows, whereas mania and anxiety showed no clear temporal window preference. Overall, these findings demonstrate the utility of daily self-reports and audio journals for dynamic symptom tracking and showcase a data-driven approach to investigating the optimal length of daily history for developing personalized monitoring tools in psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Learning a novel visual cue to update internal predictions of object weight
articles_hidden.authors: Olaf Kristiansen; Meike Scheller; Marko Nardini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background Efficient manual interactions with objects rely on accurate predictions of object heaviness, informed by both visual cues and prior lifting experience. While
arbitrary visual cues can be learned to guide motor planning, their predictive utility compared to a familiar cue like visual volume remains poorly understood.
Furthermore, it remains unknown whether presenting novel visual cues intrinsically (on the object) or extrinsically (on a screen), impacts predictive utility. This study
investigates the extent to which familiar and novel (intrinsic and extrinsic) visual cues influence anticipatory grip force adjustments.

Results: In a precision-grip lifting task with three object heaviness levels, peak grip force rate (PGFR), an indicator of heaviness predictions, was measured across four
conditions: ‘no-cue’, ‘familiar’, ‘novel intrinsic’, and ‘novel extrinsic’. Intrinsic cues were visual patterns (line orientations) on the surfaces of the objects, while extrinsic
cues were diagrammatic depictions of the same objects and patterns. Without visual cues, PGFR was strongly biased by the preceding lift’s weight. All visual cues
significantly reduced this bias. Contrary to predictions, the familiar volume cue did not exert a stronger influence than novel cues, nor did the intrinsic cues have a
stronger influence than extrinsic cues.

Conclusions: Novel visual cues can be rapidly incorporated into motor planning without a clear performance penalty relative to a familiar cue. Presenting novel cues extrinsically also does not incur a performance penalty relative to intrinsic presentation. These findings highlight the flexibility of sensorimotor control and may inform manual interactions in environments with limited or unconventional weight
predictors.

articles_hidden.title: LLM-Generated Social-Desirability Ratings for Forced-Choice Questionnaire Construction: A Preregistered Downstream Validation
articles_hidden.authors: Yui Furukawa; Kyosuke Bunji; Kensuke Okada
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce evaluative judgments, but rating-level human–model agreement does not establish whether they can replace human inputs in a downstream task. Using HEXACO personality items as a case study, we conduct a preregistered three-stage validation of whether LLM-generated social-desirability ratings can serve as inputs to forced-choice scale construction, a psychometric task that requires costly human ratings. In Stage I, three LLMs served as raters of item-level social desirability for sentence- and adjective-format items, with human ratings serving as references. In Stage II, human- and LLM-based ratings were entered into the same constrained optimization procedure. In Stage III, 400 participants completed the resulting forms, and latent trait estimates were compared using graded Thurstonian item response theory. LLM ratings showed strong item-level correspondence with human ratings (sentence: r = 0.942–0.963; adjective: r = 0.979–0.980), but optimized forms showed partial item overlap and sparse exact pair overlap. Despite these design differences, LLM-based forms produced latent trait estimates that closely matched those from human-based forms (mean r = 0.815 for sentence items and 0.768 for adjective items). These results support the conditional use of LLM-generated ratings as scalable construction inputs while showing why downstream validation is necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Substance Use Disorder Treatment: From Brain Awareness to Brain Recovery Capital
articles_hidden.authors: Tara Rezapour; Alex Baldacchino; Andrew Dalley; Jamie Berry; Shweta Chilka; Marc L. Copersino; Ali Farhoudian; Jing Jin; Steven Powers; Timothy Grigsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Substance use disorders continue to affect millions of people worldwide, yet a striking proportion never receive treatment. Poor awareness, internalized stigma, and neurobiological changes in the circuits responsible for self-monitoring all contribute to this gap in ways that conventional psychoeducation has not adequately addressed. Recent advances in addiction neuroscience offer a more precise and less stigmatizing language for understanding these barriers, one that reframes addiction as a brain disorder rather than a moral failure and opens new possibilities for how we educate patients about their condition. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation, or NIPE, builds on this foundation. It integrates current addiction neuroscience into an educational program designed to improve insight, reduce shame, and strengthen motivation for treatment and recovery. This paper proposes a clinical stage-based NIPE framework organized around the Transtheoretical Model of Health Behavior Change, mapping specific educational content and delivery priorities to seven stages of the recovery trajectory. The goal is an approach that meets people where they actually are in both their motivational readiness and their neurobiological capacity to engage. An example of a NIPE package for recovery and future directions to deliver effective NIPE and promote brain recovery are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Getting the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Ready for Clinical Practice: Population-Representative Norms That Embrace Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Zimmermann; André Kerber; Christoph J. Kemper; Katharina Weweck
articles_hidden.abstract: The Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5) is the standard measure of the maladaptive traits in the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders, but normative information for score interpretation has remained limited. Existing norms refer to the U.S. population, are not conditioned on age and gender, and report point values without any quantification of uncertainty. We derived norms for the facets, domains, and total scores of the full PID-5 and its abbreviated versions, referenced to the German general population and conditional on age and gender. A modular Bayesian pipeline combined a probability-based reference sample (N = 4,727) with three “donor” samples that completed the full instrument (N = 2,471), linked via 34 common items. The norm tables quantify uncertainty at two levels, with credible bands for every norm value and score-conditional intervals for every raw score, and can be applied through a free online scoring platform.

articles_hidden.title: The Quiet Window–Challenge Window Framework: A Conceptual Framework for Habit Formation During GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Holly R Hull; Melanie Rae Lenius Meister; Laura E Martin; Molly M. Fain; Sarah Crawford; Debra Sullivan; Alexandra R. Brown; Johanna G. Finkle
articles_hidden.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed obesity treatment by producing substantial weight loss while altering appetite, food-related cognition, and eating behaviors. Although current clinical recommendations emphasize dietary quality, adequate protein intake, physical activity, and behavioral support during GLP-1RA therapy, they primarily focus on what behavior strategies should accompany treatment rather than when they may be most effective. Emerging evidence suggests that the cognitive and behavioral effects of GLP-1RA therapy are dynamic, creating periods during which healthy habits may be more readily established and later tested. We propose the Quiet Window-Challenge Window Framework, a conceptual model that reframes behavioral opportunity during GLP-1RA therapy as a dynamic process. The Quiet Window represents a temporary period of reduced food-related cognitive burden that facilitates habit acquisition, whereas the Challenge Window reflects increasing cognitive and environmental demands during which newly established habits are tested. A central hypothesis is that durable behavior change depends on the progressive transfer of behavioral regulation from pharmacologic support to resilient, self-sustaining habits through repeated practice, increasing automaticity, and subsequent testing under greater behavioral demands. We further propose that Quiet and Challenge Windows operate across multiple time points, including broader treatment phases and recurring weekly states within weekly dosing intervals. The framework generates testable hypotheses regarding food-related cognition, habit formation and resilience, and adaptive behavioral interventions. By conceptualizing behavioral opportunity as dynamic, this Framework shifts the focus from whether behavioral interventions should accompany GLP-1RA therapy to when they are most likely to promote durable behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: A Latent Oscillator Measurement Model to Simulate Emotional-Expression Score Dynamics in Video
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandar Tomašević; Hudson Golino; Alexander P. Christensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial-expression classifiers convert video into multivariate time series of scores with measurement
error from classifiers, videos, and recording conditions. Empirical score series cannot establish whether
the score channels reflect a smaller set of latent expressive processes or whether an analysis would recover
those processes. We introduce the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a data-generating
model that separates latent dynamics, time-varying activity, and a factor-analytic observation model.
The latent processes are damped, undamped, or amplifying linear oscillators. LOMM generates bounded
scores or continuous indicators. Study 1 used four-fold cross-fitting with scores from 100 MAFW videos
to calibrate LOMM and evaluate generated series on held-out videos. Median plausibility and coverage
were 0.970 and 0.920 for LOMM, versus 0.510 and 0.370 for a calibrated static logistic-normal generator.
Study 2 tested whether Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis (DynEGA), static EGA, GraphicalVAR,
and GIMME recovered a known dimensional structure from continuous indicators generated by LOMM.
At 100 observations per clip, with failed or timed-out fits counted as incorrect, correct-dimension
recovery was 0.939 for DynEGA, 0.884 for static EGA, 0.777 for GraphicalVAR, and 0.176 for GIMME.
Replacing the common fixed initialization with independent stationary starts for stable dimensions and
bounded independent starts for amplifying dimensions reduced recovery for DynEGA, static EGA, and
GraphicalVAR. The primary initialization was optimistic relative to this alternative. LOMM provides
a controlled test of whether an analysis recovers a specified latent structure before score patterns are
interpreted psychologically.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting More Behavior More of the Time: On the Behavioral Nature of Different Personality Trait Measures
articles_hidden.authors: Niclas Kuper; Simon Mats Breil; Katharina Utesch; Mitja D Back
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research focuses on self-reported global trait ratings to approximate behavioral individual differences. However, several alternatives exist. Average self-reported states from experience sampling are thought to be closer to behavior, but little evidence supports this. Further, other-report should rely more strongly on behavior. Here, we predict interpersonal behavior from different personality trait measures, highlighting type of aggregation (global vs. average state measures) and perspective (self- vs. other-report). We provide initial, exploratory evidence with a small multi-methodological study (N = 88) including six trait measures: global self-report, global informant-report, time-based self-reported states (fortnightly diaries), time-based peer-reported states, event-based self-reported states (after social interactions), and event-based peer-reported states. Measures were compared in the prediction of actual behavior in the laboratory one year later. We focused on four behaviors (warmth, expressiveness, self-confidence, nervousness) and corresponding global/state dimensions. Self-reported states were rarely incrementally predictive above global self-report and thus not as close to behavior as commonly believed. When based on multiple raters, other-report was more consistently linked to behavior than self-report. Other-reported states averaged across peers were predictive beyond global informant-report and self-reported states, representing an underused method potentially closer to behavior. We outline future directions to go beyond self-report in behavioral personality science.

articles_hidden.title: How does Sleep Restriction Therapy work? Testing the Triple-R theory as an explanation through computational modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Jill de Ron; Tessa F. Blanken; Denny Borsboom; Hans Gommers; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Jaap Lancee; Leonie Franziska Maurer; Jason Nak; Donald Robinaugh; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep restriction therapy (SRT) is an effective treatment for insomnia, one of the most prevalent mental disorders today. The Triple-R theory has been proposed to explain the efficacy of SRT based on three processes: restricting time in bed, regulating sleep and wake times, and reconditioning of the bed-sleep association. However, based on the verbal theory alone it is difficult to determine whether the proposed processes explain the efficacy of SRT. In the current paper we test whether Triple-R theory explains the efficacy of SRT through computational modeling. Building on the productive explanation framework we (i) define empirical phenomena in sleep diary data before and after SRT; (ii) formalize the Triple-R theory as a computational model; (iii) test whether the empirical phenomena are reproduced by the model. We show that our computational Triple-R model reproduces most data patterns observed in empirical studies. Therefore, we conclude that the Triple-R theory provides a partial explanation of the efficacy of SRT. Moreover, our proposed Triple-R model makes predictions that can guide new clinical trials and provides a better understanding of the mechanisms of SRT.

articles_hidden.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: Mentoring Trainees with Lived Experience of Psychopathology: A Strengths-based, Cultural Humility Framework for Psychological Scientists
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Devendorf; Julie Cristello; Cassandra L. Boness; Irene Tung; Cecilia Hinojosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health difficulties are prevalent among psychologists, yet professionals in the field are often discouraged from disclosing their lived experience with psychopathology due to persistent stigma. For much of history, lived experience with psychopathology has been treated as a deficit within the profession. However, emerging research and perspectives are beginning to challenge this status quo by highlighting that lived experience can be an asset in psychological science and practice. Despite this shift, there remains little guidance on how to navigate this topic in mentor-mentee relationships. We outline a framework for strengths-based mentorship that is based on six pillars: 1) tenets of strengths-based mentorship; 2) foundational and functional mentorship competencies; 3) mental health literacy; 4) feminist principles; 5) cultural humility; and 6) ethical considerations. This framework can help improve mentor-mentee relationships, reduce stigma, and ultimately improve the professional development of mentees with lived experience. We apply this principle-driven framework to common professional scenarios: recruiting applicants, evaluating personal statements, and navigating situations when a mentee is distressed, requesting accommodations, or interested in leveraging their lived experiences in their work. By offering this framework, we aim to facilitate dialogue and provide actionable guidance for mentors seeking to support trainees with psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Dietary Modulation of Neurobiological Mechanisms Underlying Executive Function and Decision-Making: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Iveta Harris; Ian Evans; Jessica Bayes; Mansi Das Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive function (EF) and decision making (DM) are central to adaptive behaviour, yet evidence explaining how diet influences their underlying neurobiological mechanisms remains fragmented. This systematic review examined how dietary exposures influence the neurobiological mechanisms underlying EF and DM. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251173091). Of 12,952 records identified, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria, involving over 2,000 participants. Across the included studies, dietary exposures were associated with changes in metabolic, neurochemical, inflammatory, neural, and gut–brain pathways relevant to EF and DM. Behavioural effects were reported across all dietary domains but were less consistent than biological changes and varied according to intervention duration, task sensitivity, and participant characteristics. EF outcomes were more consistently modulated than DM outcomes, with effects most evident in working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Although less frequently studied, DM findings showed that dietary exposures could shift complex choices—including risk-taking, temporal discounting, and social decision-making—alongside changes in metabolic state and neurotransmitter precursor availability. Notably, none of the reviewed studies specifically examined ultra-processed food exposure, identifying an important gap in the current evidence. Few studies examined when or how biological changes translated into measurable behavioural outcomes.
