Together, the findings suggest that dietary effects may emerge across biological systems before consistent changes in EF and DM become detectable, potentially explaining variability in previous behavioural findings. Longitudinal, mechanistically integrated studies that account for potential confounding factors, including hormonal status, background dietary intake, and participant characteristics, are needed to test this temporal sequence and determine when biological modulation produces cognitive and behavioural change.

articles_hidden.title: A Continuous Model of Mother, Father, and Infant Relations
articles_hidden.authors: Rukmini Mukkamalla; Benito Chen-Charpentier
articles_hidden.abstract: Many couples' relationship satisfaction declines after the birth of a child, and this decline is usually strongest in mothers. Other mathematical models of couple dynamics treat the mother and father in isolation, but the infant is also an emotional agent, coupled bidirectionally with both parents. We extend the continuous marital-satisfaction model of Chen-Charpentier et al.\ to a three-agent family consisting of a mother, a father, and an infant, using measured data whenever we can. Using equilibrium and stability analysis, a global Sobol sensitivity analysis, and a time-dependent extension, we find that the family has a single stable equilibrium. The sensitivity analysis shows that all three baseline emotional states largely affect the location of this equilibrium, with the infant's and father's baselines contributing the largest share of the variance. The mother's baseline plays a different role, however. It acts as a tipping point as mild maternal depression gets absorbed by the family while severe maternal depression drives the entire family into a distressed state. A time-dependent simulation of the first year, in which the parent--infant coupling is strong early and eases smoothly, shows that the early periods govern the speed of adjustment but not the destination. For example, a healthy family reaches contentment sooner, whereas a family with severe maternal depression dips further before settling into distress. Maternal mental health is thus the key factor in whether the family's emotional outcome is content or distressed.

articles_hidden.title: Culturally Prompted Large Language Models Remain Anchored to Western Values
articles_hidden.authors: Zhao Wang; Yilin Xu; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles_hidden.abstract: One proposed solution for reducing cultural bias in large language models (LLMs) involves “cultural prompting,” in which LLMs are explicitly instructed to respond on behalf of a cultural group. However, past studies have yielded inconsistent claims about the efficacy of cultural prompting. Here we test whether these inconsistent findings can be explained through an anchoring and adjusting account, whereby cultural prompting moves LLM responses away from a default representation anchored in wealthy Western values, but this adjustment is insufficient. We test this account by prompting three commercial LLMs to answer 117 items from the World Values Survey on behalf of 66 countries. We then compare their responses with data from 97,220 humans. Consistent with our predictions, we find that cultural prompting moves LLMs closer to human responses, but the shift is insufficient, particularly for poorer and culturally distant countries. Culturally prompted LLM responses remained more secular and emancipative than human responses. We also find that the biases of culturally prompted models were clustered by cultural heritage. Countries in closer geographic proximity and with more similar religious profiles showed similar patterns of misrepresentation. In addition to these results, we find a surprising pattern for Western countries in which cultural prompting makes responses more secular and emancipative than the model’s default representations. Many of our findings are broadly consistent with an anchoring and adjustment account, but this account cannot fully explain why cultural prompting leads models to overshoot human means for Western countries.

articles_hidden.title: Canonical Correlation Analysis of Multidimensional Perfectionism and Mental Health Among Filipino Young Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano
articles_hidden.abstract: Perfectionism is a multidimensional personality trait that has been consistently linked to both negative and positive mental health outcomes. Yet recent research has increasingly reduced perfectionism to broad higher-order factors leaving specific dimensions underexamined. The present study examined how the six dimensions of Multidimensional Perfectionism according to Frost et al. (1990)—Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Personal Standards, Organization, Parental Expectations, and Parental Criticism—relate to positive and negative mental health outcomes among Filipino young adults. Canonical correlation analysis was employed in a sample of 1,093 participants (Mage = 22.10, SD = 1.66) to capture the multivariate patterning of associations between perfectionism dimensions and four mental health indicators: stress, anxiety, depression, and life satisfaction. Two significant canonical functions emerged. The first function (Rc = .649, 42.1% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Parental Criticism, Parental Expectations and Personal Standards to higher stress, anxiety, and depression, and lower life satisfaction. The second (Rc = .332, 11.0% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Personal Standards and Organization to greater life satisfaction and lower depression, with weaker associations with anxiety and stress. These findings highlight the value of examining individual perfectionism dimensions rather than broad higher-order factors. Parental dimensions, in particular, appear especially relevant in the Filipino context.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles_hidden.title: ENDS-Motivational and Affective Picture System (E-MAPS): Development and validation of a contextualized vaping image database
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Wahlers; Jonathan Westlake; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Steven Seung-Suk Kang; Delwyn Catley; Seung-Lark Lim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) use is reinforced by motivational and affective
contexts associated with repeated ENDS use. Yet, there are currently no standardized, validated
ENDS-related image cues that differentiate among motivational contexts. This study aimed to
develop and validate contextualized ENDS-related image cues.

Method
Electronic nicotine delivery system users between the ages of 21 and 35 in the United States
were recruited via Prolific (N = 253). Eighty ENDS-related images were presented. E-MAPS
(ENDS-Motivational and Affective Picture System) depicts ENDS use in four motivational
contexts corresponding to prominent vaping dependence mechanisms: positive reinforcement,
negative reinforcement, habit/automaticity, and cue-induced craving. Each motivational context
also depicts social and nonsocial ENDS use. Each participant rated 80 images on dimensions of
valence, arousal, and craving.

Results
E-MAPS images were classified consistently with their intended motivational context and ratings
of valence, arousal, and craving exhibited strong reliability within each intended category.
Several differences in valence, arousal, and craving emerged among motivational contexts,
highlighting the importance of accounting for cue-related motivational context. Regardless of
context, E-MAPS images elicited relatively high cravings while higher (vs. lower) reported
cravings were strongly associated with clinically relevant outcomes: greater vaping dependence
and reduced motivation and confidence to quit.

Conclusion
E-MAPS reliably distinguished among prominent dependence-related motivational contexts,
offering researchers tools to study the motivational mechanisms that sustain chronic ENDS use.

articles_hidden.title: An emic way of examining morality based on Moral Foundations Theory: development and validation of the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire in Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Hideya Sanada; Yoshito Tan; Haruki Oka
articles_hidden.abstract: How should morality be measured in a cross-cultural context? Although Moral Foundations Theory combines etic (universal) and emic (local) concepts, existing measures are largely etic. Therefore, we proposed an emic approach for measuring etic constructs of MFT, introduced a new construct, Moral Foundations Patterns, and developed the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire (MFPQ) in Japan. We conducted five studies to develop and validate the MFPQ (total N = 2,161), using two different sampling platforms to diversify sample characteristics. We showed MFPQ has adequate reliability and validity. Finally, we discussed how this emic MFPQ can be applied in cross-cultural research and argued that MFPQ can contribute to the stringent tests of the Moral Foundations Theory's key claims and support cross-cultural comparisons of its construct.

articles_hidden.title: Is the Useful Field all you need on the road? Hazard localization performance in a gaze contingent scotoma paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Zivli; Jiali Song; Benjamin Wolfe
articles_hidden.abstract: The Useful Field is a construct which describes a limited region of visual space around fixation, and is often misinterpreted in driving contexts as being the only portion of the visual field which supports drivers’ knowledge of their environment. This account ignores the likely contributions of peripheral vision, but this has not been studied in dynamic scenes. Studies with static scenes suggest that peripheral vision supports scene gist, but the world and road are not static. Taking inspiration from the driving literature, and using our corpus of near-collision dash camera video, we examined the separate necessity of central and peripheral information to drivers’ ability to localize dangerous objects in a rapidly-changing road scene, directly testing the strong interpretation of the Useful Field. In separate blocks, we approximated this strong interpretation of the Useful Field with a peripheral scotoma and, the reverse, a central scotoma condition, forcing observers to rely on peripheral vision alone. Blockwise, the visible or occluded region varied according to a 3-up/1-down staircase. This procedure allowed us to estimate the extent of occlusion observers could tolerate in each condition. We replicated the key findings from the static scene gist literature, extending them to dynamic scenes. Specifically, we showed that while the Useful Field can support this task, its occlusion does not render the task impossible, suggesting that we use information beyond this limited region of visual space to support task demands.

articles_hidden.title: Questionnaire Democrats? Reconsidering the Relevance of Abstract Democracy Support in the American Public
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Reel Panish; Ariel Malka
articles_hidden.abstract: The American public largely favors “democracy,” yet many citizens tolerate undemocratic actions and candidates. This raises doubts about the relevance of abstract democracy support to actual democratic commitment. In contrast, we argue that abstract democracy support is a normatively significant dimension of attitude variation among Americans. Using nineteen surveys fielded between 1995 and 2024, we show that a sizable segment of the public expresses only tepid support for democracy, and that a nontrivial minority expresses opposition. Moreover, commonly used abstract democracy support items converge on a single latent construct which displays high rank-order stability, but also meaningful within-person variation, over a two-year period. Abstract democracy support negatively predicts openness to a wide range of electoral and liberal democratic violations and is associated with greater likelihood of electorally punishing anti-democratic candidates. In panel data, positive within-person deviations in abstract democracy support precede negative within-person deviations in openness to authoritarian governance, suggesting that individual-level shifts in abstract support predict later change in substantive democracy attitudes. Overall our findings suggest that the value of ‘democracy’ is contested among Americans, with potential implications for democratic erosion. We recommend that efforts to understand the American public’s role in democratic backsliding and restoration treat abstract support as a distinct attitude construct, measure it with multi-item scales, and explore whether or not it possesses causal significance.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Childhood Experiences and Mother–Infant Bonding: A Longitudinal Path Analysis of Perinatal Mental Health and Psychosocial Resources
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Rabasa Serrano; Sandra Doval; Alejandro de Miguel Álvaro; Maria Laura Quintanilla Cobián; Marta Giménez-Dasí
articles_hidden.abstract: Maternal childhood experiences may shape perinatal mental health and mother–infant bonding (MIB). This longitudinal study examined pathways linking adverse (ACEs) and benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) to MIB through pregnancy adaptation and postpartum mental health, considering resilience and social support. We followed 404 pregnant women to 3 months postpartum. Path analyses showed that higher ACEs were associated with poorer pregnancy adaptation (β = .108, p = .020), which predicted greater postpartum depressive symptoms and poorer MIB. Social support and resilience protected against prenatal maladjustment and postpartum depression, while social support buffered the association between pregnancy adaptation difficulties and depressive symptoms (β = −.104, p = .006). BCEs were associated with better pregnancy adaptation through psychosocial resources. The model showed excellent fit (CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 23.6% of MIB variance. Similar patterns emerged for anxiety. Findings highlight indirect pathways and the protective role of psychosocial resources.

articles_hidden.title: Methodological Diversity and Heterogeneity in Psychological Evidence Syntheses
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Duco Veen; Irene Klugkist
articles_hidden.abstract: One of the fundamental problems of meta-analysis is the comparability of primary research studies and the absence of robust modes of generalisability such as formal sampling theory. The decision whether or not a set of studies ought to be mathematically pooled is therefore a complicated issue requiring both domain expertise and statistical knowledge, especially in psychological science where studies often target abstract constructs. The objective of this paper is to capture when a set of studies become so methodologically diverse that pooling the data is ruled to be inappropriate. A convergent mixed methods approach was used to combine two interdependent studies. We conducted a scoping review of current meta-analyses literature $(k = 27)$ and a qualitative content analysis of systematic reviews that decided against pooling data due to substantial methodological diversity $(k = 9)$. We find the distinction between poolable and unpoolable studies to be ambiguous. Furthermore, meta-research in psychology appears to place limited emphasis on heterogeneity and issues of generalisability. We argue that a renewed focus on generalisability through an assessment of the prototypical attributes of the scientific literature at hand would greatly improve the interpretability of meta-analytic inferences in psychology. Clearly and explicitly describing the generalisability of a review would enable authors to effectively communicate theoretically important ideas to a diverse readership. We propose the adoption of a comparability statement as a simple tool that enhances meta-research methodology without overhauling or complicating current practices in applied psychological science.

articles_hidden.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles_hidden.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Is virtual reality beneficial and for which outcomes? Comparing VR and 2D in higher education classroom learning
articles_hidden.authors: Mikko Haavisto; Johannes Halttu; Tomi Jaakkola
articles_hidden.abstract: The transition from hands-on experience to computer-aided design poses challenges for students’ understanding of 3D structures because traditional 2D computer screens limit spatial perception. Immersive virtual reality (VR) offers a potential solution but its effectiveness and feasibility compared to 2D screens in a classroom context are unclear. This experiment investigates to what extent VR affects learning, motivational, and perceived outcomes, and cognitive load compared to 2D screen environments in dental technology education. It also examines how individual differences, such as spatial ability and VR proficiency, influence these outcomes. First- and second-year dental technology students (n = 45) participated in a preregistered within-subject crossover experiment. Because participants had more than a thousand times more prior experience with conventional 2D screens than with VR, the intervention started with VR orientation lessons. Participants then studied framework partial dentures and dental bridges once in VR and once in a 2D screen environment. Data from pre- and posttests were analyzed with mixed-effects models to account for repeated measurements and individual differences. The results showed that VR increased presence/immersion, interest/enjoyment, and perceived competence, and produced a small nonsignificant advantage in 3D comprehension. In contrast, 2D screen learning led to higher factual knowledge performance and lower total cognitive load. Individual differences explained a large portion of variance in outcomes. The benefits of VR were mostly experiential and motivational, whereas 2D screens supported better factual learning with lower total cognitive load. Classroom VR may therefore be useful as an addition to conventional instruction.

articles_hidden.title: They’re All Like That! The Universality Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper investigates how humans store information within the thousands of concepts that structure our beliefs, and which ultimately guide our actions. Form Theory proposes that every concept has a central form, a unitary representational structure that encodes a compressed subset of conceptual information, captures conceptual identity, and generates a set of strong default beliefs. This paper introduces and tests a further form signature: a default universality belief. Across two experiments, participants judged central form properties as universally true of all category members. They rejected this belief for properties that were highly prototypical or causally important if they were not encoded as part of the concept's central form. This effect held across both familiar and novel categories, and across domains including animals, artifacts, institutions, places, and events. These findings identify the central form as a domain-general representational source of universality judgments, with implications for stereotyping, trauma, and ideology. They also help explain how Form Theory’s compressed conceptual structure can support complex thought.

articles_hidden.title: Embracing a new era of skill training and transfer in sports: An adaptive interface reorganization (AIR) framework
articles_hidden.authors: Sicong Liu; Wangyang Xu; Fengewei Hao; Andrew Mark Williams
articles_hidden.abstract: The value of vision-based training in sport depends on whether it transfers to competition or not. The recent debate over the utility of general vision and perceptual-cognitive training has exposed the limits of near-versus-far terminology for sport, where the practical objective is usually not improvement in a decontextualized capacity but functional change from a specified training task (i.e., practice) to a specified target task (i.e., competition). In this conceptual review, we reframe transfer in sports as a problem of multidimensional specificity and system reorganization. We develop four linked arguments. First, treating transfer distance as a single continuum obscures the dimensions on which training and target tasks correspond. Second, technologies including extended/virtual reality, eye tracking, motion capture, psychophysiology, and artificial intelligence can increase experimental control and measurement sensitivity, but cannot establish transfer without theory-led design. Third, we extend the modified perceptual training framework into a design model—the specificity cube—that profiles stimulus, response, and skill correspondence, with the skill dimension further specified by athlete state, timescale, and performance criterion. Fourth, we propose the adaptive interface reorganization (AIR) framework to help conceptualize durable reorganization of brain–body–environment relations within an athlete–environment system as a mechanism that sustains transfer. AIR makes the hypothesized reorganization testable through six complementary sources of evidence, including information sampling, action coupling, state regulation, performance stabilization, mechanism-aligned biomarkers, and untraining. The specificity cube and AIR recast the generic question of whether vision training works as a target-relative, mechanism-oriented research program, and generate applied implications.

articles_hidden.title: The Interplay of Contextual Representations Dynamically Shapes Human Defensive Responses
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Tortora; Daniel Gromer; Mario Reutter-Dieker; Sabrina Gado; Marta Andreatta; Matthias Gamer
articles_hidden.abstract: Flexibly adapting behavior to complex environments depends on the ability to process and integrate contextual information into a coherent representation. Animal research highlights the interplay between elemental and conjunctive contextual representations in guiding behavior. Here, we examined how these two forms of encoding interact to influence human defensive responses using a virtual reality context-dependent fear conditioning paradigm. The virtual environment consisted of three distinctly furnished offices, each containing the same two lamps. First, participants (N = 54) explored all offices (context encoding). Then, they repeatedly visited two of them and in each office, one lamp (e.g., yellow) predicted an aversive electric stimulation, whereas the other lamp (e.g., blue) signaled safety. Critically, contingencies were reversed across contexts (context-dependent acquisition). In the final phase (behavioral test), participants freely re-explored the offices. Subjective ratings, autonomic responses, proxemic indices, and gaze behavior were recorded. Ratings, autonomic responses, and gaze behavior showed context-dependent threat–safety discrimination, indicating a dominant role of conjunctive representations. Reduced discrimination in the context in which cue contingencies were reversed revealed a contribution of elemental representations. Interestingly, despite accurate contingency knowledge, participants adopted a “better safe than sorry” strategy during the behavioral test, avoiding both lamps across contexts, suggesting a stronger influence of elemental encoding on spontaneous defensive behavior under uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that multiple forms of contextual representation mutually interact across defensive domains, highlighting the complexity of human threat processing. This framework may provide new insights into the etiology and maintenance of maladaptive defensive responses in anxiety-related psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Dynamic and Reciprocal Within-Person Relations Between Emotion Regulation and Affect at Work: A Continuous Time Modeling Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Cort W. Rudolph; Amelia Wilcox; Hannes Zacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective emotion regulation is an important antecedent of emotional wellbeing in general, and in specific contexts, including the workplace. The impact of emotion regulation strategies, such as cognitive reappraisal and behavioral suppression, on short-term experiences of positive and negative affect (e.g., across several days or weeks) is rather well understood. In contrast, we know far less about the longer-term processes (e.g., across several months or years) by which the use of these strategies influence affect and vice versa. Based upon theories of emotion regulation, reappraisal and suppression emotion regulation strategies and positive and negative affect are posited to dynamically influence each other through a continuous process that unfolds within- person and over time. Using 47 waves of longitudinal data collected across 53 months from a sample of n = 1,458 full-time employed individuals in Germany, we hypothesize and test two distinct reinforcing “cycles” between cognitive reappraisal and positive affect, and between behavioral suppression and negative affect, respectively, in the work context. Results of continuous time modeling suggest evidence for both a “virtuous” cycle, wherein cognitive reappraisal is associated with higher subsequent levels of positive affect, and vice versa, and a “vicious” cycle, wherein behavioral suppression is associated with subsequently higher levels of negative affect, and vice versa.

articles_hidden.title: Neurophysiological correlates of time estimation in delay discounting
articles_hidden.authors: Cornelis Henrico Stam; Frederik M van der Veen; Ingmar Franken
articles_hidden.abstract:
Steep delay discounting behavior is associated with detrimental life outcomes, like addictive behaviors. It has been suggested that differences in time estimation abilities could underlie these detrimental behaviors. The research question this paper investigates is whether an association exists between delay discounting behavior and neurophysiological indices of time estimation. 
This study includes a sample of 100 participants, balanced by gender. As they performed a sequential time estimation task of 4 intervals (2, 3, 6, and 9s), the EEG was recorded while performing an error monitoring paradigm. Based on a pseudo-error condition, trials were split into correct and incorrect trials. EEG measures in the time domain were ERN and Pe, and in the time-frequency domain, trial-averaged delta, theta, alpha, and beta oscillatory power.
Consistent with expectations, delay discount rate was associated with producing shorter time estimations. For the time-domain analysis, no association was found with the ERN or Pe. But the time-frequency analysis showed that frontal theta band power was negatively associated with delay discount rate, whereas beta power was positively associated with delay discounting. Furthermore, theta power was positively associated with relative error (coefficient of variation; SD/mean). Theta band and beta band power were positively correlated, but the connection was weaker at higher levels of delay discounting.
Taken together, the time-frequency EEG results present novel evidence for a weaker temporal error monitoring ability in individuals who exhibit steeper delay discounting behavior, through a theta-beta mechanism. These individuals overestimated their time productions. This weaker ability probably results from two neurocognitive processes: 1. attenuated theta power (cognitive control deficit) and elevated beta power (magnitude distortion in memory).

articles_hidden.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Computational Models in Psychology: A Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Valeria Epelbaum; Sophie Engels; Jill de Ron; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Shirley B Wang; Derek de Beurs; Denny Borsboom; Valeria Krzhizhanovskaya
articles_hidden.abstract: There has been an increasing interest in formal models in psychology, allowing researchers to betterunderstand and intervene on psychological systems. However, the methods and tools for understandingand analysing these models are rarely used in psychological research. This is not necessarily due to a lackof methodology, but rather due to them not being familiar in this field. This paper introduces one suchmethod from computational science that can be used to determine the influence of model parameterson an output variable: (global) Sensitivity Analysis (SA). We first discuss the main goals of an SA andpotential applications, such as determining which parameters are the most relevant for causing a changein a chosen model output, such as suicidal thoughts or frequency of panic attacks. We then presenttwo methods that can be used to conduct an SA: the variance-based Sobol SA and the density-basedPAWN. Both of them are demonstrated using an existing computational model in a tutorial-like fashion,provided by (annotated) code in R. The results are connected to empirical literature and implicationsfor model evaluations are discussed. Lastly, we aggregate the entire process into a workflow and codepipeline that can be easily applied to other models. Although this paper only demonstrates the basicapplication of SA, further extensions and purposes, such as model calibration, are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Negative Bias: Disrupted Positive Valence Processing and Asynchronous Hot–Cool Development in Youth Internalizing Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Jiangli Wu; Xiaoxia Hu; Ruoyu Qiu; Guoling Zhou; Yuqing Jin; Fenfen Wang; Ye Cheng; Yudong Zhou; Jianfei Shi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective. Adolescent internalizing symptoms are traditionally attributed to negatively 
biased processing, leaving the developmental trajectory of positive-valence processing 
unclear. Using the hot–cool executive function framework, we examined whether hot 
(emotion-laden) and cool (cognitive control) systems diverge across development and 
differentially predict symptom severity. Method. A community sample of 1,042 Chinese 
students (elementary: n = 300, Mage = 10.3 years; middle: n = 434, Mage = 13.2; high: n 
= 308, Mage = 15.6; 606 boys) completed four computerized tasks assessing inhibitory 
control, cognitive flexibility, attentional bias, and emotional-word processing. Symptoms 
were indexed by developmentally appropriate measures (Children’s Depression Inventory
and Social Anxiety Scale for Children; Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21). A clinical 
reference group comprised 43 hospitalized adolescents (Mage = 14.5 years). Results. 
Cool executive functions matured linearly across school levels (ps < .001), whereas hot 
attentional bias showed no developmental change (p = .579). In childhood, elevated 
symptoms were associated with broad-based deficits in speed and accuracy; by early 
adolescence this narrowed onto crisis-word stimuli (rs up to .219). Cognitive indices 
explained an additional 12.1% of variance beyond demographics (p < .001). Clinically 
referred youth showed a reversal of the positive-word advantage (+111 ms vs. −35 ms in 
community controls; p < .001, r = .162), indicating a breakdown in appetitive processing. 
Conclusions. Hot and cool cognition mature asynchronously, cool control improving 
while hot valence processing stagnates. Crisis-word hypervigilance and blunted positive?valence processing are partly dissociable risk indicators with distinct severity profiles, 
informing age-sensitive screening for youth internalizing problems.

articles_hidden.title: Why don't the victims of bullying seek help? The effect of underestimating bystanders’ defending intentions
articles_hidden.authors: Guanghui Chen; Zhang anyi; fan Wang; Li Chao; Pei Yongshun; Wei Cui; Wenxin Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Seeking help from others is an important strategy for coping with difficult situations; however, victims of bullying are often reluctant to seek help. Using a series of behavioral experiments with 968 primary and secondary school students, the present study examined individuals’ prediction bias regarding bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective, its association with willingness to seek help, and whether this bias could be modified through an information-based intervention. The results showed that participants reported significantly lower levels of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective than from the bystander perspective, indicating a systematic underestimation of bystanders’ willingness to defend. This underestimation bias was robust across different types of bullying, genders, and educational stages. Greater underestimation of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective significantly predicted lower willingness to seek help. Positive contextual information cues significantly reduced the underestimation bias and increased willingness to seek help, whereas negative contextual information cues significantly increased the underestimation bias and decreased willingness to seek help. These findings provide a plausible explanation for victims’ reluctance to seek help and offer practical implications for enhancing help-seeking willingness in school bullying prevention and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Can We Really Leverage AI-Assisted Automatic Item Generation for Psychological Scale Development?
articles_hidden.authors: Xijuan Zhang; Deborah Laze; Kai Wen Zhou; Kentaro Suzuki
articles_hidden.abstract: With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), researchers can use chatbots such as ChatGPT to rapidly generate large numbers of items for psychological scale development. This study examines the quality of AI-generated items. Across four preregistered studies, we compared AI-generated items with human-generated benchmark scales in terms of factor structure, reliability, and validity. Items were generated by four LLMs using three prompting strategies for three diverse constructs: global self-esteem, mindfulness, and ``resolution,'' a newly proposed facet of cognitive fluency that reflects people’s desire for immediate and concrete outcomes. The initial item pools contained many low-quality items, including near-duplicates of existing items, semantically redundant items, and, most seriously, items tapping into unintended constructs. After these low-quality items were removed, the resulting AI-generated scales showed strong validity across all conditions, but their factor structure and reliability varied by construct. AI-generated self-esteem scales matched the human benchmark in terms of factor structure and reliability, resolution scales showed intermediate performance, and mindfulness scales performed worst. These findings suggest that LLMs can accelerate item generation but cannot replace expert screening and empirical validation. These limitations may arise partly because general-purpose LLMs are not fine-tuned to distinguish among closely related psychological constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Predictive coding unifies neural and behavioral signatures of contextual facilitation
articles_hidden.authors: Samer Nour Eddine; Anthony Yacovone; Gina R. Kuperberg
articles_hidden.abstract: During comprehension, words that are primed or predictable are processed more quickly and elicit smaller N400 responses than words that are less consistent with their preceding context. Although these behavioral and neural effects are both commonly interpreted as evidence of facilitated processing, they have typically been explained within different computational frameworks that impose seemingly conflicting constraints: behavioral facilitation requires more activity to accumulate over expected representations, allowing a decision threshold to be reached earlier, whereas N400 facilitation requires less neural activity to be generated overall. Here, we show that an implemented model of predictive coding provides a unified mechanistic account of both phenomena and, in doing so, resolves three longstanding puzzles. First, it explains how facilitated processing can simultaneously produce faster behavioral responses and reduced neural activity: expected representations accumulate activity more rapidly in state units while generating less activity in error units. Second, an asymmetry between top-down priors and bottom-up evidence allows context to pre-activate multiple lexical candidates without inducing premature competition or misprediction costs. Third, it reconciles apparently conflicting claims about the timing of contextual facilitation by showing that behavioral and neural measures can reflect different phases along a single continuous trajectory of lexico-semantic processing, rather than distinct processing stages.

articles_hidden.title: Differential Associations of Excellencism and Perfectionism with Mental Health Outcomes Among Licensure Examinees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Licensure examinees are vulnerable to the mental health consequences of perfectionism. However, previous work did not distinguish the pursuit of high yet attainable standards from the pursuit of exacting, inflexible ones. Guided by the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), this study examined how excellencism and perfectionism are differentially associated with well-being outcomes among Filipino adults preparing for a high-stakes licensure examination.
Method: A total of 1,206 psychometrician licensure examinees (Mage = 23.94, SD = 3.58) from two 2025 cohorts participated in the study.
Results: Structural equation modelling revealed that excellencism was significantly and positively associated with life satisfaction and positive affect while negatively associated with depression. In contrast, perfectionism was positively associated with negative affect, anxiety and depression. Comparison of predicted values for excellence and perfection strivers show better mental health outcomes for excellence strivers. 
Conclusions: These findings provide support for the MEP in the licensure examination context, suggesting that some of the desirable outcomes previously associated with perfectionism may be better accounted for by excellencism. The study contributes to the growing literature on excellence- and perfection-oriented goal pursuit and points to their potentially distinct implications for mental health in high-stakes evaluative settings.

articles_hidden.title: Immediate reward reduces procrastination in a naturalistic multi-day task
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Yijun Lin; Falk Lieder; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is costly and pervasive, and delivering rewards immediately is a widely recommended intervention in self-help advice, yet this advice lacks experimental support. A key challenge in testing it is designing a paradigm that both mimics real-world environments where procrastination arises and permits experimental manipulation. Here we introduce the Multi-day Online Reading Task (MORT), which combines these properties and enables measurement of the full time course of work. In a preregistered experiment (n = 611), participants were given seven days to complete a self-paced reading task and received payment either immediately upon task completion or one day after the deadline. Immediate reward led all participants to start earlier and led those with high trait procrastination, who need help most, to complete work units and the overall task earlier across three reward-performance relationships. The benefits were mediated by motivation and did not come at the cost of task completion or persistence. These findings provide causal evidence that immediate reward reduces procrastination.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual awareness as an information-distribution problem
articles_hidden.authors: Renzo Carlo Lanfranco
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do some sensory signals enter conscious experience while others influence behaviour without being consciously seen, heard, or felt? Research on perceptual awareness typically combines objective decisions with reports of awareness, visual clarity, confidence, or some subset of these measures, yet these outcomes are usually analysed separately. We argue that perceptual awareness can instead be approached as an information-distribution problem: how is stimulus information organised across objective decisions and subjective reports? We develop a theoretical information-theoretic framework based on mutual information, conditional mutual information, and co-information to characterise these relationships at the trial level. Crucially, the interpretation of these quantities depends on what the subjective report measures, allowing the framework to distinguish content-specific awareness, perceptual clarity, and confidence rather than treating them as interchangeable. The framework also specifies how informational relationships can be tracked across stimulus strength, used to formulate conscious–unconscious dissociations, and linked to metacognitive sensitivity. When awareness and confidence are both collected, we further introduce Subjective Access Co-information, CoI(K;A;C), which quantifies the net redundancy–synergy balance in how the two subjective reports jointly relate to decision correctness. By complementing established psychophysical and metacognitive measures with an explicit description of behavioural information structure, this framework provides new experimentally testable targets for theories and neuroscience of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles_hidden.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles_hidden.title: On Power and Sample Size Calculation for Bayes Factors: A Tutorial on the BayesPower Package
articles_hidden.authors: Tsz Keung Wong; Samuel Pawel; Jorge Tendeiro
articles_hidden.abstract:
Power analyses and sample size justifications are increasingly encouraged and required by funding agencies across disciplines such as psychology and the biomedical sciences, highlighting the growing need for accessible sample size determination tools. The present article introduces BayesPower, an R package for conducting sample size determination, power calculation, and Bayes factor calculation in Bayesian hypothesis testing without simulation. The package supports a wide range of statistical tests commonly encountered in the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences, including standardized mean differences, correlations, linear regression and analysis of variance, and tests for one and two proportions. In addition to the traditional comparison of a point-null hypothesis with a
composite alternative hypothesis, BayesPower supports sample size planning for interval-hypothesis Bayes factors (i.e., equivalence testing). For most testing problems, sample size and power are returned almost instantly, enabling researchers to design informative and efficient studies rapidly. To reach a broader audience, the package provides a user-friendly Shiny application for researchers with little or no experience coding in R, in addition to command-line functions for more experienced users. The use of the software is illustrated through five empirical examples.

articles_hidden.title: Testing AI’s abilities at closed-loop psychology research
articles_hidden.authors: Wilma A. Bainbridge; Akram Bakkour; Yuan Chang Leong
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have both incredible promise and incredible risk in becoming major contributors to scientific discovery. Psychology especially is a field that could experience major transformation, as empirical experiments can be run in fully digital closed loops via crowd-sourcing platforms. As a result, LLMs can conduct every stage of the research process: generating research questions, pre-registering its research plans, coding experiments, analyzing data, and writing the manuscript of the results. This could have the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, but also alongside many risks (e.g., false information, monoculturization, high energy usage). Here, we test the degree to which ChatGPT 5.0 can conduct a psychological experiment from start to finish—specifically, testing the degree to which humans employ hexadirectional strategies in navigating a familiar conceptual space. We discuss the model’s successes and failures at each step of the research process, and provide advice on where LLMs shine and where they need extra human observation. Our work opens a discussion of what this means for the broader field of psychological research—as these models have both high potential, but also important drawbacks and ramifications to consider.

articles_hidden.title: Cooperative care as a candidate mechanism linking prolonged childhood and brain expansion in human evolution
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias Grossmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Two traits distinguish modern humans from all other primates: an exceptionally large brain and an exceptionally prolonged childhood. What mechanism produced this combination, and why are the two traits dissociated in other hominins? Standard models predict that brain size and developmental duration should co-vary tightly, yet the fossil record reveals that they do not: small-brained hominins at Dikika, Dmanisi, and Rising Star show slow development, while large-brained Neanderthals matured fast. Evolutionary simulations show that cooperative care can offer a coherent account of these dissociations. In Experiment 1, cooperative care extends childhood and, as an emergent consequence, enhances social learning independent of brain size (+32.5% childhood extension with no change in brain size), creating a knowledge–storage mismatch that generates selection pressure for brain expansion. In Experiment 2, when the metabolic ceiling is lifted through allomaternal provisioning, cooperative care populations show significant brain expansion (+34%) co-occurring with further childhood extension and enhanced social learning. In Experiment 3, when populations lacking cooperative care achieve equivalent brain expansion through dietary improvement alone, they instead mature faster, producing brain expansion decoupled from developmental prolongation. The simulation thereby identifies two emergent routes to large brains: a cooperative-care route producing coupled brain–childhood expansion, and a nutrition-only route producing brain expansion without developmental prolongation—a dissociation that parallels the comparison between modern humans and Neanderthals. These results suggest that the distinctly human developmental package may reflect not brain expansion per se, but the cooperative care system within which that expansion occurred.

articles_hidden.title: Which Comes First: Ideology, or Moral Values? Panel evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles_hidden.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Kevin Smith; Ingrid Johnsen Haas; John Jostes
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent work has called into question the longstanding intuition that differences in political orientation are attributable to differences in moral values; instead, people may change their reported values to justify their political preferences. To identify which most plausibly causes which, we conducted a three-wave panel study, using quotas to approximate a demographically representative initial sample of U.S. adults and measuring values in four different ways, with each measure grounded in a distinct theoretical framework. We found that: 1) Ideology and partisanship consistently showed greater cross-wave stability than values. 2) Within-subject wave-to-wave shifts in political orientation and values were rarely and weakly related in either direction. Between-subjects analyses replicated existing work: conservatives and liberals tended to value different things. But during these months, respondents did not tend to become more conservative or liberal depending on what they valued, or to come to value anything more or less because of their ideology.

articles_hidden.title: Lifespan accumulated differences in semantic memory structure contribute to increases in episodic false memories
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Henderson; Ryan McCurdy; Anika Bhatia; Hita Devulapalli; Sean Matthew Polyn; Audrey Duarte
articles_hidden.abstract: Semantic memory grows across the lifespan with experience, scaffolding episodic memory processes while potentially contributing to memory errors when memory representations overlap. Prior work has attributed age-related increases in false recognition memory to executive dysfunction, but little is known about how lifelong semantic knowledge accumulation affects these episodic errors. In the current study, we recorded EEG while younger (n = 36) and older adults (n = 41) completed an episodic memory task in which study list-lure similarity was systematically varied using distributional model-derived measures of semantic similarity. We found older adults’ endorsement of lures was less dependent on semantic similarity than those of younger adults. Older adults also demonstrated reduced coupling of neural similarity to model-derived semantic similarity, and reduced encoding-retrieval reinstatement for accurate lure rejections. Together, these findings suggest that age-related increases in false memory reflect both altered semantic representational structure and reduced source monitoring, highlighting how semantic knowledge accumulated across the lifespan may simultaneously support episodic memory while increasing susceptibility to semantically driven distortions.

articles_hidden.title: Frontal midline theta tracks negatively biased affective updating in social anxiety from adolescence to young adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Elise Kortink; Öykü Gürcan; Selin Topel; Leonie Koban; Melle J. W. van der Molen
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative self-beliefs are a core feature of social anxiety, yet the neurocomputational processes that translate social-evaluative feedback into biased self-beliefs remain poorly understood. Here we examined whether frontal-midline theta (FM-theta) - an EEG signature of performance monitoring – governs how performance-based prediction errors (PEs) are incorporated into updating self-feelings based on performance feedback (i.e., affective updating). A sample of 216 adolescents and young adults (174 female; mean age 18.4 years) participated in a speech performance task during which participants provided a short speech that was evaluated by three judges. After the speech, participants were asked to appraise their own performance on the same evaluative items used by the judges. After their appraisal on each item, participants were provided with the judge’s evaluation and were subsequently asked to indicate how they felt based on the feedback received. We found that participants updated their self-feelings more strongly based on positive than negative feedback, and that this positive affective updating bias weakened with age. As hypothesized, participants with elevated social anxiety displayed more negative affective updating, and social anxiety fully mediated the age-related decline in positive affective updating. Critically, in individuals with elevated social anxiety, the magnitude of negative performance feedback was associated with stronger FM-theta modulated negative affective updating. These findings corroborate previous positive affective updating biases in healthy individuals and furthermore underscore a key role of FM-theta oscillations in feedback-guided affective updating, potentially reinforcing negative self-belief in individuals with elevated social anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: Predictors of suicide attempt in adolescents with a history of self-harm: a machine learning study combining psychosocial and actigraphy measures
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Sellier Silva; Bhavya Patwa; Dylan James; Martin Lepage; Lena Palaniyappan; Massimiliano Orri
articles_hidden.abstract:
Youth suicide attempt is an important clinical and public health concern, yet prediction of
suicide attempt among youth with a history of self-harm remains challenging. Disrupted states of
arousal may play an important role in the etiology of suicide attempt but have rarely been measured
objectively in prospective studies. In this study, we examined to what extent actigraphy-derived arousal
markers and questionnaire-based psychosocial measures collected at age 14 could predict self-reported
suicide attempt at age 17 in a population-based sample of 1,321 adolescents with a history of self-harm
from a United Kingdom cohort. We conducted both inferential analyses (univariable and multivariable
logistic regressions), and predictive (machine learning) modeling using nested cross-validation.
Cannabis use, peer problems, depressive symptoms, higher BMI, lower self-esteem, and sex emerged
as significant independent predictors of later reported suicide attempt. Machine learning models
achieved moderate predictive performance (AUROC = 0.65–0.67), with relatively high sensitivity
(0.71–0.81) but lower specificity (0.37–0.53). Peer problems and depressive symptoms were
consistently among the most important predictors across models. Although some actigraphy-derived
measures contributed to prediction in specific models, two-stage analyses suggested little incremental
predictive value beyond questionnaire-based measures alone. These findings highlight the importance
of cannabis use, interpersonal difficulties and depressive symptoms in predicting suicide attempt
among adolescent who self-harmed and suggest a limited additional contribution of actigraphy-derived
arousal markers for long-term prediction.

articles_hidden.title: Therapeutic Alliance and Perceived Closeness in MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M. Diehl; Christina Chwyl; Liliana Kennedy; Jenna Lejeune; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract: The therapeutic relationship is considered central to psychedelic-assisted therapy, yet little empirical research has examined how it changes during 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) or relates to acute MDMA experiences and clinical outcomes, particularly for social anxiety disorder (SAD). This preregistered secondary analysis examined therapeutic alliance and perceived closeness during an open-label pilot trial of MDMA-AT for SAD (N = 20; NCT-redacted-for-anonymous-review). Participants completed three preparation sessions, two MDMA dosing sessions, and six integration sessions. Therapeutic alliance and therapist closeness were assessed before and after each MDMA session using the Agnew Relationship Measure and Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale, respectively. Social anxiety severity was assessed with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale at baseline and post-treatment, and self-transcendent experiences were assessed following MDMA sessions. Alliance was high after preparation and increased significantly following the first MDMA session, with evidence of ceiling effects later in treatment. Closeness increased significantly during each MDMA session and decreased during the subsequent nondrug interval. Greater MDMA-session closeness predicted lower post-treatment social anxiety, including after adjustment for corresponding pre-MDMA closeness. Self-transcendent emotions and connection-related experiences were associated with greater MDMA-session closeness, and pre-dosing closeness predicted greater self-transcendent emotions during the subsequent MDMA session. These findings distinguish more stable therapeutic alliance from more dynamic felt interpersonal closeness and suggest that closeness may be a particularly sensitive relational process in MDMA-AT for SAD.

articles_hidden.title: Two Wisdoms, Two Pathways to Well-Being: Locus of Control among Tribal and Non-Tribal Youth in Jharkhand
articles_hidden.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Locus of control is widely treated as a near-universal predictor of psychological well-being. Most supporting evidence comes from Western, individualist samples. Whether this link holds equally in indigenous Indian communities remains unclear. Objective: This study compared locus of control and psychological well-being between tribal (Adivasi) and non-tribal youth in Jharkhand, India, and tested whether community moderates the strength of the relationship between the two. Method: A cross-sectional comparative design was used with 500 youth (250 tribal, 250 non-tribal), stratified equally by employment status and gender. Participants completed a 24-item locus of control scale and Ryff's six-dimension Psychological Well-Being scale. Results: Non-tribal youth scored substantially higher than tribal youth on both locus of control, t(449.4) = 23.76, p < .001, d = 2.12, and psychological well-being, t(326.2) = 13.83, p < .001, d = 1.24, with the largest subscale gap on Environmental Mastery, d = 2.09. The correlation between locus of control and well-being was far stronger among non-tribal youth (r = .93) than tribal youth (r = .43), a difference confirmed by a Fisher z-test, z = 13.08, p < .001. Conclusion: Community identity shapes not only mean levels of agency and well-being but also how tightly the two are linked, suggesting tribal well-being draws on pathways beyond individual perceived control.

articles_hidden.title: Combined sleep deprivation and light therapy for depression in major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Bartholomeus Haarman; Stella Druiven; Jeanine Kamphuis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Combined chronotherapy, a combination of sleep deprivation and light therapy, offers a promising approach to accelerating improvement in depression. Therapeutic sleep deprivation can have a rapid antidepressant effect, while light therapy and regulation of sleep timing are intended to maintain the initial benefit. This review examines the evidence supporting further clinical evaluation of combined chronotherapy in major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD).
Methods. We examined literature identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Europe PMC and citation searching, with the latest search conducted on 9 September 2026. Narrative synthesis was used to examine speed and persistence of response, clinical applicability and tolerability. Controlled studies of combined chronotherapy, studies of individual treatment components and observational studies were considered separately, with repeated reports linked where identifiable. We interpreted outcomes in relation to treatment schedules, comparators and study limitations.
Results. Seven randomised trials in adult patients with a depressive episode evaluated early antidepressant effects of combined chronotherapy. Several trials found rapid improvement, with benefits extending into follow-up, and outpatient studies support feasibility beyond inpatient settings. The most recent trial, including 44 randomised adults with masked outcome assessment, found greater improvement from day 5 through day 12 and discharge. Findings were not consistent across studies: one trial found an advantage confined to the first week, while two found no significant benefit on their primary comparisons. Studies of individual treatment components and clinical cohorts provide additional evidence on maintenance, patient selection and delivery.
Conclusions. Combined chronotherapy is a promising adjunctive treatment for depression in MDD and BD, with evidence of rapid improvement and persistence of benefit in some trials. Findings vary across treatment protocols and settings, and the magnitude and durability of benefit remain uncertain. Further adequately powered randomised trials are needed to establish its clinical role.

articles_hidden.title: What are we measuring when we measure moral concern?
articles_hidden.authors: Matti Wilks; Bastian Jaeger; Paul Bloom
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding the factors that shape who we consider worthy of moral concern has become a focus of moral psychology. This research generally shows that we care most about our family and close others, and less about non-humans and the environment. However, these studies sometimes yield unusual or nonsensical results. We demonstrate that these findings can be somewhat explained by issues with the conceptualization and measurement of moral concern. Study 1 reveals that many studies do not define their construct. Study 2 demonstrates weak convergent validity among five existing measures of moral concern. Study 3 highlights that laypeople actively differentiate between facets of moral concern, granting greater rights to a murderer than an apple tree, while expressing greater care and compassion for a tree. These findings indicate that treating distinct constructs, such as rights, obligations, and care, as interchangeable may limit our measurement and understanding of moral concern.

articles_hidden.title: A Systematic Review of MDMA’s Effects on Social Cognition in Placebo-Controlled Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Burmester; David Nutt; Laura Aggett; Chloe Wong; Sofia Bonito; Sophie Leigh; Tessa Bo Watford; Dasha Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is associated with distinctive prosocial and empathogenic effects, yet the consistency and scope of its impact on social cognition in humans remain unclear. Although numerous placebo-controlled studies have examined MDMA’s acute social effects, findings vary widely across subjective and behavioural domains.

Methods
We conducted a systematic review of placebo-controlled studies investigating the acute effects of MDMA on social cognition in adults. Outcomes included self-reported social and emotional experience, task-based measures of social cognition and behaviour, and relevant physiological and neurobiological indices. Studies administering MDMA as the sole intervention were included.

Results
Across 75 studies, MDMA reliably enhanced subjective social experience, including feelings of sociability, emotional openness, closeness, and emotional empathy. In contrast, behavioural manifestations of prosociality, such as cooperation and trust in economic or performance-based tasks, were inconsistent and strongly context dependent. Behavioural and neuroimaging measures showed reduced accuracy in identifying negative social cues, including fear and anger, but no study used signal-detection metrics to discriminate genuine perceptual blunting from a shift in response criterion. Neuroimaging findings were from small, methodologically heterogeneous samples.

Conclusions
MDMA consistently alters how social interactions are experienced, but subjective changes do not reliably translate into observable prosocial behaviour. MDMA reduces accuracy in identifying negative social cues, particularly fear and anger, but whether this reflects a specific blunting of threat processing or a shift in response bias and salience detection remains unresolved. Clarifying these mechanisms has implications for understanding MDMA’s therapeutic potential in conditions characterised by heightened social threat and avoidance.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive evidence for a mediated association between childhood adversity and resilience: A reexamination of Suriano and Valentino (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix published by Suriano and Valentino, we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking adverse childhood experiences with resilience. We show that the reported pattern of associations can be reproduced almost exactly by a conceptually distinct latent-variable model that does not rely on the influencing ordering specified in the original study. In this alternative framework, adverse childhood experiences, resilience, positive humor, and tolerance for ambiguity are treated as indicators of a broader latent characteristic, namely core self-evaluation. The results highlight an important challenge in observational research: a single covariance structure may be consistent with multiple theoretical explanations. As a result, correlational evidence alone provides limited justification for privileging one explanatory account over competing models. Researchers should therefore evaluate plausible alternative specifications before drawing strong conclusions about psychological mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: MEMORY RECOGNITION IN AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER ACROSS LABORATORY AND MUSEUM CONTEXTS: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY
articles_hidden.authors: Bastien Cothenet; Nicolas Navarro; Nadine Ravel; Amandine Rey
articles_hidden.abstract: Episodic memory in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has primarily been investigated using laboratory-based paradigms. This exploratory study examined recognition memory across two distinct encoding contexts: an on-site museum visit and a controlled laboratory setting. Ten adults with ASD and 25 neurotypical (NT) adults completed recognition tasks following both contexts. Recognition sensitivity (d′), recollection judgments, and detail-based versus gist-based recollection were assessed. Recognition sensitivity differed according to group and context: ASD participants showed higher sensitivity than NT participants in the laboratory, whereas no group difference emerged following the museum visit. Recollection rates for correctly recognized items were similar across groups. However, following museum encoding, ASD participants relied more on detail-based recollection, whereas NT participants relied more on gist-based recollection. These findings suggest that episodic memory differences in ASD may concern the nature of information supporting recollection, highlighting the value of studying memory in real-world settings alongside traditional laboratory paradigms.
