articles_hidden.title: The Common Format Hypothesis: The Central Form Integrates Causal Information from Different Domains into a Common Format
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper investigates the structure of human concepts within Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, and proposes and tests the Common Format Hypothesis. Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form—a unitary structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s conceptual information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a linked set of strong form-generated beliefs. The Common Format Hypothesis proposes that although causal knowledge and causal schemas differ across domains, central forms instantiate a common representational format. Across three experiments, participants learned about novel categories and their properties, with properties introduced either as satisfying a causal schema (which varied by domain) or as central form properties. The studies then tested the immediate activation of strong property-focused beliefs—specifically, beliefs about certainty, stability, and normativity. Results showed that while participants sometimes used causal cues to guide form encoding, they only exhibited these strong beliefs when a property had been encoded as part of the central form. This pattern held across domains (animals and artifacts), despite different causal structures. These findings support the Common Format Hypothesis and offer new insight into conceptual combination,  linguistic creativity, and concept learning.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Gastric State on Perceptual and Attitudinal Body Image Dimensions and Their Moderation by Eating Pathology
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Stafford; Alexandra Claire Pike; Catherine Preston
articles_hidden.abstract: Body image encompasses cognitive-affective attitudes and explicit and implicit body size perceptions. Although interoception is implicated in eating pathology, evidence directly linking gastrointestinal states to body image remains limited by caloric confounds, a dearth of research using perceptual measures, and narrow assessments of interoceptive facets. To address these gaps, this study (n=68) manipulated gastric state using the Water Load Test-II to evaluate how gastrointestinal sensitivity, over/unconfidence in sensitivity, and appraisal are related to baseline body image and disordered eating, and if gastric state can change body image and if this is moderated by disordered eating. At baseline, elevated hunger-fear and fullness-shame predicted heightened eating shame, dietary restriction/preoccupation, and reduced baseline body satisfaction, with fullness-shame uniquely predicting greater weight/shape concerns and restraint. Heightened gastrointestinal sensitivity predicted less certainty in judging an aperture as passable relative to body size, whereas underconfidence in gastrointestinal sensitivity predicted smaller waist size estimations and greater certainty in judging an aperture as passable. Controlling for baseline body image, fullness significantly decreased body satisfaction, increased the width required for an aperture to be judged as passable, and increased waist size estimations according to disordered eating severity. Eating disorder severity predicted lower certainty for aperture passability. During nutritional eating disorder recovery, where postprandial fullness is unavoidable, unaddressed negative appraisal, hypervigilance, and over/underconfidence in gastric sensitivity may directly trigger and perpetuate body image distortions and uncertainty. Eating to satiation, rather than complete fullness, may offer a behavioral goal for ongoing treatment once weight is stabilised.

articles_hidden.title: Acoustic correlates of phonological status
articles_hidden.authors: Maarten Versteegh; Amanda Seidl; Alejandrina Cristia; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles_hidden.abstract: Languages vary not only in terms of their sound inventory, but also in the phonological status certain sound distinctions are assigned. For example, while vowel nasality is lexically contrastive (phonemic) in Quebecois French, it is largely determined by the context (allophonic) in American English; the reverse is true for vowel tenseness. If phonetics and phonology interact, a minimal pair of sounds should span a larger acoustic divergence when it is pronounced by speakers for whom the underlying distinction is phonemic compared to allophonic. Near minimal pairs were segmented from a corpus of American English and Quebecois French using a crossed design (since nasality and tenseness have opposite phonological status in the two languages). Pairwise time-aligned divergences between contrasts were calculated on the basis of 7 mainstream spoken feature representations, and a set of linguistic phonetic measurements. Only carefully selected phonetic measurements revealed the expected cross-over, with larger divergences for English than French tokens of the tenseness contrast, and larger divergences for French than English tokens for the nasality contrast. We conclude that the phonetic effects of phonological status are subtle enough that only linguistically-informed (or supervised) measurements can pick up on them.

articles_hidden.title: Superior retention but not integration of information in memory in children versus adults
articles_hidden.authors: Emma James; Layla Unger
articles_hidden.abstract: Across childhood, we amass thousands of experiences from which we build knowledge about the world. Knowledge can come from both encoding memories for experiences (e.g., seeing items A and B on one occasion or A and C on another) and integrating information that spans multiple experiences (e.g., that B and C both occurred with A). Experiments that train overlapping AB-AC pairs show that when tested immediately afterwards, BC integration is relatively weak in children even when they successfully encode and remember pairs. In this study, we ask whether children can capitalise upon superior offline consolidation abilities to integrate this information at a delayed test one week later. Children aged 8-10 years (n = 137) and adults aged 18-31 years (n = 204) encoded overlapping pairs of cartoon creatures (A), objects (B), and scenes (C), as well as unique non-overlapping pairs (DE). Children showed similar memory for non-overlapping pairs to adults at the immediate test, and superior retention one week later. However, their weaker accuracy when integrating across overlapping pairs remained stable at both test points, even when both overlapping pairs had been successfully retrieved. We conclude limited evidence that children’s superior offline consolidation can compensate for weaknesses in memory integration.

articles_hidden.title: Introducing Synthetic Psychology:  Validation Across Personality and Established Relationships.
articles_hidden.authors: Michael McCormick; Todd McElroy
articles_hidden.abstract: This research introduces Synthetic Psychology (SP), a novel research approach in which large language models are configured to generate responses as synthetic individuals with predetermined psychological profiles. Across four studies with 20 replications, we configured Llama 3.3 as 32 distinct Big Five personality profiles (N = 30,400 synthetic respondents). Studies examined factor structure, personality-affect-wellbeing relationships, and personality-cognition relationships across extensive measures including risk-taking, need for cognition, thinking styles, and cognitive failures. Synthetic data replicated established patterns with exceptional fidelity and unprecedented reproducibility. Meta-analytic correlations demonstrated appropriate Big Five structure and theoretically expected relationships (e.g., Extraversion-Positive Affect r = .661-.664, Openness-Need for Cognition r = .984). While some correlations exceeded typical human magnitudes, results demonstrate SP's potential for preliminary hypothesis testing and theoretical exploration, with the caveat that synthetic data should be seen as a complement to rather than a replacement for human validation in psychological research.

articles_hidden.title: How observers decode pain from facial reactions. Distributed patterns of facial muscle contractions drive pain judgments in both naturalistic and synthetic expressions.
articles_hidden.authors: Nurefşan Üzmez; Ilaria Mirlisenna; Daniele Pugliese; Giada Dirupo; Laura Riontino; Corrado Corradi-Dell'Acqua
articles_hidden.abstract: Assessing others' pain relies heavily on facial expressions, yet how individuals translate observable facial features into pain judgements remains poorly understood. We combined a retrospective analysis of naturalistic spontaneous pain expressions across three different cohorts (Study 1, N = 398) with a reverse correlation experiment using synthetic facial stimuli (Study 2, N = 63), to investigate which facial muscle contractions (Action Units, AUs) drive pain judgments. Across both studies, we consistently found brow lowering (AU 4), nose wrinkling (AU 9) and brow raising (AU 1/2) as key contributors, alongside a more variable role of mouth movements. Multivariate pattern analysis indicated that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of facial AUs, rather than on single diagnostic cues. Finally, tailored co-engagement analysis from Study 2 identified AU pairs that, when combined, facilitate (AUs 1 + 12, AUs 4 + 24) or inhibit (AUs 4 + 9) pain assessments. Neither participants' own sex, the sex of the displayed face, nor participants' empathy traits substantially influenced pain judgments. These findings provide a first systematic mapping of the observable facial muscle contractions that drive human pain decoding. The identified facial features are best interpretable in terms of multiple, partly independent patterns of facial response, rather than a single prototypical template of pain expression.

articles_hidden.title: What Predicts Psychotherapy Outcomes Across Disorders and Treatments: an Umbrella Review
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Jacobs; Tabea Jaleta; Kevin Hilbert
articles_hidden.abstract:
The objective of assigning patients to their most promising treatment has sparked considerable interest in 
contemporary research. Many studies develop models to predict treatment outcomes and stratify treatment 
allocation. Predictive accuracy of such models, however, has remained limited due to a lack of systematic 
information used for model training, given that variables included in such datasets are often selected due to their 
availability in routine care datasets. To increase systematic information in the data, the inclusion of promising 
candidate predictors, based on theoretical or empirical considerations, is crucial. Therefore, this study 
systematically searches for and summarizes the evidence on patient level variables that predict psychotherapy 
outcome. Since the literature to answer this question is vast, an umbrella review methodology (i.e., a review of 
reviews) was implemented. Searches in PubMed, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library with preregistered 
search strings yielded 5926 articles. Title and abstract screening implemented AI-based methods alongside 
human review. N = 51 papers were extracted and quantitative evidence was descriptively aggregated. We 
identified 69 potential predictors. Using post-hoc defined criteria, reliable and relevant predictors were selected. 
Some of these were known and frequently assessed predictors (e.g., symptom severity, diagnosis) while others 
are not frequently assessed in routine care. Among the latter were social support, executive functioning, 
therapeutic alliance and motivation for treatment. The identified variables represent promising candidate 
predictors, which can inform theoretical models of therapy success, guide clinicians, or, if included in future 
analysis pipelines, have the potential to increase predictive performance in psychotherapy studies.

articles_hidden.title: Social Coercion in the Shadow of Hierarchy: State-Mediated Coercive Mobilisation and Australians' COVID-19 Vaccination Compliance
articles_hidden.authors: Katie Attwell; Joshua Lake
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: This study investigates coercive (social) mobilisation to vaccinate in liberal democracies using evidence from Australia.
Methods: We analyse how government policies can prompt non-state actors to pressure the unvaccinated. We then analyse data on COVID-19 vaccination in a representative sample of adults (N=4208), investigating the prevalence and sources of coercive mobilisation and conducting regression analyses to identify associated factors.
Results: Conceptual analysis distinguished between state-led coercive mobilisation, where authoritarian governments rely on hierarchical structures to pressure citizens, and state-mediated coercive mobilisation, whereby liberal democratic governments generate social pressure through vaccine mandates that produce encourage stigmatisation, workplace expansion, and pressures associated with collective goals. Empirically, a quarter of people vaccinated reported being coerced, and more than half reported responding to some degree of social pressure. Social coercion was most common in New South Wales and Victoria. People were more likely to attribute vaccination to social coercion when they had lower political trust, or lower trust in friends and family as sources of vaccination information. Higher trust in social media sources and stronger community connectedness were associated with increased attribution to coercion. Higher education and socioeconomic status were associated with increased attributions of employer coercion, and education workers reported more social coercion. Younger people were consistently more likely to attribute vaccination to coercive mobilisation, with some evidence this was also true for women.
Conclusion: Findings extend research on coercive mobilisation beyond non-democratic settings, revealing similar dynamics shaping vaccination decisions in liberal democracies.

articles_hidden.title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
articles_hidden.authors: Tohid Zarei; Caelan Farr; Maxx Fischer; Summer Marchiori; KJ Hepworth; Caroline Ellison; Tobias Loetscher
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic peer support, as a two-way system of help, is uniquely positioned to address high rates of loneliness and mental health challenges among autistic young adults. We aimed to inform the development of autistic peer support programs aligned with participants’ preferences and needs through a mixed methods online survey study. A total of 73 autistic young adults (aged 18-30; 34 women, 19 non-binary, 11 men, 7 transgender men, 1 transgender woman, 1 undisclosed) completed a survey covering peer interactions, peer support preferences and needs, as well as delivery preferences. While following participatory research processes, we used reflexive thematic analysis to identify an overarching theme: flying together through shared understanding and shared struggles. This maps onto participants’ desire for reciprocal connections that enable understanding and safe unmasking, and their preference for in-person programs adapted to a range of support needs with meaningful participation in decision-making. Autistic Burnout and social connection were most participants’ preferred areas to be addressed. Especially when co-produced or peer-led, autistic peer support programs can contribute to providing a sense of collective movement with preserved self-determination for participants.

articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates and behavioral outcomes of aesthetic chills and their prosthetic augmentation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Schoeller; Leonardo Christov-Moore; Ninette Simonian; NA; Yaya Shi; Abhinandan Jain; Adam Horowitz; Velu Prabhakar Kumaravel; Ben Zhang; Micah Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: Aesthetic chills, psychogenic shivers elicited by emotionally charged stimuli such as music, offer a neurophysiological marker bridging subjective experience and measurable physiology. Although neuroimaging has localized chills to reward and interoceptive circuits and behavioral work has linked them to prosocial outcomes, their electrophysiological signature and its relationship to psychological change remain poorly characterized, precluding comparison with phenomenologically similar states induced by other means (e.g., psychedelics). Here we recorded 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG; n = 103) during validated chill-inducing music and examined spectral and complexity-based signatures of chills, their relationships to self-transcendence, psychological insight, emotional breakthrough, and prosocial behavior, and whether augmenting peripheral chill sensations with a custom thermal prosthesis modulates neural activity, phenomenology, and behavior. Chills carried a spatially distributed signature of attenuated theta power, elevated gamma power, and convergent increases across four independent complexity measures. Chills predicted self-transcendent phenomenology in a graded fashion across binary, frequency, and intensity operationalizations, yet predicted neither prosocial behavior nor schema change; both were instead predicted by the chills-locked neural signature, with distinct complexity measures tracking distinct outcome families. Thermal augmentation left the behavioral incidence of chills unchanged; in exploratory mediation models, however, it shifted chills-specific dynamics toward criticality and away from undifferentiated entropy, linking embodied augmentation to phenomenological, affective, prosocial, and schema outcomes. Aesthetic chills may therefore constitute an at least partially neuro-mimetic analogue of the psychedelic state, sharing its elevated signal diversity and a theta attenuation concordant with recent psilocybin electrophysiology, while gamma correspondence and the absence of psychedelic-typical alpha suppression remain unresolved.

articles.title: Who Wants More War? Conflict Exposure, Perceptions of Public Opinion, and Preferences for Conflict Escalation in Israel
articles.authors: Nicholas Sambanis; Itamar Yakir
articles.abstract: We explore whether conformity to perceptions of public opinion shapes individual foreign policy preferences in the aftermath of a militarized conflict between Israel and Iran in June 2025. Exploiting naturally occurring variation in exposure to an Iranian missile attack, we measure Israelis' proneness to hawkish (vs. dovish) policy responses as a function of information concerning the majority's policy preferences. We find that Israelis shift their preferences to align with perceived majority opinion: when they perceive the public to be dovish, they support more dovish positions; whereas they become more hawkish when they perceive the public as hawkish. People who report having been exposed to Iranian attacks show stronger support for belligerence. Partisanship also matters as respondents are more likely to respond to cues aligned with priors that are consistent with their party's positions. We explore mechanisms of these patterns.

articles.title: Climate Change Coverage in The Guardian, 2010–2025
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Simon Wimmer; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Leading news outlets play a central role in shaping how political leaders and the public understand the causes, impacts, and solutions to climate change. Here, we provide the first comprehensive assessment of how The Guardian, a globally influential newspaper widely recognized for high-quality climate journalism, has reported on climate change between 2010 and 2025. We applied a validated methodology based on large language models to analyze N = 18,785 articles and evaluate to what extent reporting covers scientifically grounded causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and adaptation measures. We find that climate coverage increased markedly after 2018 and has remained structurally elevated relative to the preceding decade. Coverage of causes and mitigation is dominated by fossil fuels and renewable energy, whereas agriculture, overconsumption, carbon inequality, and economic growth are mentioned far less frequently. Aspects related to adaptation receive considerably less attention than aspects related to causes, impacts, and mitigation. Our findings highlight opportunities for more comprehensive coverage that better reflects full range of societal transformations needed to address climate change.

articles.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
articles.authors: Meg Small; Sally Dancer; Jonathan Wright; Blake Anthony Colaianne; Gillian Sommerville
articles.abstract: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

articles.title: The Symbolic Organisation of Political Antagonism: An Integrative Model of Cultural and Social Polarisation
articles.authors: Werner Binder; Matthias Revers; Marcus Morgan; María Luengo
articles.abstract: This article develops a cultural and relational model of political polarisation that integrates insights from currently disconnected streams of scholarship to conceive polarisation as a discursive and performative struggle over sacred meanings. Rather than treating polarisation as mere attitudinal divergence, we frame it as the symbolic organization of political antagonism. We identify three interrelated cultural dimensions and one social dimension. These are (1) ideological divergence as bifurcating responses to contested issues, conceptualized as morally and emotionally charged signifiers; (2) the ideological consistency of these divergent issues, enabling chains of signification held together by what we call 'linking signifiers' that mark group identity; (3) the mutual constitution of opposing semiotic chains and identities, which describes how antagonistic groups performatively mobilise opposing discourses to co-constitutively define themselves in relation to one another; and (4) social polarisation, which is based in e.g., inequalities, segregations, or violent conflicts.  We then present a pathway model which expresses how cultural and social polarisation drive or diminish one another over time. This model thereby offers a sociological theory of polarisation and depolarisation as interlinked processes rather than as separate phenomena requiring separate theories. This paper also maps out the implications of our model for empirical polarisation and depolarisation research.

articles.title: Who influences climate adaptation? Farmer and advisor social networks and differentiated benefits of participation in a climate adaptation fellowship program
articles.authors: Sara Delaney; Rachel E. Schattman; Janica Anderzén
articles.abstract: Due to ongoing and projected environmental change farmers and agricultural advisors need access to up-to-date and relevant information and advice to continue to be effective in their work. Education and advising services aim to transmit new information and facilitate change in behavior, often using peer-to-peer or cohort style approaches. However, given that learning and behavior is continuously shaped by interactions, we must understand the role of these interventions within broader climate adaptation networks. This study explores the social networks of a cohort of farmers and agricultural advisors who participated in a Climate Adaptation Fellowship program. Drawing on pre- and post-program surveys and interviews and longitudinal social network analysis, we first explore the range of sources that farmers and advisors in this cohort reported using for adaptation-related information, advice, and support. We also examine the impact of the program on the inter-cohort network and participants’ individual social networks. We find high diversity in the composition of interviewees’ adaptation networks. Farmers and advisors engage widely on adaptation, and while they use other farmers and advisors as resources for adaptation, they also draw on media, customers, friends, family, and the broader community. This heterogeneity has benefits for effective decision-making but also implies that messaging through single channels will only reach a limited audience. The analysis also shows that the program had variable effects among participants over time. There was a meaningful change in the social networks of approximately half of the fellows. While a subset of the group grew progressively more densely connected, others lost contact. We argue that this uneven engagement and impact is not a fault, but instead an invitation to capitalize on the energy of these most interconnected members and also find opportunities to engage those on the periphery over time. Programming can also be strategically expanded to a wider circle to help participants carry forward new learning.

articles.title: Concentration Without Representation
articles.authors: Burak Ozturan; David Lazer
articles.abstract:
A small fraction of users produces most of what circulates online, and the expectation that falling
publication costs would flatten this gradient has not been borne out. Two questions about that
concentration remain open. Published estimates of how concentrated sharing is vary by a factor
of three at comparable thresholds, with no account of why, and the demographic composition of
heavy sharers has received little systematic attention outside the study of misinformation, where
existing work does not separate the users who share the most from those whose shares reach the
most people. Using 38 million news shares by 493,237 registered US voters matched to their Twit-
ter accounts across 57 months, we address both. Observation-window length alone reproduces
the full factor-of-three range within a single dataset, holding population and content fixed. The
top one percent accounts for 22 percent of shares at a one-week window and 52 percent at 57
months. Two tests establish that the rise is compositional and not behavioral, since holding sample
size fixed does not flatten the curve and a cohort of the same users followed across all windows
stays near 21 percent throughout. Matching observation windows to prior studies that overlap our
own panel narrows the gap for comparable content almost entirely, while a residual gap against
misinformation-specific estimates reflects a difference in content class rather than window choice.
Ranking the same users by sharing volume and by audience reach identifies substantially overlap-
ping but still distinct populations, overlapping by 49.9 percent at the top one percent against one
percent expected by chance. Both elites are older and more Democratic than the panel, with mean
age rising from 40.5 years to 57.0 under activity ranking. Gender behaves differently. Male and
female users share at statistically indistinguishable rates throughout the activity distribution, and
a thirteen-point gap appears only at the extreme of the follower tail, where female share falls to
34.8 percent. Elite position is durable at the head of the distribution and close to memoryless in
the middle. The users who share the most only partly overlap with the users whose shares travel
furthest, and both groups are unrepresentative of the voting public in overlapping but distinct ways.

articles.title: Review bombing the video game industries: Sabotage as political consumer practice
articles.authors: Andrew Wirzburger
articles.abstract: Spaces of consumption have long been sites of tension and contestation between corporations and consumers. Since the late 2010s, review bombing has emerged as a persistent feature of this conflict. Consumers practice review bombing to take action in response to perceived grievances by inundating products with negative online reviews to drive down their aggregate ratings. Online reviews have been touted as part of a shift in power from producers to consumers championed by the logics of social commerce, and yet companies wield tremendous power over consumers. This study frames review bombing as sabotage, a withdrawal of efficiency. Through relational-ethnographic approaches to two cases of review bombing in the video game industries, the study argues that the efficacy of review bombing depends on a combination of spectacle and policy. While specific outcomes vary, review bombing is exceedingly effective at sabotaging the logics of the video games industries more broadly.

articles.title: Representation of Police in Television, 2020 Anti-Police Movements, and Audience Reception
articles.authors: Jenny Lee
articles.abstract: Police television is one of the most popular genres of television in the modern age. With its continued popularity and high viewership, police television, from fictional to reality shows, is often the first introduction to the criminal justice system for many viewers. Prior research has also shown that many people believe that the information they see on police television is factual and reflective of reality, whether this information is fact checked or not. In fact, the police institution relies on its cultural power to sustain its status as maintainers of social order and of regulators of deviance. However, with the 2020 anti-police brutality movements, the public atmosphere around police undeniably shifted toward a more negative outlook than before. With this question, I seek to identify whether or not there has been a change in the way police officers are portrayed in television, and if so, how change has been implemented. In addition, I seek to find how police television continues to curate a specific image of police officers without ignoring the social movements that were present. Through the qualitative observation of two television shows, I explore the changes in portrayals of police officers across the two shows. I find that there are more varied portrayals of police officers in specific categories, yet police officers are still shown to be the sole method of maintaining social order and controlling deviance. The police television shows observed in this paper adhere to the promotion of “ideal cop” principles to show the effectiveness of police officers in regulating society.

articles.title: How bibliometric indicators align with REF 2021 peer review across disciplines
articles.authors: Junjie Shen
articles.abstract: Bibliometric indicators are increasingly used to approximate expert peer review, but how well they do so varies across disciplines in ways that remain poorly understood. Existing analyses of the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) have largely correlated metrics with individual article quality scores, within single fields and using restricted-access data. This study takes a complementary approach based on publicly available data: institutional REF 2021 output GPA is correlated with a consistent set of citation-based and journal-based indicators for all submitting institutions across fifteen Units of Assessment (UoAs). Comparing the two types of indicators side by side reveals a continuum of evaluation cultures. At one end, Physics tracks citation impact far more closely than journal rank (correlations of 0.85 versus 0.42, based on the share of outputs in the top 10% of each measure). At the other end, Business and Management Studies shows the reverse (0.59 versus 0.92), among the strongest journal-based correlations across all fields examined. Of the fifteen UoAs, nine correspond best with journal-based indicators and six with citation-based indicators, a divide that cuts across the usual STEM/non-STEM boundary. Indicator validity is therefore not a property of the metric alone but of the discipline’s evaluation culture, and research assessment should choose and interpret metrics field by field.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Green: The Production of Green Conformity in European Cultural Policy
articles.authors: Vânia Rodrigues; Catarina Santos-Silva; Olga Solovova
articles.abstract:
Ecological vocabulary is nearly absent until 2021, when greening became a cross-cutting programme priority, and rises abruptly thereafter. Green, climate and sustainable increasingly appear together as an interchangeable signal of commitment. Sustainable also retains its earlier organisational meaning, binding ecological claims to claims of institutional survival. Modernisation dominates the coded projects, framing sustainability as innovation, capacity-building and better practice. Transformative elements persist only as traces, and the vocabularies of degrowth, commoning and ecological justice are absent or residual across the whole corpus. The programme's explicit greening guidance appears to supply the very terms in which compliance is demonstrated.
The article argues that this narrowing is anticipatory and sincere, which makes it harder to contest than greenwashing. It contributes to debates on travelling cultural policy and multilateral cultural governance by showing how a transnational green idiom, composed largely in English, carries a sustainability paradigm across Europe while constraining the ecological futures cultural institutions can meaningfully articulate.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz
articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. A bounded exploratory pilot applies the strategy to the publicly accessible, logged-out segment of ConsultaLEX, the Portuguese government portal for legislative and regulatory consultations. The pilot covers discovery, orientation, and authentication and assesses the availability of an entry point to expression and feedback. It identifies enabling conditions in programmatically named controls, structured consultation information, exact dates, and alternative authentication routes. Potentially constraining conditions involve relative deadlines, scripted navigation, registration and identity requirements, and human verification. Because no live commenting process was available, expression and feedback could not be inspected. The study therefore supports mechanism-level inferences rather than claims about participant exclusion or platform-wide conformance. These findings support treating accessibility as a necessary but insufficient condition for equal participation. The paper contributes a proof of concept connecting accessibility evidence to democratic analysis and identifies disability-led participant testing, live-process observation, and cross-platform comparison as priorities for future research.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Long-Term Health Financing in Chile: A Historical Analysis of the Segmented System, 1981–2024
articles.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Camilo Cid Pedraza
articles.abstract: The objective of this article is to present the results of reconstructing the historical series of health expenditure in Chile from the creation of the segmented model in 1981 to 2024, and to briefly analyze its evolution in historical context. To this end, data were collected and digitized from primary sources: the Statistical Bulletins and Public Accounts of FONASA (1989–2016; 2020–2024), the Statistical Series of the Isapre System (SUPER, 1990–2024), and the Public Finance Statistics of DIPRES (2004–2025). The results show accelerated growth in private spending until the 1990s, followed by a sustained increase in public health expenditure associated with higher fiscal contributions and mandatory contributions. However, the long-term analysis reveals periods of slowdown in public spending coinciding with the expansion of private infrastructure, revealing the persistence of a segmented and unequal financing system. The trajectory of Chilean health expenditure shows significant variation in proportions and pace, conditioned by political and economic contexts. Alongside this analysis, we make the complete series used available to researchers in open access.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: Harnessing Human–AI Interpretive Difference: Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: Recent debate over GenAI in qualitative inquiry centres on concerns that computational participation reinforces postpositivist dominance. Critical analysts propose excluding it, out-theorising it, or continuously inspecting its entanglements. In parallel, a growing body of work builds architectures to accommodate human-AI collaboration in interpretive inquiry. While most of this work relies on postpositivist assumptions, an emerging strand develops collaborative architectures grounded in interpretivism, an approach this article adopts. I propose that for computational interpretation to be part of interpretivist inquiry without being granted reflexivity or interpretive authority, it must be deliberately structured into an accountable, productive relationship alongside human interpretation. To that end, I outline Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism, an epistemological position resting on five propositions. First, productive epistemic non-equivalence holds that human and computational interpretation need not share an epistemic basis for their difference to be structured as a resource. Second, interpretive co-construction grounds computational interpretation in meanings negotiated between researcher and participant, rather than a decontextualised corpus. Third, productive divergence treats non-alignment between human and computational interpretations as a potential source of analytic insight. Fourth, interpretive traceability refers to the capacity to see the grounds upon which human and computational interpretations are made, rendering them accountable structurally. Fifth, reflexive engagement holds that computational participation can create occasions for the researcher to interrogate her relationship to her subjectivity. This position is operationalised through Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA). LICA deploys computational interpretation to anchor interpretive insights to the empirical material. It integrates explicit interpretive co-construction between participant and researcher in interviews, scrutinises divergence between researcher and computational interpretations, renders analytic reasoning traceable, and embeds the researcher's subjectivity into the computational process. Together, these features create the conditions for new insights to emerge from the interaction between human and computational interpretations.

articles.title: The Qualitative Network Approach: A Methodological Framework and Tutorial for Relational Coding
articles.authors: Ivonne Lipsch-Wijnen; Femke Nijland; Vanessa Torres van Grinsven; Szilvia Zörgő; Gjalt - Jorn Peters
articles.abstract: Relationships between concepts are often interpreted during qualitative analysis but may remain implicit within coding structures, thematic descriptions, or analytical narratives. This article introduces the Qualitative Network Approach (QNA), a methodological framework for representing qualitative codes as interconnected elements. Its associated method, QNA network coding, specifies interpreted connections between pairs of qualitative codes according to relationship type and, where relevant, directionality. A four-step tutorial demonstrates how researchers can identify two concepts in the data for relational interpretation, identify and specify their relationship using the codebook, assign the three codes to the data fragment, and document a QNA network code. A worked interview example illustrates how individual QNA network codes can form a wider QNA network code structure. QNA may be useful when relationships between concepts are analytically important. By making relational interpretations explicit and traceable to the underlying data, QNA aims to increase the transparency and inspectability of qualitative analysis.

articles.title: Sentiment change points, not peaks, mark when public opinion has yet to settle
articles.authors: Chenying Weng; Yilun Chen; Huazhen Huang; Yiting Yang; He Gong; Hongkai Wang
articles.abstract: Timing interventions during public controversies requires more than identifying when sentiment is strongest: a peak does not tell us whether public opinion can still change. We analyzed about 1.34M Weibo posts about a controversial news event (Company T vs. Company L), separating sentiment strength by referent and tracking the resulting trajectories across the event. After sudden change points (SCPs) sentiment-strength trajectories and public expression continued to change; after peak points (PPs) they largely stabilized (mean absolute displacement 3.291 times; p = 0.035), and discourse-strategy composition changed around SCPs but stayed largely stable around PPs. SCPs, not PPs, are the candidate leverage points. This suggests that the strongest moment is where public opinion settles, so mitigation should act at the SCP.

articles.title: Integrating Green Marketing and Environmental Behavior to Predict Revisit Intention in Indonesian Ecotourism
articles.authors: Andina Fasha; Cheryn Kang; Lady; Budi Setiawan
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The escalation of ecotourism as sustainability-oriented travel highlights the inconsistency of tourists' responsible actions during visits, which is also known as the attitude-behavior gap, whereas environmental concern does not necessarily translate into action, as discussed in sustainable tourism literature.

Research Methodology: A quantitative approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, collected through questionnaire surveys from 478 tourists who had previously visited Ecotourism destinations in Batam City, Indonesia, using SmartPLS 4.

Results: The findings show how direct environmental experiences at the destination were more effective in encouraging responsible tourist behavior than pre-visit digital exposure, which presumes that it is more likely to develop revisit intentions as long-term destination loyalty.

Conclusions: The study highlights the importance of environmental behavior in fostering revisit intention within ecotourism destinations and suggests that direct interpretive experiences at the destination may play a more influential role in shaping tourists’ behavior than digital promotional exposure alone.

Limitations: This study was limited to one ecotourism site in Batam City, with cross-sectional self-reported data, which may have limited generalizability.

Contributions: This study extends sustainable tourism literature by integrating digital green marketing, environmental belief, and environmental interpretation into a unified behavioral framework explaining revisit intention through environmental behavior and offer practical insights for ecotourism managers to strengthen sustainable behavior and long-term destination loyalty through effective communication and interpretation strategies.

articles.title: The nirvana fallacy and the case for friction in responding to online child sexual abuse
articles.authors: Joel Scanlan
articles.abstract: On 3 April 2026 the European Union’s temporary exception for voluntary detection of child sexual abuse material lapsed, and for three months the alternative that perfectionist arguments rarely state became policy: to do nothing. During the previous gap, in 2020–21, reports of abuse material from the EU fell by 58%. This article names the reasoning behind such outcomes as the nirvana fallacy, which Demsetz identified in 1969 as measuring the imperfect against an ideal instead of the real alternative. Four forms recur in the child-safety debate: circumvention, false positives, categorical impossibility and the slippery slope. Each states a real issue and leaves its comparator unstated. The article reframes the measures as friction, drawing on situational crime prevention, public health harm reduction and the economics of adversarial systems, then works along the offending pathway to set out what each friction layer achieves and what it cannot. Randomised trials and field deployments on Google Search, Pornhub and the Tor search engine Ahmia.fi show warnings reducing attempted access and increasing help-seeking, while hash matching, classifiers and age assurance carry known limits alongside measured effects. The article does not propose weakening encryption, and argues that most serious objections to other controls should be treated as design constraints rather than as refusals. A comparative test of four questions applies to objections and proposals alike, along with eight recommendations. Layered friction reduces measured offending-related behaviour at nearly every point it has been tested, and children are safer with it in the system than without it.

articles.title: Selection, Allocation, and Timing: Three Obstacles to Measuring the Effect of Large-Load Growth on Household Electricity Prices
articles.authors: Babu George
articles.abstract: Published estimates of how hyperscale computing load affects household electricity prices disagree about sign as well as magnitude. This article argues that much of the disagreement reflects three identification problems that existing designs often absorb rather than model directly. Large loads choose low-cost locations, making exposure endogenous. Average revenue per kilowatt-hour cannot distinguish a change in rates from a change in the composition of customers within a class. In jurisdictions that allow construction costs into rates before a plant enters service, bills may change years before the associated load appears in sales data. I examine each problem using public data. With state-level price and sales data for 2023 and 2024 for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, I find direct evidence of siting selection: the 2023 residential price level explains 22 percent of the cross-state variance in subsequent non-residential sales growth. That sorting appears to follow a state’s general cost level rather than the depth of the discount already received by large customers, a more tractable pattern for identification. Non-residential sales growth has no detectable relation to residential price growth, although the design lacks power to detect elasticities below roughly 0.9, so the null is not substantively informative. The residential-to-industrial price ratio rises with load growth, but decomposition shows that seven-tenths of the movement comes from falling non-residential prices rather than rising residential prices; the same pattern appears relative to the commercial class, and half of the association disappears after adding a four-category regional control. Translating the reduced-form slope into an implied price for incremental load shows that a pure composition account would require these kilowatt-hours to be served at about one-third of the class average, a demanding but possible figure whose confidence interval cannot adjudicate the issue. The evidence favors a regime-dependent interpretation of the literature and indicates that future work should treat capital deployment, rather than realized energy sales, as the central treatment variable.

articles.title: Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis: A Methodological Architecture for Human–AI Collaboration in Qualitative Inquiry
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: When generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is adopted without attention to its epistemological implications, postpositivist commitments to truth-seeking over meaning-making risk becoming more entrenched in qualitative inquiry, eroding reflexivity and interpretive depth. This has prompted scholars to call for the GenAI debate to move beyond binary adoption-or-refusal framings, toward how GenAI might be deployed while preserving reflexivity, theoretical depth, and epistemological plurality. I outline Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA), an interpretivist human–AI collaboration architecture, as a methodological answer to this call. LICA operationalises the position of Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism. It maintains distinct human and computational interpretive layers across six analytic steps. The architecture is centred on the live interpretation interview, which yields an initial participant narrative and a co-constructed interpretive narration negotiated between the participant and researcher. The initial narrative serves as a basis for thematic analysis, while the co-constructed interpretive narration grounds ideal-type analysis. Findings are brought together into a thematic-typological integrative analysis, which addresses what the complete thematic-typological configuration means in relation to the research question, and clarifies what it reveals about the underlying reflexive processes and human–AI collaboration. Throughout the process, human–AI divergences are retained and warranted as potential sources of analytic insights, while a traceable genealogy links successive analytic constructs to their empirical origins and interpretative context. Rather than accelerating an existing workflow, LICA relocates analytic effort to the research encounter and structures computational participation to interrogate interpretive judgement and reflexivity. For contexts where GenAI use raises strong ethical, environmental, or participant-vulnerability concerns, the method can be adapted into Layered Interpretive Analysis (LIA), a non-computational variant which retains key features of explicit meaning co-construction and thematic-typological integration.

articles.title: Automated Creativity in the Imagined Network: Creative Writer's View on Generative AI
articles.authors: Tianyu Zhao
articles.abstract:
As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies reshape the creative sector, understanding their implications for writers becomes increasingly vital. The study addresses a significant research gap by the impact of GenAI on creative writers in the United Kingdom, focusing on their perceptions and interactions within professional networks. The research explores two primary questions: how UK creative writers perceive and interact with GenAI technologies in their professional network, and what factors shape these perceptions and interactions within the creative industry. Employing a qualitative approach, the study conducts in-depth interviews with members of the Writers' Guild of Great Britain to gather rich, contextual qualitative response.

Key findings reveal the complex relationship between writers' self-identification within their professional networks and the integration of GenAI technologies. The study also uncovers writers' concerns about potential displacement by AI and examines the interplay between GenAI and capitalist forces in the creative industry. By centring the voices of creative writers, this research contributes to the ongoing discourse on technology and creativity, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of the sociotechnical dynamics in the creative industry. The study informs future discussions on the ethical use of AI in creative fields and provides an STS perspective on the evolving relationship between technology and creative professionals.

articles.title: Localizing the Sustainable Development Goals through Digitally Visible Initiatives: An Exploratory Study in Brazil
articles.authors: Cecilia Kotzias; Tamer Uzun; Hans Michael van Bellen; Roberto Pacheco; Cinthya Mônica da Silva Zanuzzi; Paulo Maurício Selig
articles.abstract: Community-based and other sustainability-oriented initiatives across Brazil address problems central to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), yet their contributions may be less visible within formal SDG monitoring because they are distributed across numerous small actors and often expressed in local rather than SDG terminology. This study frames the challenge of making the contributions of such initiatives legible within SDG localization as a knowledge-translation problem and develops an exploratory digital mapping and classification procedure for identifying and interpreting digitally visible sustainability-oriented initiatives in relation to nationalized SDG targets. An iterative snowball mapping procedure on Instagram identified 2,328 publicly visible profiles, from which 256 sustainability-oriented initiatives were classified in relation to nationalized SDG targets (230 assigned a primary SDG). A documented subset of 50 initiatives, including 47 examined using additional public sources, was analyzed in depth. Coding followed a transparent codebook, and an independent second coder recoded the documented subset, yielding moderate intercoder reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.57), followed by negotiated adjudication of disagreements. The findings indicate that many initiatives address SDG-relevant problems without using SDG terminology, that assigning a single primary SDG entails interpretive loss when representing multidimensional local practices, and that fewer than one quarter of the initiatives in the in-depth subset are directly recognized in Brazil's official civil society registry. The study introduces a transparent and auditable mapping-and-classification procedure grounded in this framing and provides empirical insights into both the analytical potential and the interpretive limits of translating situated local narratives into classifications aligned with nationalized SDG targets.

articles.title: FASTrack: A co-designed cloud-based planning support system for interactive cycling infrastructure scenario assessment
articles.authors: Ryan Turner; Afshin Jafari; Sapan Tiwari; Alan Both; Dhirendra Singh; Steve Pemberton; Chris De Gruyter
articles.abstract: Testing transport interventions using city-scale transport models is typically resource intensive, requiring specialist expertise, substantial data and computational capacity. As a result, such modelling is often concentrated on major projects and larger metropolitan areas, while smaller interventions and mid-sized regional cities have limited access to comparable modelling capabilities. This is particularly relevant to active travel, where cycling infrastructure decisions frequently need to be made with relatively limited modelling and decision-support capacity. This study presents FASTrack, a cloud-based planning support software system that integrates agent-based modelling, behavioural simulation, and interactive scenario visualisation to enable proposed cycling infrastructure assessment. A case study is applied to the City of Greater Bendigo, a mid-sized regional Australian city representative of the planning contexts that existing platforms often overlook. FASTrack was developed through a co-design process over three years with local government planning partners, to address the need to rapidly assess infrastructure scenarios, quantify changes in cycling demand and behaviour, and inform infrastructure planning and investment appraisal. These requirements underpin its design, including the use of probabilistic modelling and a cloud-based workflow designed to support rapid, on-demand scenario testing with minimal specialist modelling expertise. Scenario outcomes are presented through interactive dashboard-style interfaces that detail estimated changes in network use, level of traffic stress, mode shift, cycling usage, emissions, and cost-benefit analysis aligned with national appraisal guidelines. This study demonstrates how co-design can directly shape the development of planning support systems by translating practitioner requirements into accessible modelling platforms for cycling infrastructure planning

articles.title: Generational Imprinting: How Political Events Shape Cohorts
articles.authors: Turgut Keskintürk
articles.abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large-scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

articles.title: Mapping the Discourse Network of Cervical Cancer Screening on Reddit: A Topic-Network Approach
articles.authors: Qiyao Peng
articles.abstract: Online health communities are a primary venue where the public interprets cervical cancer screening, yet how peer discourse, which has no editorial authority, bundles screening concerns remains unclear. Drawing on network agenda setting (NAS), this study treats a peer community as a collective agenda-setter and asks how it organizes screening topics. This paper analyzes 9,851 posts and comments from seven women's-health subreddits (August 2025 to January 2026) using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and the Analysis of Topic Model Networks, with Spearman topic-loading similarity filtered to a significant backbone. Thirteen topics form three communities: a diagnostic-information agenda, an embodied exam-experience agenda, and a narrative-and-support agenda. Embodied, temporally anchored concerns hold them together: timing and bleeding, pelvic pain, and access carry the highest betweenness. Sentiment follows network position, with support positive and cancer risk negative. These findings extend NAS to agenda-less, peer-driven settings and map how health agendas emerge from the bottom up.

articles.title: Able but unwilling? Mapping citizens’ political GenAI use through the lens of Expectancy-Value Theory
articles.authors: Michael van Straelen; Christopher Starke; Patrick van Erkel; Jessica Piotrowski; Nils Köbis
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise and risk for democracy, yet little is known about how
citizens evaluate and adopt it for political purposes. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory
and Uses & Gratifications Theory, this study offers an initial account of political GenAI
adoption, mapping how citizens' cost-value perceptions and expectancy beliefs cluster into
distinct profiles. We investigate how these ‘expectancy-value profiles’ shape political GenAI
use. Using cross-sectional survey data from 947 Dutch respondents, we conduct a latent
profile analysis, identifying four profiles: optimists, cautious pragmatists, sceptics, and
indifferents. Profile differences stem largely from differing cost-value perceptions rather than
expectancy beliefs, suggesting the question is less about whether people feel able to use
GenAI, and more about whether they feel it is worth using. Across all profiles, cost
perceptions are high and political use is low, though optimists report significantly more use
than others. Individuals’ political dispositions predict usage but not profile membership and
among technological dispositions, trust in GenAI and belief in the machine heuristic predict
being an optimist. Findings raise concerns about uncalibrated trust among adopters.

articles.title: The Power of “We” in Science Funding and Publication
articles.authors: Lijian Peng; Wenwen Li; Yi Bu; Hao Peng
articles.abstract:
Linguistic communication supports all stages of scientific innovation. However, we have limited understanding of rhetorical strategies for facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science. 
Drawing on prior literature on the importance of personal pronouns in inter-personal communication, we examine the unique role of first-person plural pronouns (``We'' words, including ``we'', ``us'', ``our'') in science funding and publishing. 
Our study leverages the full sample of 13K grant proposals submitted to the Novo Nordisk Foundation and 47K research papers submitted to BMJO and ICLR between 2011 and 2024. 
We find a strong and universal positive association between ``we'' words and success rates even after accounting for important confounding factors related to content, novelty, and author impact.
Specifically, a one percentage point increase in the percentage of ``We'' words used in the full text is associated with a 36-51% increase in the odds of success for grants and papers.
Furthermore, we find that the effect of ``We'' is applicable to both editors and reviewers of BMJO papers that used the single-blind review and is predictive of more positive and engaging review feedback for ICLR papers that employed the double-blind review.
Crucially, a large-scale LLM-assisted computational experiment that replaces ``We'' words with demonstrative pronouns provides robust causal evidence of ``We'' words on paper acceptance.
Lastly, our causal mediation analysis shows that ``We'' words can lead to more acceptance mainly because they can increase the perceived teamwork, credibility, significance, and robustness in research evaluation.
By revealing the unique strength of ``We'' in facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science, our study highlights the importance of small but mighty linguistic choices in promoting knowledge discoveries and breakthroughs.

articles.title: Constructing Methodologically Robust Subnational Estimates from Survey Microdata: A Methods Review
articles.authors: Kailas Venkitasubramanian
articles.abstract:
Constructing estimates for a custom, county-defined region from survey microdata is constrained by
the geography at which respondents are identified. In the American Community Survey (ACS) Public
Use Microdata Sample (PUMS), that geography is the Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA), which
does not nest into counties and is periodically redrawn. This review surveys the state of the art in
producing methodologically robust subnational estimates under these constraints, organized into four
method families — crosswalk and allocation-factor methods, consistent-geography harmonization, areal
interpolation and dasymetric and structure-preserving methods, and model-based small-area estimation.
Each family is assessed against a reference baseline: a population-weighted allocation-factor pipeline
with Successive Difference Replication variance estimation. The review pays particular attention to the
within-zone compositional homogeneity assumption that limits direct reweighting, to the harmonization
of geographies across boundary revisions, and to the rigor of uncertainty quantification. It restricts
attention to methods implementable with publicly available data. It serves both as a standalone reference
and as the methodological foundation for a companion analysis.

articles.title: VenturePhD: A Bilateral Venture Capital Model for Doctoral Education: Reciprocal Commitments and Exit Rights
articles.authors: Koutian Wu
articles.abstract: Doctoral students may spend years building a project and a supervisory relationship before they know whether that relationship will support their training. Changing direction can be costly when one supervisor influences a student's income, research access, assessment, and references. This paper proposes VenturePhD, a policy design for doctoral education that pairs reciprocal commitments with supported transfer and exit rights. Drawing on venture-contracting research, it separates decisions about a project's continuation from decisions about student support and recognition of completed work. Students and supervisors would agree on revisable research and training plans. Universities would guarantee specified funding, appoint reviewers outside the supervisory relationship, and finance time-limited transitions. The paper specifies responsibilities and remedies, gives a worked example, and sets out hypotheses for a prospective pilot. It reports no intervention results. The empirical question is whether universities can reduce a student's dependence on a particular supervisor without weakening research quality, mentoring, or access to doctoral education.

articles.title: Demographic Segregation in Online Information Ecosystems
articles.authors: Burak Ozturan; David Lazer
articles.abstract:
Concern about online echo chambers rests on the premise that the internet sorts people
by politics. Research on online ideological segregation has accordingly measured partisanship
almost to the exclusion of other social divides, and has measured it mostly within news, which
is a small share of online activity (Allen et al., 2020; Muise et al., 2022). Whether partisan
segregation is distinctive has therefore rarely been tested against demographic segregation on
equal terms. Using a 1.6-million-user Twitter/X panel linked to voter file records (July 2018 to
May 2023), we measure age, gender, partisanship and geography with a Theil index, and race
more briefly alongside them. First, partisanship is not the dominant division of online attention.
When measured across Democrats, Republicans and Independents, partisan segregation over
general sharing behaviour is roughly a third of demographic segregation, and age separates users
more sharply than party even within news, the content category where partisan segregation is
strongest and where the existing literature has looked almost exclusively. Second, segregation is
built at the article level rather than the outlet level. People who differ on any social divide we
measure converge on the same outlets and diverge on which stories they select from them, which
places segregation downstream of the outlet choices that most audience-level research observes.
Geography is the exception and segregates at the outlet level, as local news would predict. Third,
the five-year decline in demographic segregation is produced by different mechanisms for different
divides. Gender’s decline reflects almost entirely who left the platform, partisanship’s reflects how
people changed, and age’s is an even mixture, so parallel aggregate trends can rest on unrelated
causes. Online attention is segregated along social lines that are largely not political, at a level
of granularity that outlet-based measures cannot observe. Existing estimates of partisan echo
chambers describe a narrower and less distinctive phenomenon than the polarisation literature
has assumed.

articles.title: A Stacked Deck: Ambition, Supply, Demand, and Women’s Access to Political Power
articles.authors: Mirya Holman; Lakshmi Iyer; Christina Wolbrecht
articles.abstract: Why do women remain underrepresented in positions of political power? A central challenge to answering this question is the difficulty in disentangling possible explanations, including women’s lack of interest or ambition, differences in women’s preparedness for political office, and discrimination against women by selectors. In this paper, we are uniquely able to investigate all three kinds of explanations simultaneously. Our unique dataset of applicants to appointed boards at the local level in the United States contains detailed professional, civic, and political information about the applicants, as well as about the boards to which they apply and the decisions of the appointers. We find that women are indeed less likely to apply for political positions, particularly powerful positions. The men and women who do apply are equally qualified. Despite these qualifications, women are less likely to be appointed to boards with more authority and power.

articles.title: The Latent Interview Protocol: Recovering Enacted Question Structure for Large-Scale Interview Analysis
articles.authors: Zachary Lim
articles.abstract: Interview researchers increasingly work with large corpora for which traditional line-by-line coding is costly. Current proposed indexing strategies to make the corpus more manageable still require line-by-line indexing while assuming that the planned interview protocol accurately represents what was asked in practice. This article introduces the latent interview protocol—the recurring substantive questions that organize interviews as enacted, along with the pathways linking them—and LIPE, an open-source workflow that recovers this structure by combining sentence embeddings, density-based clustering, and researcher-guided refinement. Validated protocol questions are assembled into a corpus-level structure and used to retrieve local response blocks for downstream qualitative analysis. An application to 63 semi-structured interviews on mothering during COVID-19 shows that LIPE recovers most planned protocol questions, surfaces emergent lines of inquiry, and retrieves question-anchored responses with high precision and recall. The approach makes large-scale interview indexing more tractable while preserving interpretive control over analytic boundaries.

articles.title: Accessibility as Infrastructure: A Neurodivergent Led Model for Structural Communication Safety in Disability Support Systems
articles.authors: Neil McCarthy
articles.abstract:
Disabled people frequently experience communication collapse during distress, overwhelm or coercive control, producing indirect, fragmented, masked or delayed expression rather than clear verbal articulation. National Inquiries – including the Disability Royal Commission (2023) and the NDIS Review (2023) – demonstrate that current disability and safeguarding systems are misaligned with these communication realities, relying on speech, privacy, cognitive stability and narrative coherence at precisely the moments that these capacities fail. Communication Collapse is there a predictable, embodied response shaped by trauma, cognitive load and social misunderstanding, rather than and individual deficit.
This article introduces accessibility as infrastructure, a conceptual reframing that positions communication safety as a structural requirement of safeguarding systems. Drawing on disability studies and critical social theory, it argues that safeguarding infrastructures must be redesigned to recognise neurodivergent communication as valid and actionable, particularly during shutdown, overwhelm, masking, executive- function collapse and coercive control.
Within this framework, the article presents Althing, a neurodivergent-led, trauma informed safeguarding model engineered to remain usable during distress-state communication collapse. By supporting early, low-detail, indirect or delayed signals of harm, Althing addresses structural communication failures and aligns with national reform expectations for trauma-informed, low-demand safeguarding pathways. Although conceptual, the model offers a mature foundation, for future co-design, empirical evaluation, and state-level safeguarding innovation, demonstrating how accessibility as infrastructure can strengthen communication safety at the exact moments disabled people are least able to seek help.

articles.title: Jumping to Solutions? Bureaucratic Attention Allocation in Response to Negative Performance Feedback
articles.authors: Amandine Lerusse; Joris van der Voet; Wouter Lammers
articles.abstract: Attention allocation is fundamental for governance, policy-making and management in the public administration. The attention-based view highlights how informationally and cognitively constrained bureaucrats allocate their finite attention to diagnose performance shortfalls and identify potential solutions. This study informs bureaucratic attention allocation toward solution-generation and problem-definition using a multi-method approach that combines a laboratory eye-tracking experiment with vignette-based interviews among 41 bureaucrats. We find that bureaucrats process problem-related and solution-related information in sequence and allocate more attention to solution-generation than problem-definition. The interviews demonstrate how the bureaucratic decision context gives rise to role-based, substantive, strategic and aspirational justifications for these patterns in attention allocation. We offer important implications for public administration research, theory and practice, highlighting the ever-increasing demands on bureaucratic decision-makers’ scarce attentional resources.

articles.title: Automated Suspicion: Algorithmic Workforce Surveillance and the Erosion of Internal Legitimacy in the Metropolitan Police Service
articles.authors: Paul Ford
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) pilot deployment of Palantir analytics for internal workforce monitoring, announced in April 2026 as part of the force’s post-Panorama standards programme. The force defends the deployment as lawful, since it brings together data it already holds; this article argues that defence repeats a known mistake in policing legitimacy research, treating legal compliance as the ceiling of consent rather than its floor. Drawing on procedural justice theory (Tyler 2006), the dialogic and twin-track models of legitimacy (Bottoms and Tankebe 2012; Tankebe 2013; Bradford and Tankebe 2014), Beetham’s (1991) account of institutional legitimacy, and the author’s earlier work (Ford 2021, 2026), it audits the deployment against the four pillars of procedural justice and finds it deficient on voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives. It argues that the pilot inverts Sherman’s (2007) power-few hypothesis, fails the targeting—testing—tracking discipline of evidence-based policing (Sherman 2013), substitutes a technical fix for what Heifetz (1994) calls an adaptive challenge, and entangles culture reform with surveillance in ways that risk delegitimising Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) work and, through a mirroring effect, damaging public-facing encounters.
