A subsequent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including the pilot’s Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment obtained in redacted form, tests these claims against primary evidence: it confirms an algorithmic yield of 2.6 million flags with a further-action rate of 0.075 per cent, corroborates self-acknowledged risks to trust and equity in the MPS’s own equalities analysis, and shows the force cannot establish what became of the cases its own system flagged. The article closes with implications for chief officers, police and crime commissioners, and professional standards leads.
Keywords: algorithmic management, workforce surveillance, police legitimacy, officer self-legitimacy, procedural justice, psychological safety, organisational culture, EDI, Palantir, Metropolitan Police Service.

articles.title: Thoughtforms in the Fog: Liminal Warfare and the Defense of Human Agency
articles.authors: Michael Paul Ross
articles.abstract:
Cognitive warfare is commonly framed as a contest over perception and decision-making. This
article argues that its most consequential leverage often appears during liminal periods, when
established identities, meanings, and institutions no longer provide sufficient orientation. It
introduces the thoughtform as a functional analytic construct with a long, heterogeneous
genealogy in initiation, ritual, and esoteric reflection, but does not rely on metaphysical claims.
A thoughtform is defined here as a recursively sustained symbolic formation that organizes
attention, emotion, identity, interpretation, and action across people, media, institutions, and
machines. A six-stage Liminal Thoughtform Cycle explains how threshold disruption can
produce either adaptive integration or cognitive capture. The article then advances liminal
security and Cognitive Aikido as agency-centered defenses, treating mental health and well-
being as capacities for sustaining meaning, relationships, reality orientation, and action under
pressure. The objective is capacity rather than control: preserving reflective freedom, relational
coherence, and meaningful action under persistent influence.

Keywords: cognitive security, cognitive warfare, liminality, thoughtforms, influence operations,
agency, resilience

articles.title: Maximizing Recruitment via Respondent-driven Sampling
articles.authors: Mariel Leonard; Julian B. Axenfeld; Hannah Bethge; Julia Witton; Carina Cornesse; Sabine Zinn
articles.abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS), a network-based method of sampling has become increasingly popular as a means of developing subgroup samples, particularly in web-first or web-only design (webRDS). WebRDS can reduce participant burden as well as increase the potential size and geographic scope of the sample, allowing for development of national samples with greater generalizability. However, webRDS can also introduce technical challenges as it requires all RDS processes to be mediated through internet-communication technology. In this paper, we focus on the challenges of engaging participants and reducing burden following a request to participate in webRDS. We present the results of two studies in which we tested several design features for their effects on webRDS recruitment success. We use social exchange theory as a lens through which to improve webRDS recruitment by maximizing benefits of participation and reducing burden. Based on our findings, we present recommendations for webRDS implementation.

articles.title: Digital media and social inequality : a primer in the context of Swiss digital society
articles.authors: Moritz Büchi
articles.abstract: Digital media innovations are used differently by people from different social groups and have varying consequences. Research has not found that these divides are narrowing. On the contrary, individuals who are socially better positioned appear to benefit more from digital media transformation. At the societal level, there is a need for a transparent negotiation of the values underlying the digital media infrastructure - values that can guide democratic governance.

articles.title: Geometry Proposes, Judgement Disposes: Accurate Online Proposal Clustering for Digital Deliberation
articles.authors: Tal Yaron; Fany Yuval
articles.abstract: Digital deliberation requires accurate clustering of proposals: equivalent contributions should be joined, while related interventions and opposing positions remain distinct. We study an online method implemented in Freedi that uses embeddings to retrieve candidates and focused language-model judgements to authorize synthesis, with separate themes, retained sources, and maintenance. We explain its retrieval-judgement interface and seven-stage selection process and compare it with the two main alternatives, cosine rules and LLM-only grouping. On 875 counterfactual preference triplets, a component study achieves 95.0%-96.5% accept-and-reject accuracy with original-text judging, compared with 0% for the tested cosine decision rule. On a controlled English corpus, Freedi and LLM-only baselines recover all 50 intended pairs in three arrival orders. A new 240-call probe on one authentic English deliberation compares full-list judgement with judgement over 15 retrieved proposals. Median per-decision cost reductions grow from 2.55-fold at 100 proposals to 4.29-fold at 200 and 9.38-fold at 500, under common base token prices. At 500 proposals, agreement with provisional model-authored labels is 25/40 for the restricted list and 31/40 for the full list. Retrieved targets remain available, but the restricted judge declines more merges. These refusals may preserve substantive distinctions in scope or intervention; whether they improve semantic precision or constitute missed matches requires human adjudication. A separate replay of 114 Hebrew statements shows improved automated merge precision and text fidelity after combined repairs. The evidence supports semantic judgement over the tested cosine rules and a growing cost advantage for candidate reduction at the measured scales. Equal accuracy and lower total cost for the complete Freedi pipeline remain to be established.

articles_hidden.title: The Latin American Demographic Boom in Spain. Mass Immigration and Ethnic Convergence in a New Country of Immigration
articles_hidden.authors: Miguel González-Leonardo; Guillaume Marois; Elena Ambrosetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Since the late twentieth century, Spain has undergone a rapid transition from emigration to immigration country, receiving around 510,000 immigrants annually between 2000 and 2022, approximately half from Latin America. This transformation has substantially increased population diversity, yet less is known about how diversity develops in relatively new immigration countries compared with established destinations. We combine register data, a retrospective analysis of births by parental background and a multi-state cohort-component model to examine changes in population diversity between 2000 and 2022 and project its potential evolution to 2062. The results show a rapid transformation of Spain’s population composition. Between 2000 and 2022, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background – defined by country of birth and parental origins – increased from 5% to 28%, while 13% had a Latin American background in 2022. Assuming that migration, fertility and ethnic-mixing patterns remain constant, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background would exceed 65% by 2062, with those of Latin American background reaching 32%. These findings demonstrate that the demographic consequences of immigration extend beyond the growth of the foreign-born population, as births and ethnic mixing progressively reshape the Spanish-born population. The study highlights the importance of incorporating foreign family backgrounds when assessing population diversity and provides new evidence on how diversity may evolve across generations in a recent immigration country.

articles_hidden.title: The Dual Costs of Marriage and Expectation Mismatch: A Mechanism for Understanding Gender Conflict in Contemporary China
articles_hidden.authors: Yuan Di; ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Against the backdrop of a sustained decline in marriage and birth rates in China and intensifying gender tensions, traditional explanations centered on individual preferences or gender norms are insufficient to account for the structural mechanisms involved. Drawing on the economics of marriage and the family, this paper examines how rising costs of housing, weddings, bride price, childbearing, and education affect men's decisions to enter marriage, as well as how the expansion of higher education, the shortage of standardized professional employment, and the motherhood penalty shape women's opportunity costs associated with marriage. Building on these factors, together with declining expectations of economic growth, changing lifestyle expectations, and the rising utility of singlehood as an alternative, the paper proposes the “Dual Marriage Costs–Expectation Mismatch Integrated Model” (the Di Formula) and uses “marital surplus” to characterize the comprehensive net benefits of marriage relative to singlehood. The paper argues that contemporary gender relations in China involve more than a conflict of values, but separately rising direct marriage costs for men and opportunity costs for women, together with a widening structural mismatch between modernity-based expectations and real resource constraints. When marital surplus declines and eventually becomes negative, individually rational decisions to postpone or forgo marriage may, in aggregate, contribute to declining marriage and birth rates and intensified gender tensions. Marriage is therefore increasingly shifting from a traditional mechanism of family cooperation toward a high-cost, high-risk, long-term economic decision.

articles_hidden.title: apcbound: Bounding Age-Period-Cohort Effects in Stata
articles_hidden.authors: Gordey Yastrebov
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-period-cohort analysis is complicated by the exact linear dependency between age, period, and cohort, which prevents the separate identification of their linear effects without additional assumptions. The bounding approach addresses this problem by replacing arbitrary point-identifying constraints with substantively motivated restrictions on the linear age, period, and cohort components. This article introduces apcbound, a Stata package that implements this approach. The package provides commands for describing age-period-cohort patterns, estimating identified nonlinear components and linear combinations, exploring alternative rotations, deriving bounded and semi-bounded solutions under user-specified assumptions, and visualizing the resulting identification regions. We illustrate the workflow using German data from the European Social Survey on years of education. A substantively plausible restriction that the age effect on educational attainment should be broadly nondecreasing is used to derive bounds on the otherwise unidentified linear components. The package facilitates transparent sensitivity analysis by showing how substantive assumptions translate into alternative admissible decompositions.

articles_hidden.title: Downscaling Industry Employment to European Municipalities from Economic Location Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Boero
articles_hidden.abstract: Fine-scale industry employment is largely unavailable for European municipalities, yet it is required for regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and regional input--output accounts. We present a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates municipal employment while preserving official totals at every geographical level. A reproducible dataset represents settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location using official and remote-sensing sources. Constrained allocation models are trained on data-rich United States geographies and applied to Europe under official Eurostat totals. Independent statistics for Italy, France, Germany, and Spain show that European per-step share error lies within the uncertainty derived from geographically held-out United States data. Full-chain error is neither the sum of per-step uncertainty nor the result implied by independent multiplicative compounding; it remains bounded and grows sub-linearly over four allocation steps. The framework provides open, internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates where sub-national industry data are sparse.

articles_hidden.title: To a neo-patriarchy? How anti-gender backlash shapes the youth gender gap in populist radical right voting in the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Mees Geenen; Anouk Smeekes
articles_hidden.abstract: Why are young European men more likely to vote for populist radical right parties (PRRPs) compared to young European women today? Following the concepts of cultural backlash and gender populism, we argue that anti-gender backlash, in the form of perceived status decline (PSD), opposition to gender diversity (OGD) and support for traditional gender roles (STGR), drives especially young men to PRRPs, in particular those who perceive threat from immigrants. We applied structural equation modelling on an 18–35-year-old subsample of the 2023 Dutch Parliamentary Election Study (N = 1,022). We find that the youth gender gap in PRRP voting can be explained by young men’s higher OGD, STGR, and unexpectedly also perceived threat from immigrants, but not by PSD. We conclude that gender differences in cultural backlash shape today’s youth gender gap in PRRP voting and might shape the future of European liberal democracy.

articles_hidden.title: Settler Colonial Logics: A framework for tracing the ideological currents of European colonisation of the Pacific
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Bedford
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper expands upon Patrick Wolfe’s ‘logic of elimination’ to propose a broader conceptual framework to understand the logics which underpinned European settler colonialism at large. Using the three Pacific voyages of British navigator James Cook between 1768 and 1779 as a case study, the geographic and ideological expansion of empire is positioned as a maritime endeavour which works to draw a singular geographic and political border for Empire. This view of a singular oceanic empire, rather than a collection of diverse and individual nations and peoples is further supported by the integration of the principles of the Doctrine of Discovery. This integration highlights the ways in which settler colonial logics continue to support structures founded on early modern beliefs about race, civilization and faith which, while now condemned by the institutions and cultures which established them, nonetheless continue to shape the lives of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in settler-colonial societies around the Pacific and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Role of Industry 4.0 Technologies in Enhancing Supply Chain Resilience of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs): A PLSSEM Based Empirical Investigation
articles_hidden.authors: Komal Sharma; Deepika Rathi; Jainish Bhagat; RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines how the adoption of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies – the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data Analytics (BDA), Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), Blockchain (BCT), and Digital Twin (DTW) – influences the supply chain resilience (SCR) of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), through the mediating roles of supply chain visibility (SCV), supply chain agility (SCA), and supply chain collaboration (SCC), and the moderating role of organizational readiness (ORGREAD).
Design/methodology/approach – A structural model integrating the Resource-Based View and the Dynamic Capabilities View was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) on survey data from 260 supply chain, operations, procurement, and digital-transformation executives in OEM firms across the automotive, electronics/electrical, industrial machinery, aerospace, and consumer-durables sectors. I4.0 technology adoption (I4ADOPT) is modelled as a second-order construct formed by five first-order technology dimensions; supply chain resilience is modelled as a second-order construct reflecting robustness, redundancy, flexibility, and recovery. The structural model was estimated with 2,000-sample nonparametric bootstrapping.
Findings – I4ADOPT significantly and positively predicted SCV (β = 0.487, p < .001), SCA (β = 0.254, p < .001), and SCC (β = 0.193, p < .01), and exerted a significant direct effect on SCR (β = 0.175, p < .01). SCV, SCA, and SCC each significantly predicted SCR (β = 0.237, 0.354, and 0.240 respectively, all p < .001) and significantly, partially mediated the I4ADOPT–SCR relationship. SCV additionally strengthened both SCA (β = 0.335) and SCC (β = 0.308). Organizational readiness had a significant positive direct association with both SCV (β = 0.169) and SCA (β = 0.205), but its hypothesized moderating (interaction) effect on the I4ADOPT–SCV and I4ADOPT–SCA relationships was not statistically supported. The model explained 58.2% of the variance in supply chain resilience, and all measurement-model reliability, validity, and model-fit criteria were satisfied (SRMR = 0.013).
Practical implications – OEM managers should prioritise IoT- and analytics-led visibility investment as the entry point of a digital resilience strategy, since visibility significantly amplifies agility and collaboration in addition to its own direct effect on resilience, and should invest in organizational readiness (leadership commitment, digital skills, process maturity) as a parallel, direct driver of these capabilities rather than solely as a moderating lever.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a sustainable post-pandemic growth
articles_hidden.authors: Ivan Sudibyo
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the long-run relationship between Research and Development (R&D) expenditure, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows, financial market capitalization, population, and Carbon Dioxide (CO2) emissions across five ASEAN economies–Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam– over 2000–2023. Building on the Paramati et al. (2021) framework rooted in the Impact, Population, Affluence, Technology (IPAT) theory of Ehrlich and Holdren (1971), the study applies Pedroni's panel cointegration test, the Pesaran (2007) CIPS unit-root test to address cross-sectional dependence, and Fully Modified OLS (FMOLS) estimation at both the panel and country-level. Results show that (i) population is the most consistently significant driver of CO2 emissions across all five economies, (ii) R&D expenditure carries a negative but statistically insignificant coefficient, a result consistent with the region's structurally low R&D-to-Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratios and lagged green-technology effects (Yang et al., 2025; Mehmood et al., 2022), and (iii) FDI and financial-market effects are heterogeneous, supporting a Malaysia-Singapore green-finance interpretation alongside pollution-haven dynamics elsewhere. The findings highlight the need for ASEAN policymakers to scale R&D intensity, channel financial market deepening toward green sectors, and integrate demographic-driven emission pressures into national climate plans.

articles_hidden.title: From playing computer games to achieving lexical knowledge: Linking attitudes and time allocation with vocabulary acquisition
articles_hidden.authors: Ehsan abbasi
articles_hidden.abstract:
The impact of video games on vocabulary acquisition has not received sufficient attention, despite a growing interest in the influence of digital games on vocabulary learning (i.e., DGVL) in the field of computer-assisted language learning (CALL). Particularly, it is uncertain whether the duration of time spent playing a video game and the attitude of English language learners (ELLs) have significant effects on EFL vocabulary acquisition. The present quasi-experimental study involved 40 male EFL students at a private language institute and examined the link between the students' opinions of a video game as well as the time allocated to it, in terms of vocabulary acquisition. In particular, this research explored the influence of these factors on receptive or productive vocabulary learning. Moreover, the vocabulary learning strategies employed by the participants when playing, along with the features they deemed essential for computer games to be engaging enough to support learning, were addressed in this study. The participants were required to complete a pretest, a posttest, a survey, and a self-reported timetable. The analyses did not reveal meaningful correlation between the participant's perception of the target video game and vocabulary acquisition. Additionally, it was found that the time spent playing the video game, coupled with prior language proficiency, helped to boost English vocabulary learning. Insights regarding the vocabulary learning strategies adopted and the features found appealing were also provided. These outcomes offer important insights for ESL/EFL instructors regarding the most effective approach to employing computer games as a novel vocabulary learning method.  
Keywords: Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL), Game-Enhanced Language Learning, Digital Game-Based Vocabulary Learning (DGVL), Computer games, Video Games, ESL/EFL pedagogy, TESOL, second language acquisition, Vocabulary Acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence of Non-Kin Out-of-Home Placement Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin A Campbell; Elizabeth Wendel
articles_hidden.abstract: This working paper synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence published between 1965 and 2026 on the long-term outcomes of non-kin out-of-home placement for children and describes current child welfare budget allocations in four English-speaking countries. Fourteen peer-reviewed studies using causal, quasi-experimental, or prospective longitudinal designs document elevated risks of premature mortality, adverse mental and physical health, and reduced socioeconomic attainment among placement-exposed populations relative to general-population, adversity-matched, sibling, or instrumental-variable counterfactuals; sibling-comparison and meta-analytic estimates report a roughly doubling of premature mortality risk and a roughly threefold increase in suicide risk associated with childhood out-of-home care experience. Five peer-reviewed studies argue, on methodological grounds, that observational findings have overstated the average effect, that propensity-matched analyses produce smaller estimates, that the instrumental-variable finding does not replicate uniformly across jurisdictions, and that effects are heterogeneous by age, placement type, and outcome. Within the targeted review, no peer-reviewed study was identified that reports non-kin placement producing superior outcomes relative to comparable home or kinship counterfactuals; Section 3.2 sets out the structural features of the literature that bear on how this absence should be read. Evidence on alternative pathways (parental care, intensive family preservation, community-based prevention, and kinship placement) has accumulated over the same interval; the 2018 Cochrane systematic review of 102 quasi-experimental studies finds that kinship-placed children experience fewer behavioral problems, fewer mental health disorders, better well-being, and less placement disruption than non-kin-placed children. Most recently published budget data show placement-related spending accounting for 82 percent (England, 2022/23), 72 percent (United States, SFY 2022), 64 percent (Australia, 2024–25), and 57 percent (New Zealand, 2023/24) of placement-plus-prevention expenditure within each country’s own reporting categories. Cross-national rates of children in out-of-home care, drawn from each country’s national statistics, range from 3.9 to 8.2 per 1,000 aged 0–17 across five high-income systems. The paper closes by identifying limitations and directions for further research.

articles_hidden.title: The Electoral Effects of U.S. Prison Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Ottone; Amanda Weiss
articles_hidden.abstract: From 1980 to 2000, the United States opened over 400 prisons, a rapid expansion of carceral capacity mirroring the punitive turn in public policy and public opinion. Yet few studies have examined the impact of prison construction on nearby residents and their political behavior. We develop a theoretical model tracing how prison openings affect economic, attitudinal, and electoral outcomes in surrounding communities. Using modern difference-in-difference methods and a novel county-level dataset covering forty years of prison openings, we find that prison construction decreases county-level vote share for Republican candidates, especially if Republicans represented the county during prison construction. Drawing on analyses of economic outcomes and prison bond measure support, we argue that voters sanction issue-owning Republican candidates for negative economic externalities and turn against funding for prisons. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about the political economy of prisons and have implications for how we understand contemporary expansions of carceral capacity.

articles_hidden.title: A Multicriteria Multimethod Analysis of Barriers for Green Infrastructure Implementation in Developing Countries: A Case Study of Sri Lanka
articles_hidden.authors: Udya Abeysinghe; Archana Sharma; Jagath Munasinghe
articles_hidden.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Many developed economies are considering the use of Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI) as a tool to enhance the climate resilience of urban areas and align with SDG 11 - Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. Yet, the integration of UGI in developing countries seems to be lagging. Thus, they are missing out on one of the instruments that could facilitate developing nations’ compliance with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. This review examines the current state of UGI knowledge and implementation in Sri Lanka through a comprehensive literature review, an evaluation of UGI-related policies, guidelines, plans, and projects, and an assessment of stakeholder perspectives using the Delphi technique. As a result, the study identifies five significant challenges of mainstreaming UGI in Sri Lanka, such as lack of: clear consensual understanding of UGI- definition, ecosystem service functionality, implementation facilitative classification of UGI, design tool for UGI adaptation in constrained urban context, political willingness to integrate UGI planning principles in urban planning, robust legal framework and well-specified co-governance. Furthermore, the paper identifies concepts and tools as a forward path, such as a clear acknowledgement of current enabling conditions and gaps through known/ unknown diagram, categorization of multifunctional UGI such as with ecosystem service (ES) or place-making (PM) UGI, use of design syntax for adaptable design, and enhancement of regulatory framework. This review aspires to open the conversation on usefulness of UGI as a step towards climate resilience and SDG 11, at all levels of academic institutions to governmental agencies, in Sri Lanka.

KEYWORDS: Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI), Nature-based Solutions (NbS), Climate Resilience, Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11), Urban Planning, Landscape, Design Syntax, Placemaking, Mixed method, Multimethod, Multicriteria, Analysis

articles_hidden.title: Examining Rising Life Satisfaction in Russia Amidst War: The Role of Perceived Socioeconomic Status Before and During the Ukraine War
articles_hidden.authors: Pavel Vlasov
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research has firmly established life satisfaction within the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS) as a reliable measure for assessing perceived quality of life within Russia. In this paper, we present perceived socioeconomic status (PSS) within the RLMS as a latent measure introduced to help examine levels of life satisfaction in Russia before (prewar 2018-2019) and during the Ukraine war (wartime 2022-2023). Using exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modelling (SEM), the findings indicate that PSS is a robust measure that increases the explanatory power of prewar and wartime models and positively predicts life satisfaction in both periods. Contemporary wellbeing research consistently supports the view that a key mechanism in shaping life satisfaction lies in how certain demographic conditions are psychologically interpreted. Drawing on appraisal theory, the study thus suggests that subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position provide meaningful information for understanding wellbeing that cannot be captured by demographic characteristics alone. Moreover, in the RLMS, overreliance on demographic indicators is shown to obscure the subjective mechanisms through which individuals living through wartime conditions evaluate their life satisfaction and interpret their social positions. Overall, the paper emphasizes that future research on the RLMS should consider incorporating PSS in their analyses and further developing on how subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position capture aspects of life satisfaction that are simply immeasurable in demographic only models of the RLMS. Emphasis should be placed on the major social, economic, and political disruption caused by the war that become normalized over time.

articles_hidden.title: Minimum Attainment Cost: National Benchmark Framework for Measuring Healthcare Accessibility in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias-Related Services
articles_hidden.authors: Kyusik Kim; Amber DeJohn; Weining Kan
articles_hidden.abstract: A threshold represented as travel time or distance is a key concept for determining catchment areas in cumulative opportunity and Two-Step Floating Catchment Area methods. As destinations included in a catchment area are determined by the threshold, it is a primary factor affecting spatial accessibility. In many cases, thresholds are arbitrarily determined or fixed values are used. The resulting accessibility based on these arbitrary or fixed thresholds makes it challenging to compare accessibility scores across heterogeneous geographic contexts (e.g., urban and rural areas). In this paper, we propose the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC) as a context-sensitive spatial accessibility measure using the national average facility-to-population ratio as a benchmark and explore how fixed thresholds can over- or underestimate accessibility compared with MAC in a nationwide U.S. analysis. Using the national benchmark, MAC measures the minimum travel time required to reach the national average level of a given resource in each zone, accounting for the geographic distributions of demand and resources. By comparing MAC with multiple fixed thresholds (i.e., 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes), we find that MAC is sensitive to geographic contexts in terms of the distributions of demand and resources. This approach enables direct geographic comparisons of spatial accessibility to different resources and provides evidence to support effective policy interventions by providing more context-sensitive accessibility estimates.

articles_hidden.title: Defining Nature for Policy and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Patricia Soranno; Stephen Posner; Courtney DeLoatch-Hill; Emerson Conrad-Rooney; Katie Arkema; Meena M. Balgopal; Gillian Bowser; Monika M. Derrien; Kevin C. Elliott; Tessa Francis
articles_hidden.abstract: What counts as "nature" is increasingly central to public policies, investment decisions, and scientific assessments, yet the term is often left undefined or implicit. Because nature is a complex, value-laden concept, a universal definition is unlikely to serve all uses, creating problems for comparability and auditability of claims. When users document what counts as nature and disclose the basis for their claims, measurement becomes more comparable, and accountability improves. We present a framework that pairs a concise definition with its purpose, context, and boundary rules, and apply it to develop a definition of nature that can reveal how benefits, harms, and stewardship responsibilities are distributed across people and places. Definitions should be treated as public commitments: articulating both a definition and a replicable process for revision makes governance more transparent, auditable, and open to legitimate contest.

articles_hidden.title: The Changing Gender Training Gap - A Systematic Review of Evidence from Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Marco Seegers
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on gender differences in non-formal job-related further training in Germany has produced inconsistent findings, leaving unclear how gender inequalities in training have developed and whether divergent findings reflect training forms or conceptual and meth-odological differences. This systematic review synthesised quantitative evidence from studies published between 1990 and 2026. Web of Science, Scopus, and FIS Bildung were searched in June 2026 and supplemented by backward citation searching. Forty-two stud-ies yielded 160 finding-level records, which were integrated using a structured narrative synthesis. The evidence indicates a weakening of the earlier male advantage in overall training participation, with later evidence increasingly showing no statistically detectable gender difference or higher participation among women. This convergence was weaker for employer-supported training, while population-level convergence coexisted with life-course-specific inequalities. Conceptual and methodological differences shaped the com-parability and empirical visibility of gender inequalities but did not systematically ac-count for the broader historical pattern, which remained visible under more restrictive comparisons. Overall, gender inequality in further training appears to have been recon-figured rather than eliminated or simply reversed, with inequalities remaining conditional on institutional and life-course contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Modeling Network Dynamics with Overlapping Cohesive Subgroups
articles_hidden.authors: Stepan Zaretckii; Tom A.B. Snijders; Marijtje A.J. van Duijn; Christian Steglich
articles_hidden.abstract: We introduce a longitudinal extension of the latent membership stochastic actor-oriented model (LM-SAOM) for analyzing the co-evolution of network ties and actors’ memberships in overlapping cohesive subgroups. The model treats group memberships as latent and time-evolving, giving actors frequent opportunities to update their memberships while a strong \emph{membership cohesion} effect favors membership choices that place actors in the same groups as their network contacts, thereby keeping the inferred cohesive subgroups aligned with the evolving network. In an application to a friendship network, we find evidence that students are more likely to have ties with peers with whom they share cohesive subgroup membership, beyond what is captured by dyadic and triadic effects. Goodness-of-fit assessments indicate that incorporating group-level dependence improves the representation of selected meso-level network configurations.

articles_hidden.title: Uncovering Student Thinking from Only the Answer: A GenAI Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Tommy Stell; Darryl Chamberlain; Kelvin Rozier; Yaroslav Molkov; Russell Jeter
articles_hidden.abstract: Identifying the underlying reasoning behind a student’s response to a mathematical question is a time-intensive activity for instructors. This work seeks to answer if a Large Language Model (LLM) can be used to identify potential student thinking based solely on their final response. To evaluate the LLM’s identification of potential student thinking, we developed an ordinal scale which describes how well the LLM’s identification aligns with a content expert’s identification of potential student thinking. We then utilized this scale to evaluate the ability of the Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview LLM to identify potential student thinking in a variety of College Algebra questions. We show that the LLM was able to correctly identify the mechanism encoded in the distractor, in a little over half (55.25%) of cases. This work highlights the limits of current LLMs’ ability to identify potential student thinking and further highlights the necessity of instructors to provide targeted feedback based on student thinking.

articles_hidden.title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth:  an interdisciplinary review and research agenda
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Cooiman; Julia de Groote; Isabell Stamm; Jan Ole Krieg
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the centrality of entrepreneurial activity to the accumulation, reproduction, and legitimization of wealth – and conversely, of wealth in the form of capital to foster entrepreneurship – it might be reasonable to expect a plethora of research on the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth. However, as we demonstrate in our interdisciplinary literature review, a surprising lack of engagement exists with regard to this relationship. Sociological studies of wealth inequality rarely address entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship research rarely addresses wealth. We systematically review, discuss, and synthesize the discourse in the leading journals of both fields. In the sociological discourse on wealth, we find that entrepreneurship is seen as one of many sources of income and wealth, and as a means of legitimizing its accumulation. However, the social practices, actors, and institutions that mediate the concentration of wealth through entrepreneurship, as well as the structural power of wealth in entrepreneurial activity, are rarely addressed. Similarly, in entrepreneurship research, we show that considerable attention is paid to the role of family businesses, transgenerational wealth, and non-financial wealth (“socioemotional wealth”), whilst the fundamental role of these factors in fostering wealth concentration more broadly remains largely unremarked upon in the literature. We therefore suggest future research that systematically engages with how entrepreneurial activity shapes wealth accumulation, and how wealth, in turn, structures entrepreneurial opportunities and outcomes. With this review, we contribute to advancing debates on inequality, social mobility, and economic development.

articles_hidden.title: Global Trends in Widowhood Prevalence, 1970–2020: The Role of Population Ageing, Mortality, and Union Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Elder Lara-Castaneda; Zachary Van Winkle
articles_hidden.abstract: Widowhood is the predominant marital status at older ages, especially among women. Although population ageing is expected to increase widowhood, evidence on this trend remains scarce or fragmented across countries. This study contributes to the global understanding of widowhood by addressing two questions. First, how has widowhood prevalence changed among women and men across countries and world regions between 1970 and 2020? Second, to what extent are changes in overall widowhood prevalence attributable to changes in population age structure rather than to changes in age-specific widowhood prevalence, i.e. mortality and union dynamics. We gathered marital-status tabulations from censuses, registers, and nationally representative surveys covering 222 countries and territories, and trace crude and age-standardized widowhood prevalence from 1970 to 2020. A Kitagawa decomposition separates change between 1980 and 2010 in 135 populations into age-structure and age-specific-prevalence components. Widowhood prevalence declined globally and in most regions, especially among women. Although population ageing contributed to increasing widowhood prevalence, changes in age-specific prevalence more than offset this effect. An ageing world is not necessarily one in which an increasing share of people are widowed, but it may still be one in which large, socially vulnerable populations live with the consequences of spousal loss.

articles_hidden.title: Why Do Immigrant Girls Participate Less in Organized Leisure Activities? The Role of Parental Influence Across the Transition from Adolescence to Adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Frank van Tubergen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles_hidden.abstract: Research documents immigrant-native gaps in girls’ participation in organized leisure activities across Western Europe, particularly among Muslim immigrant-origin girls. While parental characteristics are often assumed to shape these gaps, less is known about which parental factors matter most and how their influence unfolds from adolescence into adulthood. Using German longitudinal data from CILS4EU and CILS4EU-DE, we address these questions by examining participation gaps among non-Muslim and Muslim immigrant-origin girls relative to native girls across the transition from adolescence to early adulthood.In doing so, we estimate a structural equation model that distinguishes between initial parental effects in adolescence, path-dependent effects linking adolescent and adult participation, and persistent parental effects in early adulthood. Differences in parental participation andsocioeconomic resources explain a substantial share of theimmigrant-native participation gaps, whereas parental gender values explain comparatively little. Although participation gaps narrow over time, they persist, primarily through path-dependent processes, as lower participation during adolescence is carried forward into adulthood. Persistent parental effects remain but are comparatively modest. While participation gaps are larger among Muslim immigrant-origin girls, the underlying mechanisms are broadly similar across immigrant-origin groups. The findings highlight how family-based inequalities shape participation trajectories and contribute to the production and reproduction of participation gaps across the life course.
