articles_hidden.title: Políticas industriais regionalizadas e estado desenvolvimentista em rede como orientadores do desenvolvimento policêntrico no Brasil
articles_hidden.authors: Isaias Albertin de Moraes; Humberto Martins
articles_hidden.abstract: O artigo trata da trajetória da indústria de transformação brasileira no período recente, observando a evolução de seu peso na estrutura produtiva, bem como sua dinâmica regional nas escalas macro e microrregional. Diante da identificação de um processo de desindustrialização (1985-2024) simultâneo a uma tendência de desconcentração regional limitada, ressalta-se a importância da dimensão regional das políticas industriais. Nessa perspectiva, discute-se o potencial de um Estado Desenvolvimentista em Rede (EDR) para estabelecer políticas industriais regionalizadas no Brasil com vistas a favorecer a ampliação, integração e a sofisticação da estrutura produtiva, bem como a reduzir as desigualdades regionais e estimular o desenvolvimento policêntrico do país.

articles_hidden.title: Unbundling Support for Political Violence
articles_hidden.authors: Sam Fuller; Jack T. Rametta; Alexa Federice
articles_hidden.abstract: Measures of support for political violence (SPV) vary drastically across what violence they describe, who performs it, against whom, and the stated justification. We argue that these measures are not interchangeable operationalizations of a single latent attitude but rather represent correlated, distinct subdimensions of SPV. Across three studies, we iteratively develop and validate concise batteries that 1) differentiate between actor-target combinations and reactive versus proactive violence and 2) vary across justification and the response's severity. We find that SPV is a multidimensional concept: levels of reactive support are remarkably higher than proactive; support for state-on-mass and mass-on-state violence are only weakly correlated, with Republicans supporting state-on-mass and Democrats supporting mass-on-state violence at significantly higher rates; common SPV measures correlate with proactive more than reactive; and we find mixed evidence that survey disengagement influences SPV. Our findings contextualize disparate and conflicting literatures, offering measurement strategies tailored to specific research questions.

articles_hidden.title: Homeschooling as Racial Retreat: The Impact of School District and Leadership Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Maranda Joyce
articles_hidden.abstract: What explains the decision to homeschool? This study examines whether local racial context influences families’ decisions to homeschool their children. I argue that many white parents exit public school systems due to concerns about the distribution of school resources to racial out-groups, particularly in racially diverse and resource-constrained districts. I conduct a state-representative survey of over 30,000 respondents to describe the homeschooling population in the United States. Then, using data from Virginia that link student and district leadership demographics (school board members and superintendents) to district-level homeschooling rates, I examine how racial composition and leadership diversity shape educational exit. I find that higher levels of non-white students and certain kinds of leadership diversity are positively associated with increased homeschooling, especially where resources are limited. By showing that homeschooling is often motivated by perceived racial threat, this study informs debates about the regulation and public subsidization of homeschooling.

articles_hidden.title: Specific Support, Diffuse Trust: Central Banks and the Mass Politics of Unconventional Monetary Policy
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth
articles_hidden.abstract: Central banks relied for a decade on unconventional monetary policies (negative interest rates, large-scale asset purchases, and forward guidance) that carry significant distributive consequences and became intensely politicized. Yet little is known about the mass politics of central banking, or whether contestation over specific instruments threatens central banks' broader legitimacy. We provide evidence from two pre-registered survey experiments in Germany and the Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that citizens strongly oppose negative interest rates, the most penalized levels in the design, and are skeptical of unconditional asset purchases. A framing experiment shows support for negative rates responds to both egotropic and sociotropic arguments, with pocketbook concerns resonating most strongly. Exploiting a within-respondent measure of trust in the European Central Bank (ECB), we show that these same frames shift citizens' specific support for the policy without eroding their diffuse trust in the ECB, a highly insulated, technocratic, non-elected institution.

articles_hidden.title: How Intergenerational Closure Shapes Parental Aspirations in a Highly Differentiated Educational System: Evidence from Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Monja Schmitt; Kerstin Schörner; Felix Bittmann
articles_hidden.abstract: According to James Coleman's theoretical considerations, intergenerational closure, defined as social ties among the parents of children's peers, is a crucial factor in the formation of educational inequalities. Empirical studies report positive associations between intergenerational closure and academic success, while indicating that these associations cannot be understood in isolation from the social contexts in which closure is embedded. Nothing is known about its impact on parental aspirations that precede the children's educational success. From the perspective of the Wisconsin Model, aspirations are not only precursors of educational attainment but are themselves shaped through social interactions with significant others. Educational systems structure the social contexts in which children and parents form networks and become significant to each other, and the extent to which educational outcomes, including educational aspirations, are shaped by the degree of educational stratification. Germany represents a highly differentiated educational system with secondary school tracks that differ in their student composition and educational opportunities. No study has examined whether parents of classmates function as significant others for parental educational aspirations, nor whether this role varies across school tracks. Using unique data from a National Educational Panel Study (n = 6,162), we examine whether intergenerational closure is associated with parents’ realistic and idealistic aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. Results from linear probability models indicate that intergenerational closure significantly increases realistic aspirations only among parents with children in intermediate educational tracks, suggesting that significant others shape realistic aspirations primarily as models providing information and resources, rather than through normative mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: What’s Worth Dreaming of? The Gendered and Classed Logics Behind Occupational Aspirations
articles_hidden.authors: Diego Strassmann Rocha; Marie Labussière
articles_hidden.abstract:
Even though occupations have multiple characteristics that make them more or less likely to
be aspired to, research has yet to capture which characteristics matter most for which
adolescents. This limits our understanding of inequalities in aspirations because different
theories emphasize the role of certain occupational characteristics over others. This article
examines whether and how evaluations of multiple characteristics combine into distinct logics
of aspirations based on adolescents’ gender, class, and gender-class intersection. We combine
Swiss data from the DAB Panel Study on adolescents’ aspirations with O*NET data on
occupational characteristics. Using conditional logit models, we estimate the relationships
between occupational characteristics and the choice of aspired occupation. Results show that
girls prioritize occupations satisfying female-typed interests and those requiring higher
education levels, while boys avoid occupations with high shares of women and high
educational requirements. High-class adolescents favour artistic and investigative occupations,
whereas low-class adolescents are averse to highly educated and high-income occupations.
Intersectional analyses reveal that low-class boys are particularly disadvantaged, exhibiting the
strongest aversion to highly educated occupations. Overall, findings highlight that aspirations
are shaped by multiple occupational characteristics rather than a single dimension,
underscoring the importance of a multidimensional perspective to better understand
inequalities in adolescent aspirations.

articles_hidden.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro di Molfetta; Valeria Notarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3,225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2,991 priced capital increases on 1,330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

articles_hidden.title: Do genes modify earnings trajectories following job loss?  Gene-environment interactions with endogenous and exogenous forms of job loss
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Arno Van Hootegem; Henri Salokangas; Gaia Ghirardi; Henrik Dobewall; Laura Jernström; Maria Vaalavuo
articles_hidden.abstract: Job loss is a disruptive event that results in long-term economic scarring, though effects vary across social groups. This study explores a new potential source of inequality in the impact of job loss by examining whether genetic traits can amplify or attenuate earning declines following job loss. To address bias from gene-environment correlations, we compare interactions between polygenic indices (PGIs) and both endogenous job loss (individual unemployment) and exogenous job loss (plant closures). We focus on PGIs for depression, educational attainment, and risk-taking. Using Finnish population register data linked to genetic information for approximately 10,000 individuals observed over ten years, we apply a difference-in-differences design. We find persistent earnings losses following job loss, with larger declines for endogenous unemployment spells. Genetic moderation is observed only for plant closures: individuals with higher depression-related PGIs experience greater earnings declines. No comparable interactions emerge for endogenous job loss or the other PGIs.

articles_hidden.title: From Working Life to Retirement: Changing Educational Inequalities in Income Trajectories in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Ordemann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Previous literature has mainly focussed on either income trajectories of higher education graduates in working life or in retirement. This paper advances this literature by investigates the inequalities of income trajectories at the transition into retirement and compare the trajectories to other educational graduates for the case of Germany. While cumulative advantage theory suggests that education-based income inequalities widen throughout working life, the institutional design of the German pension system fundamentally alters these trajectories. 
Using data from 1,741 (11,740 observations) baby boomers from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (SOEP) I combine descriptive income trajectories with fixed effects regression and replacement rate analysis. find a stratified pattern by educational degree in pre- and post-retirement income. However, income inequality by education degree is more pronounced during work life than in retirement: At the transition into retirement income differences are compressed relative to pre-retirement disparities. This compression operates through heterogeneous replacement rates. Higher educated individuals have lower replacement rates than the rest of the educational groups. Germany’s contribution-capped statutory pension system therefore constitutes a structurally induced erosion of the income advantage that higher education generates over a working lifetime.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Multidimensional Structure of Subjective Well-Being: Evidence from Mexico
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Alberto Arellano-Esparza
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research on subjective well-being (SWB) relies on the classic tripartite model of life satisfaction, positive affect, and negative affect, which may obscure its multidimensional character. Using nationally representative data from Mexico, this study compares alternative structural models of SWB through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, evaluating configurations that integrate eudaimonic, affective, and cognitive components to test whether a multidimensional structure provides a better statistical account of the data than a unidimensional alternative. Several competing models (correlated three-factor, hierarchical, and bifactor) display robust and largely equivalent fit. This multidimensional representation consistently outperforms a unidimensional one and remains largely stable across sex and region, indicating that no single structural model uniquely captures SWB, calling for more flexible approaches to its study.

articles_hidden.title: 植民地から自動車へ、イノベーションが帝国主義の終焉を齎すメカニズム
articles_hidden.authors: Charles Kongō
articles_hidden.abstract: 植民地と帝国主義の世界はなぜ終わったのか？ウラジーミル・レーニンは資本主義の最高段階を「帝国主義」と位置付けたが、実際には次が存在したからである。本稿が提唱する現代資本主義は「モータリズム」であり、これと対比することで帝国主義を再定義した。「帝国主義」とはプロセス・イノベーションによる供給増加が優勢な段階であり、経済成長には植民地の需要を必要とした。これに対して「モータリズム」はプロダクト・イノベーションによって自ら需要を作り出すため、植民地市場を必要としない段階である。本稿が主張する帝国主義の終焉は1908年のフォード・モデルTが起点であり、ウッドロウ・ウィルソンの民族自決、戦争違法化、そして第二次世界大戦後の英仏の脱植民地まで、国際秩序の変化は「帝国主義」から「モータリズム」へのトランジションによって引き起こされたことを明らかにした。また、本研究の副次的結論として、経済成長における「供給が需要を生み出す」という命題は、生産物効用が労働不効用を上回るという限定的条件下でのみ成立することを示した。この状況においては、需要創出に資するプロダクト・イノベーションの役割が特に重要となる。

articles_hidden.title: Bucks for Bumps: How Paid Parental Leave Pays Off for Firms
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Cookler
articles_hidden.abstract: Firms use benefits such as paid parental leave (PPL) to attract and retain employees. In the U.S., which lacks broad public PPL benefits, firms increasingly provide this benefit. Systematic evidence of its benefits remains limited, due in part to the absence of comprehensive data on firm policies. Using a novel, hand-collected database of firm policy changes, this paper estimates the causal effect of PPL expansion on employee retention using a differences-in-differences approach. PPL expansions reduce departure rates by 3.1%, an effect equivalent to a permanent wage increase of 1.8%. Retention gains for women are concentrated among the lowest paid and those in the most junior roles, while retention gains for men are broad-based. At the firm level, retention gains concentrate in the interior of the internal labor market flexibility distribution and among firms with moderate firm-specific human capital, and they are robust to concurrent benefit changes and to firm revenue trajectories. Public PPL programs, by contrast, show no comparable retention effect, consistent with the non-portability of firm-provided benefits. Combining fertility estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) with worker and firm data, the paper calculates the expected costs of PPL provision and compares them to retention gains: at realistic utilization rates, PPL expansions generate positive net returns to firms.

articles_hidden.title: A Rough Revised Estimate of Exclusive Breastfeeding at 6 Months in England Based on the 2024 Infant Feeding Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Emily H Emmott
articles_hidden.abstract: The 2024 Infant Feeding Survey likely overestimates exclusive breastfeeding prevalence at 6 months in England. Roughly correcting for probable selection and attrition bias, true prevalence is more plausibly in the region of 4–17%, with an upper bound estimate of 21.4%. More precise estimates would require individual level data, which would allow formal modelling and direct estimation of differential attrition by feeding status.

articles_hidden.title: No Reform, No Election: CHADEMA's Campaign and the Legacy of Incomplete Political Reform in Tanzania, 1991–2025
articles_hidden.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles_hidden.abstract:
On 23 March 2025, the Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo (CHADEMA) launched its “No Reform, No Election” campaign in Mbeya City, demanding substantive electoral and political reforms as a condition for participation in Tanzania's forthcoming general election. Although the campaign emerged in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 local-government elections, its political rationale was rooted in a much longer history of incomplete institutional reform dating from the Nyalali Commission of 1991. This article examines the campaign within the historical trajectory of Tanzania's major presidential commissions and reform initiatives, including the Nyalali Commission, the Warioba Commission on corruption, the Kisanga Committee, the Warioba Constitutional Review Commission, and the Presidential Taskforce on Multiparty Democracy chaired by Professor Rwekaza Mukandala.
The article argues that Tanzania's reform trajectory is characterized by a recurring gap between the identification of institutional problems, the production of reform recommendations, and their comprehensive implementation. This article conceptualizes this phenomenon as the reform implementation gap and argues that its cumulative effect has generated a reform expectation gap between citizens' and political actors' expectations and the institutional outcomes delivered by successive governments. The 2025 CHADEMA campaign should therefore be understood not simply as an electoral boycott strategy but as a political claim concerning the relationship between electoral participation and institutional legitimacy. The article further examines the 2023–2024 electoral and political-party legislation, CHADEMA's invocation of President Samia Suluhu Hassan's “4Rs” philosophy, and the opposition's increasing reliance on digital mobilization in a constrained political environment. It concludes that democratic consolidation in Tanzania requires not merely additional reform initiatives but credible implementation of existing recommendations, stronger institutional independence, and political conditions capable of sustaining meaningful electoral competition.

articles_hidden.title: Lexical Integration: Introducing Aymara Corpus Evidence into Global English
articles_hidden.authors: Robert D. Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: Indigenous Andean languages have traditionally been preserved through oral traditions, especially following the historical destruction of non-alphabetic record-keeping systems like khipus (Coletta, 2023). In the face of imperial linguistic hegemony, traditional documentation efforts often prove insufficient for long-term epistemic preservation (van den Berg, 2024). As Global English expands, the decline of Indigenous languages threatens profound Andean ways of knowing with systematic erosion (van den Berg, 2024). This paper proposes a conceptual framework to preserve Highland Andean epistemology by integrating targeted, untranslatable Aymara words—such as ch’ixi, taypi, and suma qamaña—into Global English lexicons using international corpus evidence (Bosch & Griesel, 2020). Anchored in translanguaging theory and decolonial macro- and microethics, this approach maps translational deficiencies where English lacks single-word equivalents for complex Andean concepts. The study demonstrates that bridging these lexical gaps transforms Global English into an additive vehicle for cultural preservation, counteracting academic extractivism and projecting Indigenous philosophies onto the global stage.

articles_hidden.title: The Growing Transatlantic Sanctions Divide
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Peez
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilateral cooperation on sanctions is a key determinant of their success, yet transatlantic collaboration on sanctions is steeply declining. This transatlantic sanctions divide is a symptom of increasingly divergent US and EU foreign policies. Sanctions are likewise best terminated multilaterally to effectively wield them as leverage. Here too, trustful US-EU collaboration is increasingly difficult to imagine. Nonetheless, strong public support for sanctioning Russia in both the EU and US offers a basis for continuing forceful Western sanctions as Russia escalates its war of aggression against Ukraine.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining the Decline of impal Marriage among the Karo: An Epidemiological Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Geoff Kushnick; Sam Passmore; Fikarwin Zuska; Karmila br. Karo; Daniel M.T. Fessler
articles_hidden.abstract: The Karo of North Sumatra, Indonesia, have long expressed a preference for matrilateral cross-cousin (impal) marriage, yet the practice has declined sharply over the past century. To identify the demographic and sociocultural factors underlying this change, we applied an epidemiological approach to cultural evolution, using a case-control design coupled with structural equation modeling (SEM). Ethnographic data from 176 married individuals across 62 villages were analyzed to assess the effects of demographic, alliance, religious, cosocialisation, and modernisation variables on the likelihood of impal marriage. The model fit was strong (CFI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.04), revealing significant direct and indirect effects. Marrying an impal was positively associated with the number of marriageable impal and with arranged or strategically motivated unions but negatively associated with reported religious conflict between spouses. Indicators of modernisation such as schooling and infrastructure were non-significant. These results indicate that the decline of impal marriage reflects demographic contraction and the weakening of alliance-based strategies rather than a rejection of the cultural norm itself. Framed within an epidemiological model of cultural transmission, the findings demonstrate how social practices may fade when the ecological and demographic conditions sustaining them erode, even as their normative value persists.

articles_hidden.title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey Swindle; Matthew Blanton
articles_hidden.abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

articles_hidden.title: Generative AI and Society
articles_hidden.authors: Laura K. Nelson; Daniel Karell; Thomas Davidson
articles_hidden.abstract: For sociologists, generative AI inherits the legacy of earlier computational technologies: it is an advancement of machine learning already adopted as a methodology, and it intervenes in a society already shaped by algorithmic systems. Yet it also has a dimension that distinguishes it from previous computational methods, and one that makes it inherently sociological: its interactivity. In this review, we conceptualize the interactivity of generative AI and introduce a framework for understanding how it operates across individual, organizational, and institutional life. Specifically, the framework specifies how generative AI expands users, functions as a proxy for society, and expresses power, both in sociological practice and in society. We conclude by suggesting three dynamics driven by generative AI that sociology will face in the near future: the transformation of scientific practice, the reorganization of social interaction, and the acceleration of algorithmic governance.

articles_hidden.title: Do AI Occupational-Exposure Scores Measure AI? AIOE and Eloundou (2024) Largely Capture Cognitive Content; Webb (2020) Does Not
articles_hidden.authors: Sudhanshu Rai
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing empirical literature uses pre-built "AI occupational exposure" scores (most prominently the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index of Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021) and the GPT-4 task-exposure measure of Eloundou et al. (2024)) as occupation-level treatments or predictors for AI's labor-market effects. We show that two of the most-cited scores, AIOE and Eloundou's GPT-4 measure, substantially re-label cognitive task content rather than capturing AI-specific exposure, a construct-validity problem that does not extend to a third, differently-built score (Webb 2020, patent-based). This note horse-races these three measures against transparent cognitive/manual task-content indices and the established Autor–Dorn Routine Task Intensity (RTI) measure. Across 773 occupations: (i) the ten-plus AI "applications" underlying AIOE collapse to a single factor (first principal component ≈ 88%); (ii) AIOE and Eloundou each correlate strongly with a cognitive-ability index (+0.85 / +0.70) and negatively with a manual-ability index (−0.91 / −0.83), correlate 0.86 with each other, but only moderately with RTI (−0.33 / −0.30): the confound is specifically cognitive ability level, not the classic routine-task polarization axis; (iii) each score's positive wage association reverses sign controlling for cognitive content but is barely affected by controlling for RTI; and (iv) the much-cited pre-ChatGPT "AI foresight" wage-divergence pattern collapses to near-zero under the cognitive control (not under the RTI control). Critically, this collapse is not universal: Webb's patent-text-overlap score is essentially uncorrelated with AIOE (r=0.03) and Eloundou (r=−0.03), only weakly related to cognitive content (r=0.13), and its modest wage associations do not reverse under cognitive control. The cognitive-content collapse is a signature of how a score is built: subjective crowd-relatedness ratings (AIOE) or LLM/human task judgments (Eloundou), not an inherent property of occupational AI-exposure measurement. Studies using relatedness- or judgment-based exposure scores should control for cognitive content and re-interpret accordingly; a patent-based measure is not shown here to have the same problem, though its own construct validity is untested.

articles_hidden.title: The Kia-Hyundai vehicle theft surge: the roles of anti-theft devices and co-occurring offenses
articles_hidden.authors: Graham Farrell; John Roman
articles_hidden.abstract: Between 2020 and 2024, vehicle theft in the United States increased 40 percent. This study addresses this as a natural experiment, using a quasi-experimental design for causal inference to attribute the increase to theft of Kia and Hyundai vehicles manufactured without engine immobilizers. It is conservatively estimated that by the end of 2024 there were over 1.1 million excess vehicle thefts and over three hundred thousand excess co-occurring offenses including homicides, violence and other serious offenses. The evidence indicates that the withdrawal of situational crime prevention measures can increase crime and criminality and that the long-term national crime declines cannot be taken for granted. Additional implications are identified.

articles_hidden.title: Turning Votes into Power: New Women Voters and Access to Local Governance
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Christina Wolbrecht; Lakshmi Iyer
articles_hidden.abstract: Do voting rights secure access to political power for previously excluded groups? We theorize that organizational capacity and ideological congruence with political regimes determine whether voting rights produce access to governance. We test this theory with the case of American women’s suffrage and a new measure of access to power: representation on local appointed boards. Using a new dataset of more than 30,000 appointees, hundreds of women’s organizations, and local political regimes in four major cities, we find that suffrage facilitates descriptive representation, but this connection is limited to when women are ideologically aligned with the political regime. Strength of women’s organizations is associated with women’s representation, but only before suffrage. Women’s representation remained concentrated on boards concerning children, arts, and welfare. Even with the vote, women’s access to governance depended on the preferences of the established male elite.

articles_hidden.title: Questionnaire Design and Rater Cognition in 360-Degree Performance Appraisal
articles_hidden.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani; Simin Ebrahimi Lialekol
articles_hidden.abstract:
Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering.
Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias.
These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

articles_hidden.title: Seizing the Agenda: Polarization and Legislative Autonomy in Brazilian Presidentialism
articles_hidden.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Fabiano Guilherme Mendes Santos
articles_hidden.abstract: Brazilian coalitional presidentialism has long been read as a system in which the executive sets the agenda and the legislature holds a veto. We argue that, since the mid-2010s, the Congress has been building agenda-setting power. We account for the shift with a formal spatial framework in which a legislature weighs the cost of acquiring agenda power against the costs caused by the executive it expects to face. Two forces drive the investment: the rightward movement of a median legislator dissatisfied with the status quo and the recent polarization of the Executive, a partner that became too radical and costly to legislate with. Reading the record from Lula's first governments through Lula III, we show how the realignment of agenda power came to constrain the president who now has to both manage the coalition and to accommodate increasing policy demands from the legislature.

articles_hidden.title: Economic Growth and Working-Class Representation: Evidence from Brazil
articles_hidden.authors: Jamil Civitarese
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic growth may lead to more resources for the working class to solve collective action problems and demand political representation, but not all instances of economic growth do unequivocally reduce economic inequality. When productivity gains accrue disproportionately to economic elites and political parties lack durable ties to labor, it may instead deepen class-based political exclusion. I test this argument using a novel panel that identifies the occupational background of every city council candidate in Brazil from 2004 to 2020, a period of economic growth led by agribusiness productivity increases. Within municipalities, increases in GDP are associated with a smaller share of campaign funding going to working-class candidates and a lower share of elected councilors from working-class backgrounds. Leveraging individual-level data on career trajectories of incumbents, I confirm these results. Additionally, I study the scope conditions for my theory, showing that non-leftist parties and rural areas drive my results. A qualitative comparison design reveals that discretionary choices by party leaders serve as a channel through which unequal growth can reinforce exclusion in political representation.

articles_hidden.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo; Kani Khalaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles_hidden.title: Six-Year Trends in LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Keith Robert Head
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of trends in LGBTQ+ youth mental health from 2019 through 2024, drawing on data from The Trevor Project’s annual national surveys. We examine five consistently measured indicators across six years of survey data including: suicidal ideation and attempts, discrimination due to SOGI (sexual orientation and gender identity), physical threats and harm exposure, and conversion therapy exposure and threats. Suicidal thoughts among LGBTQ+ youth rose to a significant peak before easing, while actual attempts showed a steady decline, especially among adolescents, yet younger teens remained disproportionately vulnerable throughout. Over the same period, discrimination remained persistently widespread, while reports of physical violence swung sharply but ended higher than at the outset, and exposure to conversion therapy spiked briefly during the pandemic era before settling back to its earlier yet still troubling level, highlighting the significant risks young LGBTQ+ youth and young adults face. The findings highlight continuing disparities, alongside small improvements in some areas. In conclusion, we summarize key insights and recommend actions to bolster mental health support, reduce stigma and victimization, and expand affirming resources for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles_hidden.title: Start-up certification and prices: Evidence from markups and a statutory expiry in Italy
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Italy grants registered innovative start-ups fee exemptions, investor tax relief and guaranteed credit, and removes that status sixty months after incorporation. This paper asks whether certification changes firms’ markups. Markups are estimated from a translog production function on 76,466 firm-years of certified start-ups, certified innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs over 2015–2024. Certified firms price about 12 per cent below ordinary SMEs, but within firms the gap shrinks to 2 per cent and vanishes once persistence is modelled: registration selects firms rather than changing their pricing. Exploiting the statutory expiry, and a 2020 extension that shifted it by one year for adjacent cohorts, the loss of status leaves markups unchanged on average (2SLS −0.005, first-stage F = 750). An unsupervised partition shows this null combines falls of five to six per cent in capital- and materials-intensive firms with none elsewhere; regression learners and double machine learning confirm the central estimates.

articles_hidden.title: The Human Cost of Port-Centric Development in Dar es Salaam: Displacement, Congestion and Development Without Distribution
articles_hidden.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles_hidden.abstract: Dar es Salaam's transformation into a major regional logistics hub illustrates both the developmental promise and distributive risks of infrastructure-led growth. Modernisation of the port, expansion of inland container depots (ICDs), and investment in rail and road connectivity are essential to Tanzania's trade ambitions. Yet infrastructure expansion can generate a second problem when the costs of urban transformation are concentrated on communities living in strategically valuable locations. This article examines the relationship between port-centric development, displacement, compensation and urban congestion in Dar es Salaam, drawing particularly on the experience of Kurasini, the Chamazi community-led resettlement response, recent concerns surrounding ICD expansion, and evidence from the Msimbazi flood-risk project. The analysis argues that the central problem is not simply displacement without compensation but development without distribution. Compensation systems centred principally on recognised property interests can leave tenants and economically dependent residents without adequate assistance to reconstruct their livelihoods. At the same time, the conversion of residential land into logistics infrastructure can create substantial future economic value from which displaced communities have no continuing claim. The article further argues that the proliferation of ICDs within the metropolitan area risks transferring the congestion problem from the port to surrounding communities unless logistics planning is integrated with land-use and rail infrastructure. The appropriate policy response is therefore not to reject port expansion, but to redesign its distributional architecture so that affected populations participate in compensation, resettlement, employment, value creation and the longer-term development dividend.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Intelligence and Money Anxiety:  “An Empirical Study on Financial Stress Coping Mechanisms Among  Generation Z
articles_hidden.authors: Deepika Rathi; Jainish Bhagat; RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA; Komal Sharma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Generation Z has entered adulthood under a distinctive combination of economic precarity, 
digital financial exposure, and social-media-amplified comparison, making financial stress a 
defining feature of their early financial socialisation. While emotional intelligence (EI) is well 
established in organisational and educational psychology as a predictor of stress regulation, 
its role in shaping how young adults respond to money-related anxiety remains 
underexamined in the financial-behaviour literature. This paper develops and specifies a 
structural model linking Emotional Intelligence, Money (Financial) Anxiety, and Coping 
Mechanisms among Generation Z, incorporating Financial Self-Efficacy as a boundary 
condition and Financial Literacy as a control variable. Drawing on the ability model of 
emotional intelligence (Salovey & Mayer, 1990), the transactional model of stress and coping 
(Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the financial-anxiety literature (Archuleta et al., 2013), 
seven hypotheses are proposed and a measurement model is specified using established, 
validated scales — the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (Schutte et al., 1998), 
the Financial Anxiety Scale (Archuleta et al., 2011), and the Brief COPE (Carver, 1997). A 
Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) approach is proposed as the 
Page 1 of 23 
analytical strategy, given its suitability for exploratory, prediction-oriented models with 
formative and reflective constructs. The paper details the full measurement instrument, 
sampling strategy, and a step-by-step PLS-SEM assessment protocol (measurement model 
validity, structural model evaluation, mediation and moderation testing, and PLS predict) so 
that the study can proceed directly to data collection and empirical estimation. [Once data 
collection is complete, this abstract should be revised to state the actual sample size, key 
path coefficients, and principal findings.]

articles_hidden.title: The effects of childhood family disruption on sexual attitudes, experiences and well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Yucheng He; Yao Ma; zhuofei lu
articles_hidden.abstract: More than 40% of children in the representative UK Millennium Cohort Study experienced a risk of family disruption (i.e., not living with both biological parents by age 14), a circumstance widely recognized as shaping the early developmental environment. Yet the longer-term implications of family disruption for offspring’s sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being remain surprisingly underexamined. Drawing on 10,624 respondents from the most recent wave (2010–2012) of Natsal-3, and combining weighted OLS and logistic regression models, this study yields several novel findings. First, individuals who experienced family disruption by age 14 face elevated risks of non-volitional sex. Family disruption is also associated with more permissive sexual norms and greater involvement in boundary-testing sexual practices. Moreover, it is linked to slightly poorer sexual functioning and more frequent symptoms of low sexual mood. Taken together, these results provide new evidence that childhood family disruption has enduring consequences for sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being, underscoring the need for greater attention to interventions supporting children who experience family disruption.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Developing Indicators of Environmental Sustainability for Kathmandu, Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
articles_hidden.abstract: Sustainability is now considered one of the key objectives in urban planning. However, due to inappropriate planning, weak institutions, limitation of resources, and poor implementation of policies, many big cities in developing countries have become even less environmentally, economically, and socially sustainable than they were in the past. Historically, the Kathmandu Valley enjoyed a unique tradition, rich heritage and a moderate state of sustainability in all areas, particularly in the environmental arena. However, the rapidly expanding and modernizing cities in the valley are facing serious problems of sustainability on all fronts: economic, social, environmental, and ecological. Whereas, environmental and economic sustainability were tacitly embedded in the traditional planning practices in Nepal, the rapid growth and modernization of the major cities in the valley are making them increasingly unsustainable. This paper proposes major indicators of sustainability and discusses an approach to implement sustainable practices in urban planning and development in Kathmandu.

articles_hidden.title: Rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961
articles_hidden.authors: Alfredo Antonio Pérez Sánchez
articles_hidden.abstract:
La presente investigación analiza el rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961. El estudio parte del interés por comprender la relación establecida entre la Iglesia y el Estado, así como la influencia que dicha vinculación ejerció en la legitimación del régimen y en la difusión de valores, prácticas y discursos orientados a fortalecer el poder político durante la Era de Trujillo. La investigación se desarrolló desde un enfoque cualitativo, mediante un estudio histórico-documental sustentado en el análisis crítico de documentos oficiales, legislación, publicaciones periódicas, correspondencia, obras historiográficas y otras fuentes primarias y secundarias relacionadas con el tema. El análisis realizado permitió establecer que la Iglesia católica ocupó un lugar importante dentro de la estructura ideológica del régimen, al ejercer una influencia significativa en los ámbitos educativo, moral y simbólico de la sociedad dominicana. Además, se observó que esta relación no permaneció estática, ya que en los años finales de la dictadura comenzaron a manifestarse diferencias entre la jerarquía eclesiástica y el poder político, motivadas por el incremento de la represión y el deterioro de la situación nacional. En ese sentido, la investigación ofrece una interpretación histórica que amplía la comprensión de las relaciones entre religión, poder e ideología durante el trujillato y aporta una visión integral sobre este proceso de la historia dominicana.

Palabras clave: Iglesia católica; dictadura de Trujillo; aparato ideológico del Estado; legitimación política; ideología.

articles_hidden.title: The Accountability Gap in Sub-Sovereign ESG Finance: A Case Study of Police Administration Oversight in Chiba Prefecture, Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Takashi Miyazawa
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures—specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically documents the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Road Network: A Three-Layer Multimodal Accessibility Framework for Island and Remote Settings
articles_hidden.authors: Weining Kan; Amber DeJohn; Kyusik Kim; David Van Riper
articles_hidden.abstract: The majority of transport accessibility studies rely on road networks to calculate travel costs. This approach penalizes regions like Alaska and Hawaii, where roads are not the only mode used to reach nearby communities. As a result, contexts such as these are typically excluded from accessibility research. To address this gap, we propose a three-layer routing method: layer 1 uses standard road routing; layer 2 adds commercial flights for places roads do not reach; layer 3 connects the remaining communities to the nearest airport by straight-line distance, for cases where there is not a road at all. We tested this method in Alaksa and Hawaii on 13 types of healthcare facilities using census block groups as the unit of analysis. Road-only routing misses a lot: depending on the service type, 10% to 44% of Alaska block groups have no reachable facility within three hours by road. Adding flights and snap-routing resolves most of these gaps, bringing coverage above 96% for most service types in both states. The improvement is largest for services with few facilities, like medical labs and imaging centers, where flight routing alone adds 18% to 32% more block groups. Fewer than 6% of block groups remain unreachable after applying the full method, with these communities constituting the most remote and unreachable. The framework is highly adaptable and only requires three inputs: (1) a remote region where the road network is disconnected, (2) flight or ferry time data, and (3) a road network for the local legs of the trip. This approach is generalizable for other isolated regions both in the United States or globally, and offers an opportunity to expand how traditional accessibility measures capture remote and isolated geographies.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Negotiating mobility: Methodological insights from older adults' activity diaries
articles_hidden.authors: Amber DeJohn; Ainsley Bowie
articles_hidden.abstract: Older adults' mobility is a growing area of research, with multiple methods being employed to understand whether older adults can adequately access key destinations. This has resulted in increased interest in older adults' activity spaces, and a concomitant rise in methods employed to work with these individuals. While GPS-based data collection has advantages, traditional paper surveys remain in use due to their perceived low barriers to entry for participants and researchers. Relatively little is known regarding the appropriateness and validity of paper-based, self-reported activity diary data collection with older adults. Using qualitative feedback on activity diary surveys deployed in rural and urban communities and the activity diaries themselves, we argue that paper, self-reported activity diaries are viable instruments for recording older adults’ geographies. Further, qualitative feedback demonstrates how older adults confront their mobility, memories, and communities. We identify perceived mobility deficits, difficulties remembering, community visibility, and positive affect among our participants. Our findings suggest participating in activity diary surveys is a generally positive experience for older adults, but for some may engender a sense of inadequacy regardless of their activity level. We make recommendations for methodological enhancements specific to working with older adults.

articles_hidden.title: The Illusion of Precision: Interpreting International Rankings Within Their Measurement Limits
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: International rankings publish precise country positions. We ask which comparisons the evidence behind five of them supports, by reproducing published tables, optimising weights, applying multiplicity-adjusted rank inference and two source checks, within a framework separating invalid measurement, insufficient validation, normative trade-offs, underrepresentation of uncertainty and misleading communication. In every programme the adjacent ordering is unsupported, each for a different reason: Report Card 19 trades off dimensions in all 35 adjacent pairs; World Happiness Report countries move a median of 30 places when affect replaces life evaluation; 23 of 38 countries can lead the Better Life Index under unrestricted weights; retrospective rescoring moves Global Health Security Index countries a median of seven places within one year; only 4 of 80 adjacent PISA pairs are distinguishable. Broad contrasts survive throughout. Two unrepresented uncertainties are documented: rotated administration behind Report Card 19's social-skills indicator, and unlinked assessment vintages behind the Human Capital Index.

articles_hidden.title: Are stereotypes of warmth and competence intersectionally complex? Investigating intersections of gender, sexuality, ethnicity, and religion.
articles_hidden.authors: Ely Strömberg; Valentina Di Stasio; Jeremy Michael Jesse Kuhnle; Vasilena Lachkovska; Bram Lancee; Stefanie L. Sprong; Stephanie Steinmetz; Sanne van Oosten; Susanne Veit; Elli Zey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intersectional stereotype research has consistently found that stereotypes vary simultaneously
across categories such as race and gender. Recently, studies have started to investigate the
complex interplay of multiple (more than two) categories, with some finding that stereotypes
are best viewed as based on independent categories. By contrast, other studies find that
stereotypes are intersectionally complex, meaning that they result from unique combinations
of categories. We fielded a harmonized factorial survey experiment across nine European
countries (n = 20,339) in which respondents evaluated perceived warmth and competence of
vignette profiles that varied on gender, sexuality, ethnicity, and religion. We find that while
main effects account for 95% of stereotype variance, compared with 5% of interactions,
single category stereotypes still show effect variation; sometimes to the degree that a negative
stereotype turns positive. Our study shows that stereotypes are primarily explained by
categorical effects, but with small but consistent intersectional effects.

articles_hidden.title: Structured Literature Analysis on Sustainability Report Disclosure in Public Sector Organizations
articles_hidden.authors: Muhammad Arifai; Mariana; Heru Fahlevi; Mirna Indriani; Darwanis Darwanis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: This study examines the adoption of sustainability reporting in Public Sector Organizations (PSOs),
focusing on (1) stakeholder expectations, (2) implementation challenges, and (3) the impact on accountability and
value creation. It also identifies existing gaps in sustainability reporting frameworks and provides strategic
recommendations to enhance transparency and effectiveness in public sector sustainability disclosures.
Methodology: A Structured Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 97 articles from Scopus (1990–2024), selected
using keywords such as "sustainability reporting," "public sector," "GRI framework," and "public sector
organizations." Inclusion criteria ensured relevance to the public sector and methodological diversity. The articles
were categorized by sustainability focus, country, research methods, and theoretical frameworks. This approach
enabled the identification of research trends, key gaps, and best practices to support policy improvements in
sustainability reporting.
Findings: The review reveals that (1) research on sustainability reporting in PSOs is still limited and predominantly
conducted in developed countries, (2) there is an increasing trend in sustainability reporting driven by demands for
greater transparency and accountability, (3) major challenges include inconsistencies in reporting frameworks, varied
stakeholder expectations, and difficulties integrating sustainability metrics, and (4) adoption is influenced by
regulatory environments, political commitment, and resource availability. Although digital reporting tools are
emerging, standardization and performance measurement issues remain unresolved.
Conclusion: Despite progress, sustainability reporting in PSOs suffers from a lack of consistency, comparability, and
stakeholder engagement. To improve credibility and effectiveness, harmonized standards, stronger regulatory
oversight, and capacity-building initiatives are essential. Addressing these gaps will enhance accountability and foster
long-term value creation in the public sector.

articles_hidden.title: The Kia-Hyundai vehicle theft surge: the roles of anti-theft devices and co-occurring offenses
articles_hidden.authors: Graham Farrell; John Roman
articles_hidden.abstract: Between 2020 and 2024, vehicle theft in the United States increased 40 percent. This study addresses this as a natural experiment, using a quasi-experimental design for causal inference to attribute the increase to theft of Kia and Hyundai vehicles manufactured without engine immobilizers. It is conservatively estimated that by the end of 2024 there were over 1.1 million excess vehicle thefts and over three hundred thousand excess co-occurring offenses including homicides, violence and other serious offenses. The evidence indicates that the withdrawal of situational crime prevention measures can increase crime and criminality and that the long-term national crime declines cannot be taken for granted. Additional implications are identified.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Children’s Family Complexity: A Multi-Conceptual Approach with Dynamic Sequence Analysis and Fixed Effects Models
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Rowold; Martin Gädecke; Zachary Van Winkle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The association between a wide range of family complexity indicators and children’s educational outcomes was assessed. 

Background: Previous research documented a negative impact of disadvantageous family transitions and family instability on children’s educational outcomes. However, there is a theoretical and empirical debate surrounding the most appropriate measure of family complexity during childhood.

Method: Numerous theoretically conceptualized sequence-based complexity measures are applied to parents’ life history data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, which were linked to children’s test scores in the National Pupils Dataset. Average within-child change in boys’ and girls’ math and English tests scores following change in mothers’ and fathers’ family complexity were estimated with fixed-effects regressions.  

Results: Family complexity measures were largely found to be negatively associated with children’s academic performance, however with differences across indicators. The number of transitions as well as the uncertainty and sum of disadvantage indicators were most tightly associated with children’s test scores. In addition, results varied by parents’ and children’s gender. For example, family complexity for fathers was often positively associated with children’s educational outcomes and associations were often stronger for boys compared to girls.

Conclusion: Findings highlight the importance of theoretically derived measures of family complexity. In this study, measures associated with family instability and parental absence were shown to be most strongly linked with children’s educational outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS
articles_hidden.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles_hidden.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles_hidden.title: The weaponised Ocean and marine spatial planning
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph Scott Boyle; Diana Volpe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Restrictive asylum and border policies force people into dangerous maritime crossings and lead to record numbers of deaths at sea. Yet marine spatial planning (MSP), despite commitments to social benefit and expanding attention to diverse marine uses and stakeholders, has largely overlooked irregular migration and the governance regimes that shape these routes and their lethality. Applying border geographies literature to European seas, we highlight the Ocean as a weapon used to control migration and allow states to shift responsibility onto migrants.

In this Short Communication, we argue that the weaponisation of the sea through deterrence, pushbacks, neglect, and externalised border control should be recognised as an issue of marine governance. While MSP has limited scope to resolve structural drivers of displacement or border violence, it can no longer remain silent on spatially patterned forms of ‘liquid violence’. Analysing irregular migration through MSP could support more just and humanitarian Ocean governance through improved spatial understanding of migration routes, risks, and sites of death, and by aligning planning more explicitly with the protection of human life at sea. We argue that irregular maritime migration and death at sea should be understood as concerns for marine governance because they are spatially patterned, politically produced, and shaped by the allocation of visibility, safety, and responsibility at sea. As migration drivers continue to increase, acknowledging and addressing these neglected realities is an urgent task for marine policy and planning.

articles_hidden.title: Mezi kontinuitou a změnou: Městské názvosloví a postsocialistická transformace v perspektivě kritické toponymie /  Between Continuity and Change. Urban Toponymy and Post-Socialist Transformation from the Perspective of Critical Toponymy
articles_hidden.authors: Lydie Kárníková
articles_hidden.abstract: The naming of public spaces is a popular tool that ruling regimes have used since the second half of the 19th century to imprint their values on the public sphere and to express symbolic power. However, due to frequent changes in the political and social context, urban naming systems also change frequently. The most recent significant intervention in Central and Eastern Europe was the collapse of the Eastern Bloc in the early 1990s. Among the main features of the wave of post-socialist renaming were a widespread “cleansing of sins”—that is, the restoration of original names to places that had been renamed during the communist dictatorship—as well as numerous disputes and dilemmas regarding which names to remove and what to replace them with. Naming policy stems from a broader political and historical context, but ultimately it is always the result of negotiations within specific local conditions. This paper examines changes in city names—known as urbanonymy—through the lens of critical toponymy, which links cultural and political geography with history, memory studies, or anthropology. It presents the main trends in the transformation of urbanonymy in the period following the collapse of the socialist bloc and, based on selected works, offers insight into specific situations involving the renaming of public spaces, with a particular focus on Czech and Slovak cities. At the same time, it highlights a renewed wave of interest in lingering socialist toponyms and their repoliticization in the context of Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine after 2014.

articles_hidden.title: ‘My spiritual path is Belonging’: Belonging as a valued and sought after affective state for spiritual but not religious individuals.
articles_hidden.authors: Kathryn Diane Ford; Sotirios Kolios; Lora Adair; Matthew Michel Gervais; Aiyana Koka Willard; Michelle Ann Kline
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Objective: Spiritual but not religious (SBNR) beliefs are often characterised as hyper individualistic and lacking community. This study explores concepts of belonging and community among spiritual seekers to assess these claims. 
Methods: This study entailed 30 semi-structured interviews of SBNR individuals combined with long term ethnographic research in Glastonbury UK, a small town with a reputation as a spiritual hub. 
Results: Thematic analysis of participant interviews highlighted the importance of affective belonging to participants. Participants left social contexts where they experienced a lack of affective belonging. Participants invested time and effort into finding sources of affective belonging and in creating sources of affective belonging for others.
Conclusion: Affective belonging is important to SBNR individuals. Prior research suggesting that spiritual but not religious do not value belonging is due primarily to miss-measurement and a lack of conceptual clarity. 
Key words: Spiritual but not Religious, Belonging, Community, Glastonbury, Belief, Qualitative, Interviews

articles_hidden.title: Capacity development approaches and strategies in climate change adaptation projects in Latin America: A typology
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Nye; Paul Cisneros; Sarah-Lan Mathez-Stiefel; Manuel Fischer
articles_hidden.abstract: The success of climate adaptation projects globally is dependent upon a multitude of factors, including the various actions which are designed into a project, as well as more contextual factors affecting the delivery of those actions. Capacity development, sometimes referred to as capacity building, is one type of action which has been identified as having the potential to improve the delivery of a project but perhaps, more importantly, ensure its impact and sustainability beyond the limitations of a project. Using mainland Latin America as a focus region, this paper analyses 60 ‘real world’ climate adaptation project proposals, funded by three different multilateral climate finance mechanisms, in order to highlight the principal characteristics of the capacity development strategies across all projects. Through the manual coding of each proposal, a typology of twelve different ‘types’ of capacity development actions was created, which seeks to outline the specific delivery modality and strategic approach employed by a project, taking into account learning dynamics and possible power relationships. In addition to the typology as an output, findings demonstrate that consideration of capacity development elements remains insufficient across many projects, and that, while there has been movement towards strategies emphasising empowerment, local ownership and long-term change, a significant shift is still required: one which moves away from a reliance upon traditional top-down methods of developing knowledge and coordinating stakeholders, to initiatives which include more participatory, iterative and enabling actions.
